headings: SpatialBrain: Spatial Intelligence Growing from Experience
body_start:
Abstract

Spatial reasoning requires more than access to geometric tools: a reasoner must decide when direct observation is sufficient and when to reconstruct, measure, or change reference frames. We present SpatialBrain, a framework that retains experience about these decisions while keeping its vision-language backbone fixed. The key distinction is between evidence about a scene and experience about how to reason with that evidence. 3DFusionMemory fuses current-scene observations into queryable spatial relations. A Spatial Skill Library provides reusable tool procedures, and Spatial Cognition associates task conditions with experience about when and how to use memory and skills. Completed trajectories are abstracted into process records and consolidated between task blocks, allowing later decisions to draw on earlier execution without transferring scene coordinates or reference answers. Across five spatial-reasoning benchmarks, SpatialBrain improves on direct answers from the same backbone on four and ties on the fifth. Component comparisons, experience-coverage curves, and traced resource decisions characterize how the framework accumulates and uses these resources.

## 1 Introduction

The same visual scene can pose very different reasoning problems. A visible attribute may be read directly, an object-relative direction requires a reference frame, and a distance estimate may require geometric evidence from several views. Route questions additionally require keeping track of successive movements. Spatial benchmarks expose these differences through multi-image reasoning, limited-view scene construction, dynamic spatial aptitude, and degraded observations [28, 24, 12, 19, 33]. A useful reasoner must therefore choose the computation as well as produce the answer. Reconstructing every scene can add unnecessary cost and noisy evidence, while answering directly can overlook information that must be integrated across views.

Spatial representations learned through training [4, 6] and tools for perception, reconstruction, and simulation [17, 5, 7, 35] expand the computations available to a reasoner. Agent methods also retain reflections and reusable workflows from earlier tasks [21, 23, 32, 25]. Access to a resource, however, does not specify when it is useful. A procedure for computing relative directions can be reused across scenes; the coordinates on which it previously operated cannot. The challenge is to retain experience that informs resource use while grounding each answer in the current scene.

SpatialBrain separates scene evidence, reusable computation, and experience
about resource use. It operates as an agent: a vision-language reasoner that
can select and call tools. After completing tasks, it retains abstract
records of the conditions encountered, resources used, and execution
feedback. Later tasks consult these records to choose a reasoning route,
memory-access mode, or skill. We call this cross-task adaptation
self-evolution. The model weights remain fixed; the external
experience available to the controller changes. Unlike correcting an answer
within one task, self-evolution changes the state available to subsequent
tasks.

Figure 1: SpatialBrain: spatial reasoning with experience reuse.
Spatial Cognition chooses how to use direct reasoning, spatial skills, and scene evidence. Completed trajectories update procedures and resource-use experience for later tasks; 3DFusionMemory is rebuilt for each scene. The scene is illustrative.

Our core contributions address three parts of this reasoning process
(Figure 1):

• 

3DFusionMemory grounds reasoning in a shared scene state by
fusing object, pose, camera, and route observations into queryable spatial
evidence with supporting views and uncertainty.

• 

Spatial Skill Library makes recurring spatial computations
reusable through parameterized tool procedures, separating the operation
from the scene-specific inputs on which it acts.

• 

Spatial Cognition accumulates condition-specific experience
about when and how to use memory and skills. Past process feedback and costs
inform resource selection, connecting completed trajectories to later
reasoning decisions.

Tasks within a block share prior experience and maintain separate scene
memories. Updates occur after the block finishes, without reference answers.

Evaluation with GPT-5.6-sol shows improvements over direct answers on four
of five benchmarks and a tie on the fifth. Component comparisons and execution
traces examine resource use and how earlier
experience changes later decisions.

## 2 Related Work

Spatial intelligence.

SpatialVLM and SpatialRGPT develop spatial representations through targeted supervision [4, 6], while Thinking in Space studies cognitive maps for video reasoning [27]. Tool-based approaches expose visual programs, geometric constraints, stateful computation, and simulation to a reasoner [11, 17, 5, 7, 35]. Structured representations include S-Agent’s scene and agent memories and AlloSpatial’s allocentric maps [8, 20]. SpatialCLI provides specialist tools, and SATURN and OmniView-Space emphasize perspective-aware reasoning [34, 13, 16]. SpatialBrain uses execution experience to decide when and how to invoke spatial representations and computations.

Agent skills and memory.

Executable skills and recurring workflows provide reusable computation, as in Voyager and Agent Workflow Memory [23, 25]. Skill-3D distills scene-aware tool workflows and failure lessons from rollouts for skill-guided inference and agentic post-training [14]. SpatialBrain focuses on blockwise, reference-label-free test-time resource adaptation with fixed model weights, separating current-scene geometry from persistent resource-use experience. Episodic reflection and linked memory notes retain broader experience [18, 26], whereas object-centric scene graphs and exploration snapshots retain spatial evidence [9, 29]. In SpatialBrain, the Skill Library stores how to execute a procedure, strategic experience records when and how to use it, and 3DFusionMemory represents what the current scene supports.

Self-evolving agents.

Self-evolving agents differ in what they update. Reflexion retains verbal feedback for subsequent trials [21], while ExpeL distills experience from training tasks for later inference [32]. Agentic Context Engineering consolidates contextual playbooks through generation, reflection, and curation [31]. Automated Design of Agentic Systems searches agent programs using an expanding archive [10], while the Darwin Gödel Machine modifies and tests agent code [30]. SpatialBrain updates external spatial strategies and procedural records from completed test-time trajectories.

## 3 SpatialBrain

## 3.1 Overview

Given images $I_{1:K}$ , a question $q$ , and optional answer choices $O$ ,
SpatialBrain solves a task $x_{i}=(I_{1:K},q,O)$ using a fixed vision-language
backbone and perception and geometry tools. Spatial Cognition selects the
reasoning route and access to memory and skills. Tool observations populate
the scene memory, and skills carry out reusable computations on the current
inputs. An execution trajectory records these decisions, calls, returned
evidence, and process checks. Completed trajectories supply experience for
later tasks without updating model weights, as illustrated in
Figure 2.

Figure 2: Self-evolution from earlier trajectories. (a) Initial reasoning leaves the reference frame unresolved. (b) Completed earlier trajectories are abstracted and consolidated between task blocks. (c) Accumulated experience guides memory access and skill selection for the same target. The trajectories and outcomes are illustrative.

This separation gives two timescales of state: scene evidence changes
within a task, while experience about using evidence changes between
task blocks. Let $i$ index tasks, $t$ a within-task execution step, and $b$ a
block. The state available to the reasoner is

 $\mathcal{S}_{i,t}=(\mathcal{G}_{i,t},\mathcal{H}_{b}),\qquad\mathcal{H}_{b}=(\mathcal{L}_{b},\mathcal{P}_{b}).$ 

(1)

Here $\mathcal{G}_{i,t}$ is the current scene graph, $\mathcal{L}_{b}$ the skill
library, and $\mathcal{P}_{b}$ the strategic experience used by Spatial
Cognition. Observations update $\mathcal{G}_{i,t}$ during
execution; all tasks in a block read the same committed snapshot
 $\mathcal{H}_{b}$ and keep separate scene graphs. A procedure for comparing
object-relative directions can thus persist without carrying its earlier
object coordinates into a new scene.

## 3.2 3DFusionMemory

Different views expose different objects and different sides of the same
object. 3DFusionMemory fuses these observations into a shared scene frame,
where object identities connect evidence across views and spatial relations
connect objects. The memory for the current task is

 $\mathcal{G}_{i,t}=(\mathcal{V}_{i,t},\mathcal{E}_{i,t},\mathcal{C}_{i,t},\mathcal{R}_{i,t}),$ 

(2)

where $\mathcal{V}_{i,t}$ contains object nodes, $\mathcal{E}_{i,t}$ spatial
relations, $\mathcal{C}_{i,t}$ camera states, and $\mathcal{R}_{i,t}$ ordered
route history. Nodes retain detections,
3D centers, available point sets and extents, pose, semantic axes, and
supporting views. Depth and camera poses place observations in the scene
frame; matched observations update an object’s center through
confidence-weighted fusion (Appendix D).
Repeated observations support the same node, while complementary views add
objects that a single view does not cover. Relations are then computed
between these fused object representations (Figure 3).

Figure 3: Multi-view observations become spatial relations.
Three of six input views, a saved fused 3D scene, and view support for five
estimated object nodes. Colors link identities. The RGB surface uses saved
depth and camera poses; edges show unambiguous stored relations. Labels give
stored directions and 3D measurements derived from object centers.
Coordinates use A as origin and reconstruction-world axes; lengths are in
units of $d_{0}=|AB|$ , not meters.

Queries return distances and camera- or object-frame relations together
with confidence, supporting views, and ambiguity. Ordered route state
supports successive translations and rotations. The planner may receive
compact spatial facts, or memory may be reserved for answer checking.
Skills and reasoning steps can therefore refer to the same grounded objects
instead of reconstructing their relations independently.

## 3.3 Spatial Skill Library

Recurring spatial operations can reuse a computation even when the objects
and images change. The library represents each skill as a procedure with an
explicit applicability condition and input–output interface:

 $\ell=(A_{\ell},X_{\ell},P_{\ell},Y_{\ell}),\qquad\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{b}.$ 

(3)

In equation 3, $A_{\ell}$ specifies applicability, $X_{\ell}$ 
typed input requirements, $P_{\ell}$ a parameterized tool procedure, and
 $Y_{\ell}$ its returned evidence. For example, a relative-direction procedure
binds a reference frame before computing a displacement. Its parameters
refer to the current task’s objects, so the same procedure can operate on
different scenes.

Seed skills initialize the library. Completed trajectories add recurring
execution patterns and records of their use. Spatial Cognition can withhold
a skill, expose it as a planning hint, or permit execution. The executable
configuration also compiles compatible primitive calls into parameterized
procedures and tests them under a limited budget; earlier hint-based
configurations retain procedural records without this compilation. A change
in an existing skill’s availability is consequently distinct from the
creation of new skill code.

A skill may build or query the current scene memory, but cannot supply an
earlier answer or bypass a disabled memory interface.

## 3.4 Spatial Cognition

Deciding when and how to use resources.

Spatial Cognition turns execution experience into conditional resource
decisions. Its strategic store associates input-visible task conditions
with past resource choices, process checks, failures, and costs. A task
signature $\sigma_{i}$ describes the reference frame, relation scope, output
form, temporal structure, metric demand, and view count. It uses neither
reference answers nor benchmark category labels. Given this signature and
the available experience, the controller selects

 $g_{i}=\pi(\sigma_{i};\mathcal{P}_{b},\mathcal{L}_{b})=(r_{i},m_{i},\mathcal{K}_{i},\nu_{i}).$ 

(4)

Here $r_{i}$ chooses direct-first or tool-assisted reasoning, $m_{i}$ controls
memory access (off, answer-checking only, or planner-visible),
 $\mathcal{K}_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{L}_{b}$ gives permitted skills, and $\nu_{i}$ 
specifies verification and revision. Equation 4 is resource
selection, not answer prediction. A skill’s how describes a computation;
Cognition’s how describes how to use that computation and its evidence.
The controller combines initial rules with stored experience rather than
training an additional model.

Resource changes require supporting experience. In the executable
configuration, route and memory alternatives must have sufficient historical
support, acceptable process risk, and lower estimated token cost; otherwise
the default remains. At most one learned route or memory factor changes per
request. Skill selection requires compatible inputs and availability, while
verification and resource limits follow fixed rules.
Appendix D specifies these conditions.
Process feedback is not a correctness reward: it describes execution
reliability and cost, not agreement with a reference answer.

The self-evolution loop.

Tasks first execute using the fixed block snapshot. After task $i$ finishes,
its trajectory $\tau_{i}$ is projected to a label-free record
 $d_{i}=\operatorname{Abs}(\tau_{i})$ : task signature, resource decisions, tool
sequence, process checks, failures, and available costs. This abstraction
excludes answers, literal scene coordinates, and raw task content from the
transferable state. For completed block $\mathcal{B}_{b}$ , let
 $\mathcal{D}_{b}=\{d_{i}:i\in\mathcal{B}_{b}\}$ . Only then do the stores update:

 $\mathcal{P}_{b+1}=U_{\mathrm{policy}}(\mathcal{P}_{b},\mathcal{D}_{b}),\qquad\mathcal{L}_{b+1}=U_{\mathrm{skill}}(\mathcal{L}_{b},\mathcal{D}_{b}).$ 

(5)

Here $U_{\mathrm{policy}}$ consolidates condition-specific strategic records
and statistics; $U_{\mathrm{skill}}$ updates procedural records and their
availability. Equation 5 is a state update, not a gradient
step. The next block can retrieve these records and make different resource
choices. No task in $\mathcal{B}_{b}$ reads these updates, future observations,
or reference answers, allowing parallel execution within each block.

## 4 Experiments

## 4.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate MMSI, MindCube, OmniSpatial, SpaceDG, and SAT on 1,000, 1,050,
1,533, 1,000, and 150 items, respectively [28, 24, 12, 33, 19].
We report accuracy, using mean relative accuracy (MRA) for numeric SpaceDG
questions. SpaceDG uses a fixed 1,000-item subset, and SAT uses fixed option
order. The direct-answer baseline and SpatialBrain both use GPT-5.6-sol on
the same items. Predictions are fixed before scoring; experience updates
use neither reference answers nor future tasks.

Table 1 includes foundation VLMs, spatially trained models,
and agentic frameworks. It combines published results with our evaluations,
so backbones and protocols vary across methods. These comparisons position
the framework among available approaches, while the shared-backbone pair
measures its gain over direct answers. Appendix A
gives evaluation settings and comparison details.

## 4.2 Main Results

SpatialBrain improves on direct GPT-5.6-sol answers on four benchmarks and
ties on SAT (Table 1), raising the unweighted mean from 67.5
to 72.6. MindCube accounts for the largest gain, at 20.4 percentage points;
the smaller changes on OmniSpatial and SpaceDG show that the benefit
depends on the task setting.
Category-level changes are mixed, including regressions on OmniSpatial’s
egocentric questions and SpaceDG’s distance and counting questions.

## 4.3 Error Analysis

Figure 4 breaks errors down by benchmark
task type. On MindCube, errors decrease in all three categories, from 344
to 130 overall, a 62.2% reduction. On MMSI, SpatialBrain makes 33 fewer errors
overall, but the
direction of change varies: positional and attribute errors decrease,
with no uniform reduction across all task types. The left panel groups MMSI
into its four official families. The right panel pools the two benchmarks
by input-derived reasoning demand, showing the largest reduction for
motion and rotation. These groups describe what a question requires, not
an inferred cause of failure.

title: LLM-Based Exogenous World Modeling for Dynamic Scheduling
abstract: Dynamic scheduling requires dispatching online arrivals while anticipating future jobs, as poor decisions can compound downstream costs under nonlinear tardiness objectives. We show that a pretrained large language model (LLM) can serve as the exogenous component of a structured world model, forecasting uncertain future job arrivals. Specifically, we exploit an afterstate decomposition, which separates known deterministic shop transitions from uncertain exogenous job arrivals, enabling the LLM to forecast only the latter through a compact belief representation. Building on this, we develop Afterstate World-Model Planning (AWMP), which combines an evolved, belief-conditioned dispatching strategy with short scenario-based rollouts. A surprise-triggered refresh mechanism queries the LLM only when newly observed arrivals deviate sufficiently from previous forecast, and online residual self-calibration further conditions the LLM on its recent forecast errors to handle nonstationary arrivals. Across diverse arrival distributions, AWMP reduces weighted tardiness by 6-21% on dynamic job-shop and 22-46% on flexible job-shop benchmarks, relative to the best of eight classical priority-dispatching rules.

## LLM-Based Exogenous World Modeling for Dynamic Scheduling

Ni Zhang

Haofeng Yuan

Jianan Zhou

Shiji Song

headings: LLM-Based Exogenous World Modeling for Dynamic Scheduling
body_start:
Abstract

Dynamic scheduling requires dispatching online arrivals while anticipating future jobs, as poor decisions can compound downstream costs under nonlinear tardiness objectives. We show that a pretrained large language model (LLM) can serve as the exogenous component of a structured world model, forecasting uncertain future job arrivals. Specifically, we exploit an afterstate decomposition, which separates known deterministic shop transitions from uncertain exogenous job arrivals, enabling the LLM to forecast only the latter through a compact belief representation. Building on this, we develop Afterstate World-Model Planning (AWMP), which combines an evolved, belief-conditioned dispatching strategy with short scenario-based rollouts. A surprise-triggered refresh mechanism queries the LLM only when newly observed arrivals deviate sufficiently from previous forecast, and online residual self-calibration further conditions the LLM on its recent forecast errors to handle nonstationary arrivals. Across diverse arrival distributions, AWMP reduces weighted tardiness by 6-21% on dynamic job-shop and 22-46% on flexible job-shop benchmarks, relative to the best of eight classical priority-dispatching rules.

1Singapore Management University 2Tsinghua University 3Nanyang Technological University

ni.zhang.2025@phdcs.smu.edu.sg, yhf22@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn

jianan004@e.ntu.edu.sg, shijis@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn, zgcao@smu.edu.sg

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: 
Illustration of dynamic scheduling with online job arrivals and dispatching decisions under unknown future arrivals.
At the current time $c_{t}$ , the scheduler observes the released jobs
and current shop state and selects the next operation to dispatch.
Here, $J_{i}$ denotes job $i$ , $J_{i}$ – $O_{j}$ denotes the $j$ -th operation of job $i$ ,
and “due” indicates the corresponding job due date.
Future job arrivals remain unknown.

Scheduling determines how a collection of jobs should be processed on limited machine resources while satisfying operational constraints such as precedence, machine capacity, and delivery commitments (Pinedo and Hadavi 1992; Smit et al. 2025a). Classical scheduling formulations assume that all jobs and their processing requirements are known in advance, allowing optimization over a fixed problem instance.
Real manufacturing systems, however, are inherently dynamic (Vieira et al. 2003; Ouelhadj and Petrovic 2009). New jobs arrive dynamically over time while machines are already processing previously released work, and the scheduler must repeatedly dispatch operations without knowing the future workload.

Under such uncertainty, scheduling performance is typically evaluated by due-date-oriented objectives. A widely adopted objective is total weighted tardiness, which incurs no cost before a job’s due date but imposes a growing penalty once the due date is missed.
This nonlinear objective creates sharp due-date thresholds: a dispatching decision that appears locally beneficial may occupy critical machine capacity, delay a later high-priority job past its due date, and incur a disproportionate downstream penalty.
Consequently, effective dynamic scheduling requires more than reacting to the currently available operations, but also anticipating how future job arrivals will reshape shop congestion and incorporating those expectations into decisions.

Existing approaches address this challenge either by reacting to the current workload or by explicitly modeling the future.
1) Classical priority-dispatching rules (PDRs), such as weighted shortest processing time (WSPT) and apparent tardiness cost (ATC), are fast and training-free (Panwalkar and Iskander 1977; Haupt 1989), but they rank only the currently available operations and carry no explicit representation of future arrivals.
2) Anticipatory optimization methods, including rolling-horizon replanning, sample-average approximation (SAA), and multiple-scenario approaches (MSA), evaluate decisions against future scenarios sampled from a prespecified stochastic model through repeated reoptimization (Powell 2007; Kleywegt et al. 2002; Bent and Van Hentenryck 2004; Li et al. 2025). Their performance relies heavily on the fidelity of the assumed model, and the repeated reoptimization can be extremely expensive.
3) Recent neural methods learn dispatching policies from simulated trajectories with stochastic arrivals (Chang et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2024b; Tang et al. 2026). While capable of capturing complex dynamic patterns, they typically entangle the exogenous arrival process with dispatching decisions and require task- and distribution-specific training, with retraining needed once either changes.
These limitations motivate an anticipatory scheduler that can exploit observed arrival patterns without presupposing a parametric stochastic model, and that adapts without heavy retraining or reoptimization.

In this paper, we leverage a pretrained large language model (LLM) to model the exogenous component of a structured world model by forecasting future job arrivals, while explicitly accounting for known scheduling dynamics. Specifically, we employ an afterstate decomposition to separate the deterministic effects of dispatch actions from the uncertainty associated with future job arrivals.
At each decision step, a dispatch action transforms the current state into an afterstate, representing the resulting shop configuration before subsequent arrivals are incorporated. This afterstate captures endogenous changes, including machine availability, operation progress, and precedence status, governed by known deterministic dynamics, leaving future job arrivals as the sole source of exogenous uncertainty.
Accordingly, the LLM estimates a compact, decision-relevant belief over future arrival pressure, represented by the expected numbers of jobs arriving in the early and late portions of a fixed prediction horizon.
The belief summarizes anticipated arrival intensity without specifying individual job identities, machine requirements, or operation-level dynamics.
This compact interface makes the forecast directly usable by a dispatching planner while avoiding the need to learn a high-dimensional transition model.

Building on this decomposition, we develop AWMP, an Afterstate World-Model Planning framework for dynamic scheduling. At each decision step, AWMP maps every feasible dispatching action to its deterministic afterstate, and scores the action using both its afterstate features and the belief-derived features that capture future arrival pressure.
A scenario generator then converts the early-late belief into concrete arrival scenarios, under which the retained action candidates are evaluated through short rollouts, and the action with the best aggregated evaluation is selected for dispatching.

Moreover, AWMP makes the LLM forecast adaptive and efficient for online planning through three mechanisms.
First, online residual self-calibration feeds recent prediction-outcome pairs and forecast errors into subsequent prompts, enabling the LLM to adapt its arrival forecasts to nonstationary patterns through in-context learning.
Second, belief amortization caches the forecast across all candidate evaluations and rollouts within a decision step, while the cached belief is also reused across decision steps, where the LLM is queried only when realized arrivals deviate sufficiently from the current belief. This surprise-triggered refresh reduces the number of LLM calls from one per rollout to a handful per episode.
Third, meta-evolution searches over compact, human-readable strategy objects, comprising the scoring and value functions, rollout parameters, and forecast-refresh threshold, to automatically discover an effective belief-conditioned planning strategy.

Our main contributions are as follows:

• 

We formalize dynamic scheduling through an afterstate decomposition that separates the uncertain, exogenous job arrivals from known, deterministic scheduling dynamics.

• 

We instantiate the exogenous arrival-belief component of the structured world model with an LLM to forecast a compact arrival belief, and make this forecast adaptive and efficient through online residual self-calibration and belief reuse with surprise-triggered refresh.

• 

We develop AWMP, a belief-conditioned afterstate planner integrating coarse action screening and short-rollout evaluation under fixed scenario generation, with the planning strategy discovered offline via meta-evolution.

• 

Experiments across four arrival distributions show that AWMP discovers strategies that outperform the best of eight classical PDRs, reducing total tardiness by 6-21% on dynamic job-shop instances and 22-46% on dynamic flexible job-shop instances, while running in seconds.

## 2 Related Work

Classical dynamic scheduling methods. Classical methods for dynamic scheduling broadly fall into reactive dispatching and anticipatory optimization. Reactive PDRs, such as WSPT and ATC, re-rank eligible operations whenever the shop state changes (Panwalkar and Iskander 1977; Haupt 1989). They are fast and training-free, but evaluate only the current observable workload with no explicit representation of future arrivals. Anticipatory methods, including rolling-horizon optimization, SAA, and MSA, instead evaluate decisions against expected or sampled future workloads (Powell 2007; Kleywegt et al. 2002; Bent and Van Hentenryck 2004; Li et al. 2025). Their lookahead quality depends on the assumed arrival model, while repeatedly solving the resulting subproblems can be computationally expensive. AWMP occupies a middle ground: it retains low-latency online dispatching but augments it with a compact arrival forecast inferred by an LLM from the observed arrival history, without requiring the arrival pattern to be specified as a parametric stochastic process.

Neural dynamic scheduling methods. Neural combinatorial optimization has introduced graph and attention encoders combined with policy-gradient or value-based reinforcement learning (RL) for routing and scheduling (Kool et al. 2019; Zhang et al. 2020). Recent methods extend learned dispatching policies to dynamic job-shop scheduling problems (JSSPs) and flexible job-shop scheduling problems (FJSPs) with random job arrivals (Luo 2020; Liu et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2023; Smit et al. 2025b; Yu et al. 2026). These methods can capture complex interactions among jobs, operations, and machines, but they generally learn from specific simulated trajectories and may require retraining when the arrival process or optimization objective changes. In contrast, AWMP trains no neural policy, but uses a frozen pretrained LLM to estimate aggregate arrival pressure, and converts it into dispatching decisions through a compact planning strategy that is evolved offline and frozen before evaluation.

Learned world models for planning. Model-based RL learns a transition model of the environment to evaluate and select future actions. Representative approaches include MuZero (Schrittwieser et al. 2020; Antonoglou et al. 2022), Dreamer (Hafner et al. 2021), and TD-MPC (Hansen et al. 2022). These methods are designed for settings in which substantial environment dynamics must be learned from interaction. Dynamic scheduling has a different structure: once an action is specified, the transitions in shop status are deterministic and known. Our afterstate decomposition exploits this structure by retaining exact endogenous dynamics and isolating the future arrival stream as the only exogenous uncertainty. AWMP forms a structured world model from two parts: a low-dimensional predictor of exogenous arrival pressure and the deterministic scheduling simulator.

LLMs for optimization and heuristic discovery. LLMs have recently been used to generate and refine algorithms, heuristics, and environment dynamics simulators (Romera-Paredes et al. 2024; Liu et al. 2024a; Ye et al. 2024). AWMP uses LLMs in two separate roles. During online scheduling, a pretrained LLM instantiates the exogenous component of the structured world model by forecasting aggregate arrival pressure. During offline meta-evolution, a proposer LLM evolves a compact, human-readable planning strategy incorporating the scoring rule, value estimator, and rollout parameters, rather than an independent solver program.

## 3 Methodology

Figure 2: 
Overview of our AWMP framework.
1) The dynamic scheduling environment provides the current shop state and the observed arrival history.
2) The afterstate decomposition separates the known, deterministic shop transition from the exogenous job-arrival process.
3) A pretrained LLM forms the exogenous component of the structured world model and, with online residual self-calibration, forecasts a compact early-late arrival belief.
4) The belief-conditioned planner first scores feasible actions, retains the top- $K$ candidates, and evaluates them through short scenario-based rollouts.
5) Meta-evolution optimizes planning strategies offline.
6) The best strategy is frozen and evaluated on held-out dynamic JSSP and FJSP benchmarks.

Our methodology is organized around three questions: what to forecast, how to forecast, and how to plan with a structured world model, and AWMP addresses them through a modular design, as illustrated in Fig. 2. First, we formalize dynamic scheduling through an afterstate decomposition, which separates the known endogenous shop dynamics from unknown exogenous job arrivals. This decomposition identifies future arrivals, rather than the complete shop transition, as the only object that requires forecasting (Section 3.1). Then, we instantiate the exogenous component with a frozen, pretrained LLM to forecast a low-dimensional belief of early-late future arrival pressure from the observed arrival history, and introduce residual self-calibration to adapt the forecast in an online manner, especially under nonstationary arrivals (Section 3.2). Building on this, we develop AWMP, a belief-conditioned afterstate planner that first identifies promising actions with a compact scoring rule, and then evaluates them through short rollouts under arrival scenarios generated from the forecast belief (Section 3.3). Intra- and inter-step belief caching and surprise-triggered belief refresh amortize LLM calls without repeatedly forecasting at every rollout or decision step.
Finally, meta-evolution discovers a compact, human-readable planning strategy offline, which is then frozen for held-out evaluation (Section 3.4).

## 3.1 Afterstate Decomposition

We consider dynamic JSSPs and FJSPs, where jobs arrive online and dispatching decisions must be made before observing future workload. Let $t$ index decision steps and $c_{t}$ denote the corresponding physical shop time. At decision step $t$ , the scheduler observes the current shop state $s_{t}$ and selects a feasible dispatch action $a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}(s_{t})$ , where $\mathcal{A}(s_{t})$ is the set of all feasible operation-machine assignments. In JSSPs, the machine for each operation is fixed, while in FJSPs, machine selection is part of the action. The state $s_{t}$ contains the current shop configuration, including machine availability, job progress, precedence status, and observed arrival history $h_{t}$ .
The effect of an action can be separated from that of subsequent arrivals. Applying $a_{t}$ first produces an afterstate

The afterstate captures the updated machine availability, operation progress, and, for FJSPs, the selected machine assignment before any new arrivals are incorporated. These changes are endogenous: once $s_{t}$ and $a_{t}$ are specified, they are fully deterministic.

We define the set of future job arrivals as:

 $\mathcal{Z}_{t}=\left\{(\rho_{j},\zeta_{j}):\rho_{j}>c_{t}\right\}\sim P_{\beta}(\cdot\mid h_{t}),$ 

(2)

weight, and $\beta$ controls the arrival pattern such as intensity.
The arrival process is exogenous: dispatching actions do not affect which jobs arrive or their release times.

Nevertheless, an action may change the physical time of the next decision step, and hence which portion of $\mathcal{Z}_{t}$ becomes observable before that decision. The next state is therefore determined by an event-advance function $g$ :

This decomposition provides direct insight into how a world model can be structured for dynamic scheduling. Because the endogenous shop transitions are known exactly, AWMP retains them in the scheduling simulator and models the uncertain exogenous arrival process separately. A pretrained LLM estimates the decision-relevant effect of $\mathcal{Z}_{t}$ as a low-dimensional, compact belief from the observed arrival history $h_{t}$ , while the planner combines this belief with the exact transitions $T$ and $g$ for rollout evaluation. Together, the exogenous predictor and deterministic simulator constitute the structured world model used by AWMP.

As discussed above, reliably predicting the complete arrival stream $\mathcal{Z}_{t}$ , such as the exact release times and job attributes, is difficult and unnecessary. We instead forecast a compact projection, referred to as the belief, of the future

We introduced AWMP, an afterstate world-model planning framework for dynamic scheduling under online arrivals. The afterstate decomposition separates known deterministic shop dynamics from the exogenous uncertain arrival stream, forming a structured world model in which a pretrained LLM models the exogenous component while the scheduling simulator retains the known endogenous transitions exactly. Residual self-calibration adapts the belief forecast online under nonstationary arrivals, while a meta-evolved, belief-conditioned planner converts it into dispatching decisions through candidate screening and short rollouts under a fixed, non-learned scenario generator. Experiments show that combining a low-dimensional LLM-based forecast of exogenous uncertainty with exact scheduling dynamics supports effective anticipatory scheduling without learning the complete shop transition or training a task-specific neural dispatching policy. Future work includes enriching the arrival belief with more job-level information and evaluating AWMP on real-world and more diverse arrival processes. We will also explore more efficient forecasting models to further reduce online inference latency. More broadly, the structured world-model framework may extend to robust optimization and stochastic programming settings.

Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support consequential decisions, yet their reliability under equivalent representations of uncertainty remains unclear. Existing work has documented prompt sensitivity, cognitive biases, and confidence miscalibration, but it is still unknown whether high-stakes advice changes when the same probability is expressed through complementary gain and loss frames. We introduce FrameBench-HPS, a controlled benchmark of 2,880 prompts derived from 240 high-stakes scenarios across healthcare, finance, education/career, and legal/consumer-rights domains. Across seven LLMs, gain-loss framing changes the recommendation category in 32.4% of complete groups, with most changes involving uncertainty rather than direct reversals. Human evaluation confirms corresponding shifts in perceived risk and directiveness. Robustness experiments show that framing effects persist under conversational paraphrases and exceed ordinary repeated-generation variability. Probability canonicalization substantially reduces framing sensitivity, identifying probability representation as a practical target for improving consistency in high-stakes LLM decision support.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable of supporting complex decision-making tasks. Beyond retrieving information, current models can compare alternatives, synthesize evidence, reason over uncertain outcomes, and generate action-oriented recommendations. These capabilities have motivated applications in healthcare, finance, legal reasoning, and other consequential settings, where users may ask whether to pursue a treatment, make an investment, or take a legal action Hu et al. (2026); He et al. (2026). As LLMs become more capable and more frequently used as decision-support assistants, the reliability of their recommendations becomes increasingly important.

However, stronger task performance does not guarantee stable decision behavior. Recent studies show that LLM outputs can change under paraphrases, question-wording variations, and other meaning-preserving prompt reformulations Takayama et al. (2026); Alhetelah and Ahmad (2026). Related work also reports framing and decision biases in applied settings, as well as unreliable abstention and confidence under uncertainty Cocchieri et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026).
These findings raise a practical concern for high-stakes advice: two users may express the same decision-relevant probability differently and receive different recommendations. Gain-loss framing provides a controlled test of this problem. For example, “60% chance of a favorable outcome” and “40% chance of not achieving the favorable outcome” describe the same binary probability structure but foreground different outcomes.
Despite recent efforts to improve prompt robustness Tan et al. (2026), it remains unclear whether probability-equivalent framing systematically alters high-stakes recommendations beyond ordinary generation variability, and whether such sensitivity can be reduced through lightweight inference-time interventions.

Figure 1: 
Overview of FrameBench-HPS and the evaluation framework.

We address these gaps with FrameBench-HPS, a controlled benchmark of 2,880 prompts derived from 240 high-stakes scenarios across healthcare, finance, education/career, and legal/consumer-rights domains. Figure 1 summarizes the benchmark construction and the evaluation components corresponding to the three research questions. We study three questions:

RQ1: What forms of decision-support variation emerge under probability-equivalent gain-loss framing?

RQ2: How robust is framing sensitivity across models, probability levels, surface formulations, and repeated generations?

RQ3: To what extent can probability-representation interventions reduce framing sensitivity?

We evaluate seven LLMs on recommendation decisions and structured response measures, validate observable response properties through a three-annotator study, and conduct a three-model robustness evaluation using conversational paraphrases and repeated generations. We further test probability canonicalization and frame-robust prompting as inference-time interventions. Figure 1 summarizes the evaluation framework. Across the seven-model evaluation, gain-loss framing changes the recommendation category in 32.4% of complete groups, while direct yes-no reversals remain rare. Under conversational prompting, cross-frame disagreement remains substantially higher than same-frame repeated-generation disagreement. Probability canonicalization reduces matched-repeat category changes to 6.7% and nearly removes the mean framing-related risk shift.

Our contributions are:

• 

We introduce FrameBench-HPS, a controlled benchmark for evaluating probability-equivalent framing sensitivity in high-stakes LLM decision support.

• 

We characterize framing sensitivity across seven LLMs and test its robustness using human judgments, conversational paraphrases, and repeated generations.

• 

We show that probability canonicalization substantially reduces framing-induced variation, identifying probability representation as a practical intervention point.

## 2 Related Work

LLMs for high-stakes decision support.
Recent work evaluates LLMs in consequential decision settings, including finance Hu and Zhao (2026), legal judgment Hu et al. (2026), and calibrated decision frameworks He et al. (2026). In healthcare, models may still fail to abstain appropriately under uncertainty Machcha et al. (2026); Cocchieri et al. (2026), while confidence estimates can remain poorly calibrated Lovering et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2026). We study a complementary reliability property, which is whether advice remains stable under equivalent probability representations.

Cognitive biases and framing in LLMs.
Gain-loss framing is a well-established human bias in which equivalent descriptions can produce different judgments Tversky and Kahneman (1981); Levin et al. (1998). LLM studies report related effects across broad bias benchmarks Malberg et al. (2025), negotiation settings Takenami et al. (2025), generated content Alessa et al. (2025), persona-conditioned decisions Yoshikawa et al. (2026), and risky-choice tasks Ge et al. (2026). DeFrame further studies semantically equivalent framing and framing-aware debiasing Lim et al. (2026). Our work focuses on complementary probability framing in high-stakes advice and distinguishes uncertainty-mediated changes from direct recommendation reversals.

Prompt sensitivity, robustness, and consistency.
LLM behavior can vary across meaning-preserving prompt changes, including general reformulations Liu and Chu (2026), wording variations Takayama et al. (2026), paraphrases Alhetelah and Ahmad (2026), and non-adversarial prompt variants Bhat and Varma (2026). Recent work evaluates sensitivity and consistency directly Errica et al. (2025); Nalbandyan et al. (2025), examines evaluation artifacts and human perceptions of consistency Hua et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2025), and improves robustness through consistency training or uncertainty calibration Hejabi et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026). FrameBench-HPS fixes the scenario and underlying probability, compares framing effects with repeated-generation variability, and evaluates inference-time mitigation without retraining.

## 3 FrameBench-HPS Dataset

FrameBench-HPS is designed to isolate changes in model decision support induced by probability-equivalent gain-loss framing.

## 3.1 Scenario Abstraction

We construct high-stakes probabilistic decision scenarios across four domains: healthcare, finance, education/career, and legal/consumer rights. Each scenario describes an actor considering a consequential action under uncertainty, such as adopting a treatment, making an investment, enrolling in a program, accepting a career opportunity, or pursuing a consumer remedy.

Each base scenario is represented using a structured abstraction containing the domain, decision target, potential benefit, potential downside, probability-sensitive outcome, expected decision type, and high-stakes factor. The high-stakes factor records why the decision may have consequential personal outcomes. The abstraction separates scenario semantics from surface realization, allowing all framing variants of a scenario to be generated from the same underlying representation.

The decision target specifies the action under consideration, while the benefit and downside fields encode consequences that remain fixed across framing conditions. The probability-sensitive outcome identifies the event whose likelihood is expressed differently under gain and loss framing. The expected decision type ensures that each scenario poses a concrete decision for which a recommendation can be elicited. All probability and framing variants derived from the same base scenario therefore share the same decision target, contextual facts, and outcome structure, enabling controlled comparisons under
semantics-preserving transformations
Hong et al. (2025).

## 3.2 Probability and Framing Conditions

For each base scenario, we instantiate positive-outcome probabilities of 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%. These levels span a broad range of uncertainty while avoiding near-deterministic endpoints. The benchmark targets framing sensitivity in uncertain decision regions. Gain-loss framing follows the established distinction between equivalent outcome descriptions that foreground favorable versus unfavorable outcomes Tversky and Kahneman (1981); Levin et al. (1998).

Each probability level is paired with neutral, gain, and loss conditions. The neutral condition states the positive-outcome probability without explicit gain-oriented or loss-oriented lexical cues. Because it still refers to the favorable outcome, we treat comparisons involving this condition as secondary. The gain frame states the probability of the favorable outcome. The loss frame states the complementary probability that the favorable outcome will not occur. For example, “80% chance of success” and “20% chance of not succeeding” encode the same binary probability structure and differ in linguistic orientation.

## 3.3 Prompt Generation and Quality Control

We use an LLM-assisted, human-in-the-loop process to construct the benchmark, motivated by recent evidence that LLM-generated evaluation data require explicit validity and quality controls Gill et al. (2025). GPT-5 generates an initial pool of 288 candidate decision scenarios, corresponding to 72 candidates for each of the four domains. We manually screen the candidates for decision clarity, realistic uncertainty, domain relevance, and the presence of a consequential action that can be expressed as a concrete recommendation. We then select and refine 60 base scenarios per domain, yielding 240 scenarios in total.

Fixed generation templates instantiate each retained base scenario at four positive-outcome probabilities (20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%) and under neutral, gain, and loss framing. For benchmark quality control, we first apply automated structural validation to the instantiated prompts. The checks verify required fields and formatting, domain balance, framing-group completeness, and exact probability complements within each gain-loss pair.

All structurally valid scenario groups then undergo human semantic review. Two annotators review all 240 base scenarios and their instantiated gain-loss formulations to verify that each pair refers to the same decision problem, expresses complementary probabilities of the same outcome, preserves the same decision target, contextual facts, and consequences, and introduces no additional asymmetric severity or evaluative cues beyond the intended framing manipulation. Any scenario that fails these criteria is revised, re-instantiated, and reviewed again. Revised instances are also rerun through the automated validation checks before inclusion in the final benchmark.
The resulting benchmark contains 2,880 prompts. Within each probability-equivalent group, the decision target, contextual information, and decision question remain fixed while the probability representation varies according to the framing condition. Representative scenario abstractions and instantiated prompts are provided in Appendix A.

## 4 Experimental Setup

Models. We evaluate seven LLMs spanning multiple providers and model families: GPT-4o-mini OpenAI (2024), GPT-4.1-mini OpenAI (2025a), GPT-5 OpenAI (2025b), Claude Sonnet 4.6 Anthropic (2026), Qwen3-VL-235B Bai et al. (2025), Gemini 3 Flash Google DeepMind (2025b), and Gemini 2.5 Pro Google DeepMind (2025a). Exact model/API identifiers and inference configurations are reported in Appendix G.

Benchmark conditions. We evaluate all 2,880 prompts in FrameBench-HPS. Each query is issued independently and does not expose other framing variants from the same probability-equivalent group. All models receive the same scenario format and structured-output schema. Of 20,160 expected model responses, 20,111 were recorded; the remaining 49 were not obtained after exhausting the predefined API retry procedure. Of the recorded responses, 20,079 contain verifiable final structured answers.

Output schema and inference.
The requested JSON output contains a categorical recommendation (yes, no, or uncertain), a 1-5 model-assigned risk score indicating how risky the proposed action is presented to be, a 1-5 actionability score indicating how strongly the response supports a concrete course of action, a 1-5 self-rated confidence score indicating the model’s stated confidence in its recommendation, and a brief natural-language explanation. Appendix B provides the complete prompt and field definitions. We use temperature 0 for all models. The maximum output length is 1,500 tokens except for Qwen3-VL-235B, for which we use 8,192 tokens to accommodate its longer exposed reasoning trace. These values are truncation ceilings; all framing variants within a model use identical inference settings.

We apply explicit validity checks to all stored responses. Recommendations must belong to the predefined three-category set, scalar fields must contain integer values from 1 to 5, and an explanation must be present. Integral numeric strings are normalized without altering their value. For outputs containing visible reasoning, a structured answer is retained only when a complete JSON object appears after the closing </think> marker.

Metrics.
Following recent work that treats prompt sensitivity and consistency as reliability properties distinct from task accuracy Errica et al. (2025); Nalbandyan et al. (2025), we quantify whether probability-equivalent gain and loss inputs produce different observable outputs. Let $i$ index a scenario-probability-model combination and let $y_{i}^{G}$ and $y_{i}^{L}$ denote recommendations under gain and loss framing. The two inputs encode complementary outcomes of the same binary event:

Positive $\Delta r$ indicates higher model-assigned risk under loss framing, while positive $\Delta a$ indicates higher actionability under gain framing. Because the 1-5 fields are elicited without detailed scale anchors, we treat them as structured model outputs rather than validated psychological measures.

Statistical analysis.
For the seven-model evaluation, we report 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals from 5,000 resamples of the 240 base scenarios. Each resampled scenario carries all associated probability levels and model observations, preserving within-scenario dependence. Scenario-level sign-flip tests provide inference for signed scalar differences, with Holm correction across risk, actionability, and signed self-rated confidence. All hypothesis tests are two-sided with a predefined significance threshold of $\alpha=.01$ .

## 5 Results and Analysis

Overall, we find that (1) gain-loss framing changes recommendation categories in 32.41% of complete groups, with 98.1% of these changes involving uncertain; (2) framing sensitivity persists under conversational reformulations and remains substantially larger than same-frame repeated-generation disagreement; and (3) probability canonicalization reduces matched-repeat category changes from 34.20% to 6.68%. We examine these findings below.

## 5.1 RQ1 Framing Primarily Shifts Recommendations Through Uncertainty

Setups. We use 6,644 complete framing triplets for the primary analysis, where neutral, gain, and loss responses are all valid. To test whether the complete-triplet restriction affects the gain-loss comparison, we additionally analyze all 6,658 valid gain-loss pairs. We further conduct a human evaluation on 140 gain-loss response pairs selected through stratified random sampling, with 35 pairs per domain, 35 pairs per probability level, and 20 pairs per model, and all pairs drawn from distinct base scenarios. Three annotators independently rate both responses on 1-5 scales for risk presentation, directiveness, and expressed certainty. conclusion:
Framing sensitivity and recommendation uncertainty. The central finding is that probability-equivalent gain-loss framing produces substantial recommendation variation without frequently causing direct reversals. Recommendation categories change in 32.41% of complete groups, while direct yes-no reversals occur in only 0.63%. Among the 2,153 observed category changes, 98.1% involve uncertain. Framing therefore primarily changes whether the model commits to a categorical recommendation rather than simply reversing affirmative advice into negative advice. This distinction matters for evaluating decision-support systems. A model may appear directionally stable when evaluation considers only direct reversals, while still changing between recommending an action, withholding a recommendation, and advising against it under probability-equivalent descriptions. Evaluations based only on direct reversals would therefore miss most of the observed sensitivity.

The structured-output and human-evaluation results further suggest that framing affects how the decision is characterized, although the correspondence between model-generated scores and perceived response properties differs across dimensions. Loss framing increases model-assigned risk and is accompanied by higher human ratings of risk presentation and directiveness. The association between perceived risk and the structured risk field is relatively strong ( $\rho=.704$ ), while the association between directiveness and actionability is smaller ( $\rho=.307$ ). Expressed certainty shows no significant directional gain-loss difference despite substantial variation in self-rated confidence, with a moderate association between the two measures ( $\rho=.407$ ). These differences caution against treating structured scalar fields as direct measurements of human-perceived response properties. They are useful indicators of systematic response variation, but their interpretation depends on the construct being measured.

Recommendation-category change is observed across all seven evaluated models, ranging from 21.58% for Qwen3-VL-235B to 63.33% for GPT-4o-mini. Framing-related risk shifts also vary with the underlying probability, decreasing from 0.535 at a 20% positive-outcome probability to 0.109 at 80%. title: ARCANA: A Benchmark for Abstraction and Analogical Reasoning
abstract: Analogical reasoning is widely considered a fundamental component of human intelligence. Few benchmarks are designed to explicitly test far analogical reasoning - reasoning between domains that are superficially dissimilar yet share deep relational or structural similarities. In this work, we introduce an analogical reasoning benchmark called Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus of ANAlogy (ARCANA). The tasks of ARCANA require performing far analogical mappings from real-world objects or physical phenomena to abstract grid-based transformations, different from the well-known ARC-AGI benchmark which primarily emphasized innate human priors. We validate ARCANA through a human study, demonstrating that humans solve these tasks reliably. In contrast, evaluations across a range of large language models show a distinct performance gap compared to humans, revealing systematic failure modes that remain challenging for current models. To address this gap, we propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection. Experiments demonstrate that ConceptSIR enables standard LLMs to solve several challenging ARCANA tasks that were unsolved by direct prompting in our evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that far analogical reasoning remains an open problem for contemporary LLMs. All the materials are available at sites.google.com/view/arcanacogtest. The complete codebase, including benchmark, and ConceptSIR, is publicly available at https://github.com/density-11/arcana-test. All ARCANA data and task instances can be accessed and explored at https://arcanacogtest.org/.

Analogical reasoning is widely considered a fundamental component of human intelligence. Few benchmarks are designed to explicitly test far analogical reasoning—reasoning between domains that are superficially dissimilar yet share deep relational or structural similarities. In this work, we introduce an analogical reasoning benchmark called Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus of ANAlogy (ARCANA). The tasks of ARCANA require performing far analogical mappings from real-world objects or physical phenomena to abstract grid-based transformations, different from the well-known ARC-AGI benchmark which primarily emphasized innate human priors.
We validate ARCANA through a human study, demonstrating that humans solve these tasks reliably. In contrast, evaluations across a range of large language models show a distinct performance gap compared to humans, revealing systematic failure modes that remain challenging for current models. To address this gap, we propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection. Experiments demonstrate that ConceptSIR enables standard LLMs to solve several challenging ARCANA tasks that were unsolved by direct prompting in our evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that far analogical reasoning remains an open problem for contemporary LLMs.
All the materials are available at sites.google.com/view/arcanacogtest. The complete codebase, including benchmark, and ConceptSIR, is publicly available at https://github.com/density-11/arcana-test. All ARCANA data and task instances can be accessed and explored at
https://arcanacogtest.org/.

## 1 Introduction

Analogical reasoning has long been regarded as a central component of human intelligence and a characteristic of general intelligence more broadly [1, 2, 3, 4]. Humans routinely draw analogies between domains that are superficially dissimilar yet share deep relational structure, allowing them to generalize knowledge flexibly from limited experience. This capability for far analogy—mapping abstract relations across distant domains—plays a critical role in human learning, reasoning, and problem solving.

In recent years, substantial progress has been made in evaluating the general reasoning abilities of artificial intelligence systems, such as Humanity’s Last Exam [5] and SWE-Bench Pro [6]. However, these benchmarks are not designed to explicitly probe far analogical reasoning. Among the most challenging existing benchmarks, ARC-AGI-1&2 evaluate abstraction, reasoning, and analogy through grid-based tasks that require inferring latent rules from a small number of examples [7].
In general, ARC-AGI-1&2 primarily focus on testing near analogy based on relative surface-level feature similarity (e.g., color, shape, position, number, center, copy, and count). While instances of far analogy may arise implicitly, explicit far analogical reasoning—particularly that requiring mappings from real-world concepts or physical phenomena to abstract symbolic representations—is rare and limited in scope. This leaves a substantial gap in the systematic evaluation of fluid intelligence and far analogical reasoning.

Inspired by ARC-AGI-2 and to address this gap, we introduce ARCANA (Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus for ANAlogy), a benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate far analogical reasoning.
ARCANA inherits the form of ARC-AGI-1&2, each task of which consists of 3-5 examples and 1-2 tests.
As shown in Figure 1, unlike ARC-AGI-1&2 which largely emphasizes innate human priors (e.g., copying the 3×3 pattern to the purple grid, filling in the grids with different colors using discovered rules), ARCANA focuses on far analogical mappings from real-world objects or physical phenomena to ARC grid transformations (e.g., threading 3D rings onto a column with physical constraints).
The benchmark draws from a broad and diverse set of conceptual sources, including physical principles (e.g., buoyancy, levers, gears, melting, the Doppler effect, Kepler’s second law), natural phenomena (e.g., planets, sunset), and object-level abstractions (e.g., cats, ducks, fireworks, 3D rings, 3D sushi).

To assess the validity and difficulty of ARCANA tasks, we conduct a human study with undergraduate participants. The results show that humans reliably solve ARCANA tasks, indicating that the benchmark captures forms of reasoning that are natural for human cognition. Meanwhile, we evaluate ARCANA across a range of large language models (LLMs), the results of which reveal lower performances, suggesting that far analogical reasoning remains a challenge for current models and exposing systematic failure modes beyond simple pattern matching.

Inspired by the Copycat model of analogical reasoning proposed by [3], we propose ConceptSIR, an analogical reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection. ConceptSIR is designed to approximate key aspects of the human problem-solving process when constructing and solving ARCANA tasks. Empirical results show that ConceptSIR enables large language models to solve several ARCANA tasks that are otherwise unsolved by standard prompting strategies, providing insight into the potential of our ConceptSIR.

In summary, this work makes three contributions:
(1) we introduce ARCANA, a benchmark explicitly targeting far analogical reasoning;
(2) we present a human and model evaluation that reveals a substantial performance gap; and
(3) we propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework that improves model performance while highlighting remaining challenges.
Together, our results suggest that far analogy remains an open problem for contemporary AI systems and that the reasoning pipeline of ConceptSIR offers a promising direction for studying analogical reasoning.

## 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Cognitive Theories of Analogical Reasoning

Although the computational nature of analogy is not yet fully understood, a number of cognitive theories have been proposed to formalize how analogical reasoning operates. Structure-Mapping Theory (SMT) characterizes analogy as a mapping from a source to a target that prioritizes the preservation of relational structure over surface features [1]. SAGE, a later extension of SMT, incorporates frequency information over alignable structures, enabling probabilistic generalization across analogical instances [8]. The Analogical Constraint Mapping Engine (ACME) is a classic computational model that formulates analogical mapping as a process of constraint satisfaction [4].

Among these theories, our ConceptSIR draws particular inspiration from Copycat [3, 2], which involves a Slipnet, a workspace and a population of perceptual agents. Although originally developed for letter-string analogy problems, Copycat has been influential as a general cognitive theory of analogical reasoning. In fact, we believe that ARC-AGI tasks are similar to 2-dim Copycat analogy tasks to some extent: Copycat letter-string analogy tasks primarily focus on letters, numbers and symbols, while ARC-AGI tasks focus on numbers and 2-dim concepts.

Concept Slippage, a core mechanism in Copycat [2, 3], describes how activating one concept can trigger related concepts and higher-level relational structures, thereby expanding the search over possible interpretations.
One task from Copycat theory is shown in Figure 2. Given an example: $a\ b\ c\to a\ b\ d$ , what will $x\ y\ z$ change to? If we assume the alphabet is not cycle, i.e. the next letter of $z$ is not $a$ but nothing, $x\ y\ z$ might change to $x\ y$ , which is obviously not a preferred answer. If we notice that $a\ b\ c$ and $x\ y\ z$ are the beginning and last three letters of the alphabet, the concept “opposite” will be activated in the Slipnet. Therefore, the concept “successor” might slip to the concept “predecessor”, resulting in the answer $w\ y\ z$ . The process of one activated concept causing another related concept is concept slippage.

Figure 2: One task from Copycat theory. In workspace, the task is given as: if $a\ b\ c$ changing to $a\ b\ d$ , then what will $x\ y\ z$ change to? The concept “opposite” activated from $a\ b\ c$ and $x\ y\ z$ in the alphabet will promote the concept “successor” to slip to the concept “predecessor”. This will finally result in the answer $w\ y\ z$ .

## 2.2 Analogical Reasoning Benchmarks and Models

A variety of cognitive tests and benchmarks have been developed to assess analogical reasoning ability, among which Raven’s Progressive Matrices (RPM) are a canonical example and are widely used to measure human fluid intelligence [9, 10]. Other benchmarks, such as the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) [11, 7], place a stronger emphasis on abstraction and analogical reasoning, posing persistent challenges for contemporary artificial intelligence systems. Compared to ARC-AGI-1, ARC-AGI-2 [7] introduces substantially more complex and abstract conceptual compositions, significantly increasing task difficulty. Developed from these two benchmarks, ARC-AGI-3[12] is introduced as an interactive benchmark for studying agentic intelligence from novel environments and in which agents must explore, infer goals, build internal models of environment dynamics, and plan effective action sequences without explicit instructions. Nevertheless, systematic evaluation of far analogical reasoning grounded in real-world concepts remains limited, which motivates us to propose ARCANA.

Among models for analogical reasoning, large language models (LLMs) have emerged as the dominant approach for solving ARC-AGI-1&2, owing to their extensive pretraining and strong general-purpose reasoning capabilities. Beyond LLM-based approaches, alternative methods include train-from-scratch models such as Vision Transformer (ViT)-based picture-to-picture mappings [13], as well as approaches inspired by the Minimal Description Length (MDL) principle [14].
In parallel, several methods have been proposed for analogical reasoning beyond the ARC setting, including vector-based matching approaches that leverage BART embeddings [15], as well as models that integrate encoder–decoder architectures with Structure-Mapping Theory to induce structured correspondences [16].

## 3.1 Dataset Creation

## 3.1.1 Target-concept-target Generation Loop

ARCANA tasks are grounded in diverse real-world objects, concepts, and physical phenomena, which we refer to as targets. Each target can be abstracted into a small set of higher-level concepts that govern the grid transformation. For instance, the “threaded rings" target (shown in Figure 1(c)) can be summarized by three concepts—move, shelter, and 3D—where 3D rings move and partially occlude (“shelter") the column pattern. Once such concepts are extracted from targets, they can be slipped and re-grounded to other targets (e.g., candles burning on a cake, as shown in Figure 8(a)). With this target-concept-target generation loop, we have created several different targets that nevertheless instantiate the similar underlying rules or concepts on ARC grids.

Although some tasks in ARCANA might be mapped from physical phenomena, ARCANA still holds a crucial difference from physical reasoning benchmarks. Many tasks in ARCANA are non-physical, including cat1, shoes1, etc. Even physical inspired tasks are highly abstracted away from real physics: melt1, melt2, melt4 encode conservation of colored cells and a horizontal surface rather than density, or strict fluid dynamics; buoyancy2 concerns grid relations rather than buoyant-force calculation; and even Kepler_second_law_or_area1 can be solved through a grid invariant without knowing Kepler’s law. Therefore, we address that ARCANA evaluates explicit transfer from real-world concepts to abstract grids, and physical phenomena are only one possible source of analogy; the source concept should not be confused with the capability being evaluated.

The target-concept-target generation loop can also be viewed as an explicit process of analogy. We source targets from diverse domains (e.g., water, windmills, flags, and physical laws) and classify tasks into 34 concept categories plus an “other" class. Example concepts include wave propagation, 3D cuboid motion and shadows, fluid flow, state transitions, object-induced rotation, light propagation, and game-rule dynamics. Many tasks are compositional, combining multiple concepts (e.g., motion with rotation).

## 3.1.2 Grounding Targets into Grids

Concept attention.

Bridging targets and discrete ARC grids requires concept attention: emphasizing task-relevant concepts of a target while suppressing concepts that are secondary or irrelevant to the core rule. For example, in the melt target (shown in Figure 3(b)), ice melts only upon contact with hot water (red cells); after melting, both the ice and the hot-water become cold water (blue cells). The final cold-water volume (the number of grid cells) equals the sum of the initial ice volume and hot-water volume. We therefore focus on the melting condition and this discrete conservation rule, while ignoring physical nuances such as density differences across phases and temperatures.

Concept expansion.

Beyond concept attention, we sometimes augment a target with additional concepts (e.g., time) to fully specify its dynamics and complicate the tasks. We refer to this as concept expansion. For instance, in the charge target (shown in Figure 3(c)), green cells (analogous to charge or data) propagate along directed “wires” from a source container at the red terminal to a sink container at the green terminal. At each time step, each wire transfers one cell if the sink container has remaining capacity. Introducing an explicit temporal process (and treating it as effectively continuous) is necessary to correctly solve the test. Overall, concept expansion substantially increases the difficulty and diversity of ARCANA tasks.

Figure 4: Visualization of cat1 task in animal category. The task requires recognizing topology of the true cat, and changing the color of eyes, ears and tail into red.

Generation principles

We construct the benchmark according to four principles that are intentionally simple and human-grounded:
(1) Human-familiar targets. The targets are common and recognizable to humans; given the target, most people who are familiar with it can solve the task accurately with little effort.
(2) Concept-faithful grounding. The ARC grids inherit the target’s core concepts, and the grid-target analogy is intended to be explicit.
(3) Multiple targets, one rule. A task may admit multiple plausible analogical targets, but they must agree on the same underlying transformation rule, such as claw and chopsticks.
(4) Human-aligned correctness. When multiple rules are consistent with the examples, we choose the one most natural to humans, best aligned with everyday concepts, and lowest in cognitive burden.

## 3.2 Discussion on ARCANA Tasks

ARCANA comprises 200 tasks spanning 35 distinct concepts, with each task targeting a unique analogical mapping. We have provided the categorization of ARCANA tasks in Appendix F.

All tasks are named by the abbreviated target from the designer’s perspective followed by a numeric suffix, while different tasks are guaranteed to correspond to different rules. For example, in water_transform category, melt1, melt2 and melt4 tasks correspond to the following rules respectively: (i) ice melts if it touches hot water (as shown in Fig. 8), (ii) ice melts only if sunlight shines on it, and (iii) ice melts only if there is no light-blocking glass above it. limitations:
ARCANA is currently limited in scale and representation. When we constructed ARCANA, we have tried our best to distinguish each task from each other, i.e., similar tasks could be generated from existing tasks to expand the benchmark. We mainly focus on the diversity but not the quantity of ARCANA, while leaving scaling up an unsettled problem for the community. Moreover, although ARCANA covers diverse targets, the space of real-world concepts and analogical sources is effectively unbounded, making larger benchmarks difficult without community effort. We view ARCANA as a starting point for such expansion. Furthermore, ARC-style grid abstraction provides conciseness, precision, and cognitive challenge, but limits expressivity for structures such as oblique lines, circles, and ellipses (e.g., the ellipses of Kepler_second_law_or_area1 task shown in Figure 5 are not strictly faithful expressions), motivating richer representations for future far-analogy benchmarks.

We also note several limitations of ConceptSIR. Future work should evaluate it on a larger set of ARCANA tasks beyond the current challenging subset. Although code execution offers a faithful and reproducible way to apply hypothesized rules, it is not fully expressive for all ARCANA targets, especially topology-heavy ones (e.g., animal category); extending the executor to atomic grid operations with explicit where-to-apply instructions, or expanding the framework to a true agent which could judge output the answer as code or direct matrix may improve generality. Moreover, our code-mutation procedure selects the “best” candidate solely by prediction error, which is a rigid proxy for solution quality. Additional modules, such as explicit memory or human feedback, may further improve robustness and generalization. More limitations are also mentioned in Section 7.

title: CrashGym: Measuring the Decision Value of Experimentation for LLM Agents in Counterfactual Market Crashes
abstract: Language-model agents are increasingly asked to run experiments, yet benchmarks rarely measure whether those experiments improve the decisions they are meant to inform. We introduce CrashGym, a deterministic, replayable limit-order-book simulator in which an agent must choose between a deleveraging intervention and a liquidity backstop for a market about to suffer a shock-triggered crash. Before committing, the agent may query intervention experiments in a laboratory realization of the market. Its choice is then scored on an independently seeded target realization in which the simulator executes every feasible intervention, so regret relative to the best intervention is computed by directly simulating every alternative on the same target repeats, with no human or model-based judging. The simulator implements each amplification channel---persistent price impact, liquidity withdrawal, margin-driven liquidation, and an evolving strategy mix---as an explicit mechanism that can be switched on in stages. In a prospectively specified study on 24 newly sampled worlds, laboratory access reduces the mean regret of the one deployment with a complete record (Luna) from 8.878 to 3.785, a paired reduction of 5.092 utility units (nominal 95% world-bootstrap interval: 1.028--9.507), or 57.4% of the OBSERVE-ONLY mean. Prospective comparisons for two further deployments are incomplete; in a separate exploratory study, mean regret is lower with laboratory access for all four deployments evaluated. A laboratory whose strategy mix evolves endogenously yields no established advantage over one with a fixed mix. CrashGym thus measures the value of experimentation as avoided decision loss and lets simulator detail be judged by the decisions it supports.
