Abstract

Language-model agents are increasingly asked to run experiments, yet benchmarks rarely measure whether those experiments improve the decisions they are meant to inform. We introduce CrashGym, a deterministic, replayable limit-order-book simulator in which an agent must choose between a deleveraging intervention and a liquidity backstop for a market about to suffer a shock-triggered crash. Before committing, the agent may query intervention experiments in a laboratory realization of the market. Its choice is then scored on an independently seeded target realization in which the simulator executes every feasible intervention, so regret relative to the best intervention is computed by directly simulating every alternative on the same target repeats, with no human or model-based judging. The simulator implements each amplification channel—persistent price impact, liquidity withdrawal, margin-driven liquidation, and an evolving strategy mix—as an explicit mechanism that can be switched on in stages. In a prospectively specified study on 24 newly sampled worlds, laboratory access reduces the mean regret of the one deployment with a complete record (Luna) from 8.878 to 3.785, a paired reduction of 5.092 utility units (nominal 95% world-bootstrap interval: 1.028–9.507), or 57.4% of the Observe-only mean. Prospective comparisons for two further deployments are incomplete; in a separate exploratory study, mean regret is lower with laboratory access for all four deployments evaluated. A laboratory whose strategy mix evolves endogenously yields no established advantage over one with a fixed mix. CrashGym thus measures the value of experimentation as avoided decision loss and lets simulator detail be judged by the decisions it supports.

## 1 Introduction

A market is about to fall sharply. A policy agent must recommend one of two interventions: force leveraged holders to cut their positions, or post a standing bid that supplies liquidity. Both are defensible a priori. Deleveraging can pre-empt the cycle of margin calls and forced selling, whereas a liquidity backstop can absorb that selling before it moves prices [1, 11, 25]. Which intervention is better depends on which amplification channel dominates in the market at hand. We ask whether an agent that can first experiment on a laboratory copy of the market chooses better, and by how much.

Language-model agents are increasingly evaluated as experimenters: they design studies, run code, and report findings [22, 15, 16]. Most evaluations, however, score the research process or its products—task completion, explanation quality, or recovery of a latent structure. Completing an experiment and benefiting from it are different outcomes. Measuring the benefit requires two ingredients that are rarely available together: the same decision-maker observed with and without experimental access, and the counterfactual outcome of every action it could have taken. The second ingredient is unobservable in historical data.

Approach. CrashGym supplies both ingredients inside a deterministic agent-based market (Figure 1). An agent receives a public observation, may query intervention experiments in a laboratory realization, and then commits to one intervention. The simulator executes every feasible intervention on an independent target realization that the agent never observes. Regret—the utility gap between the best intervention and the chosen one—is therefore exact for the realized target repeats. Comparing regret across information conditions yields the gross decision value of experimentation, a realized counterpart of the classical value of sample information [21, 14, 23]. Because the simulator’s amplification channels are explicit mechanisms that can be enabled in stages, the same outcome also tests whether added simulator detail improves the decision it is meant to support.

Contributions.

• 

A counterfactual market laboratory. We describe an exchange core with exact integer accounting, event-sourced replay, and counter-based randomness, together with a crash construction whose amplification channels can be enabled in cumulative stages (Section 3).

• 

A decision-grounded evaluation task. A laboratory in which the agent acquires interventional evidence is separated from an independently seeded target on which every feasible intervention is executed and scored. This yields exact counterfactual regret for every decision (Section 4).

• 

Controlled evidence. With identical targets, we compare no access, two laboratory designs, and a tool placebo, sampling new worlds prospectively and using a stratified whole-world bootstrap (Section 5). Laboratory access lowers Luna’s mean regret by 5.092 units on 24 newly sampled worlds, meeting the prespecified criterion. An evolving strategy mix in the laboratory yields no established additional benefit (Section 6).

The measured value is avoided loss in simulator utility units. Net value would additionally require the costs of experimentation and inference, which we do not measure.

## 2 Related work

LLM agents as experimenters. Tool-using language models interleave reasoning with external actions [33, 24], and a growing set of environments evaluates them as scientists. ScienceWorld and DiscoveryWorld assess task completion and discovery in simulated worlds [29, 16]; MLAgentBench evaluates machine-learning experimentation [15]; and end-to-end systems generate complete research papers [22]. CausaLab distinguishes predictive success from recovery of causal structure, and CausalGame evaluates causal reasoning and experimental protocols in games [32, 5]; see also Kıcıman et al. [17]. We measure a different quantity: how much an agent’s experiments improve a subsequent, independently scored decision. An agent may use informative intervention results well without reconstructing the latent mechanism.

LLM agents in finance. Domain-adapted models and agents have been applied to financial analysis and trading [30, 34, 31], and InvestorBench evaluates financial decision-making across tasks [20]. These evaluations typically rely on historical data, in which the outcomes of untaken actions are unavailable. Our simulator supplies those counterfactuals for a policy intervention, at the cost of using synthetic rather than historical markets.

Market simulation. Agent-based models have long been used to study market dynamics [12, 19, 9]. ABIDES supports high-fidelity, message-level market research [2]; JAX-LOB targets accelerated, parallel limit-order-book simulation [10]; and realism metrics assess how closely simulated order books reproduce stylized facts [28]. Our crash construction draws on the leverage-cycle and fire-sale literature, in which margin constraints, forced selling, and liquidity withdrawal reinforce one another [1, 11, 26, 25]. Rather than maximizing realism, we use the simulator as an instrument that supplies exact counterfactual intervention outcomes and lets each amplification channel be switched on or off.

Value of information and decision-aware model evaluation. Statistical decision theory values an experiment by the improvement in the expected utility of the decision it informs [21, 14, 23, 4]. Our gross value $V_{b}$ (Section 7) is a realized, empirical counterpart for an LLM agent. A related literature argues that models should be judged by the decisions they induce rather than by predictive accuracy alone [6, 8, 18], and the value-equivalence principle motivates retaining only those model distinctions that matter for planning [13]. Our comparison of laboratory designs examines this motivation empirically; it does not test Bellman-operator equivalence. The setting also relates to sim-to-real transfer, in which the deployment environment differs from the training simulator [27].

## 3 The CrashGym simulator

The simulator is a discrete-time, single-asset market with a central limit-order book. We describe its components in turn: the exchange core, the participants, the episode schedule, the amplification mechanisms, the evolving strategy mix, the mechanism stages, and the determinism and replay layer. Parameter values refer to the crash construction used in all experiments; Appendix A lists them in full.

## 3.1 Exchange core

Order book and matching. Prices are integers in ticks. Each side of the book maps a price level to a first-in-first-out queue, giving strict price–time priority. The only order primitive is a limit order, together with cancellation by the owning account. A marketable order is emulated as a limit order priced 100 ticks through the best opposite quote; any unfilled remainder is cancelled immediately, so it behaves as an immediate-or-cancel order with a price band. Incoming orders walk the opposite side best-first, and each fill executes at the resting order’s price for the smaller of the two quantities; a partially filled resting order keeps its queue position. The reference price $m_{t}$ is the sum of best bid and best ask, i.e. the midpoint in half-tick units, so it remains an exact integer. If one side of the book is empty, the reference falls back to the last two-sided quote, and aggressive orders are priced from the last published bid or ask. Book invariants—no empty levels, no zero quantities, strictly increasing priorities, and no crossed book—are checked after every mutation.

Accounts, risk admission, and fees. Each participant owns an account with integer cash and inventory, with positions tracked as first-in-first-out lots. Before an order is accepted, the exchange checks a position limit ( $10^{6}$ lots) and a leverage limit: the worst-case position notional along the order’s potential fill path may not exceed $20\times$ the account’s initial cash. Rejected orders are logged and have no effect. A fee of one cash unit per lot is charged to both counterparties of every fill; resting orders that never fill pay nothing. Every fill must conserve total inventory and total cash plus fees, global invariants are re-checked after each operation, and a full canonical audit closes every run.

## 3.2 Participants

Table 1 summarizes the six participant classes and the two exogenous accounts. Each step, a market maker posts a 40-level ladder on each side, at offsets of $2+k$ ticks ( $k=0,\dots,39$ ) around a center that tracks the previous reference price. Its depth per level is a world-specific $\bar{Q}\in\{24,\dots,56\}$ lots in the initial ladder (step 0), 400 lots during steps 1–7, and $\bar{Q}$ again from the shock onward. Every world therefore experiences a scheduled liquidity cliff at the shock, in addition to the stress-driven withdrawal described below. Ladders are reconciled rather than rebuilt: unchanged levels keep their queue priority, and superseded orders are cancelled. Noise traders submit eight marketable orders of four lots per step, each a buy or sell with probability $1/2$ . A fundamental trader trades four lots per tick of deviation between the fundamental value $v$ and the midpoint. A trend follower trades $4e_{t}$ lots, where $e_{t}=\operatorname{trunc}\bigl((3e_{t-1}+r_{t-1})/4\bigr)$ is a moving average of past returns $r_{t}=m_{t}-m_{t-1}$ (half-ticks) and $\operatorname{trunc}$ rounds toward zero. The fundamental value is held constant at $v=10{,}000$ ticks: no news arrives, so post-shock dynamics are responses to the shock, the scheduled post-shock depth, and the intervention. The leveraged trader builds a long position at step 1 and afterwards trades only through forced liquidation or the deleveraging intervention. The adaptive participant chooses each step between two candidate strategies (Section 3.5).

## 3.4 Amplification mechanisms

The shock is a burst of order flow, not a change in fundamentals. Three mechanisms convert it into a crash whose depth and duration depend on the world (Figure 3b).

Persistent impact. The maker’s quote center shifts by $40\,x/D_{0}$ ticks, where $x$ is the executed shock volume and $D_{0}=10\bar{Q}$ is the depth of the ten best bids in the initial (step-0) ladder; integer remainders are carried forward. The shock therefore moves the price permanently rather than only transiently.

Liquidity withdrawal. After the shock, the maker measures stress $\sigma_{t}=\max\{0,\,m_{t_{0}-1}-m_{t-1}\}+|r_{t-1}|$ in half-ticks and thins its ladder to

 $Q_{t}=\bar{Q}\cdot\max\bigl\{0.25,\;1-\beta\,\sigma_{t}/\kappa\bigr\},$ 

(1)

where $\beta\in[0,1]$ is the world’s withdrawal strength and $\kappa\in\{24,\dots,56\}$ its stress scale. Withdrawal reduces depth but never widens the spread or empties the book.

Margin-driven liquidation. At the start of step $t$ , the leveraged trader’s equity is $E_{t}=c_{t}+q_{t}p_{t}$ , where $c_{t}$ and $q_{t}$ are its cash and inventory at the close of step $t-1$ and $p_{t}=m_{t-1}/2$ is the previous closing midpoint in ticks; its maintenance requirement is $M_{t}=\mu\,|q_{t}|\,p_{t}$ with $\mu\in[3\%,7\%]$ . From step $t_{0}+1$ onward, whenever $E_{t}<M_{t}$ it must sell

 $\ell_{t}=\bigl\lceil\alpha\,|q_{t}|\bigr\rceil$ 

(2)

lots at market, where $\alpha\in[0,1]$ is the world’s liquidation strength. Because forced sales lower the price and therefore equity, the rule can repeat over consecutive steps and form a liquidation spiral.

The strengths $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are both held at zero until the shock order has filled, and they define the four world strata used in sampling: neither mechanism, liquidation only, withdrawal only, or both (Section 4.1).

## 3.5 Reflexive strategy ecology

The adaptive participant holds shares $(s_{\mathrm{F}},s_{\mathrm{Tr}})$ over two candidate strategies, initialized at $(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2})$ . Both candidates are inactive until the
conclusion:
The value of an experiment is the decision it changes. The task links an agent’s research process to a consequence: avoided intervention loss. Writing $\bar{R}_{b}$ for mean regret under an experimental budget of $b$ calls, the gross value of experimentation is

 $V_{b}=\bar{R}_{0}-\bar{R}_{b},$ 

(6)

the loss avoided relative to observation alone. For Luna on new worlds, $V_{8}=5.092$ with the adaptive laboratory. This quantity makes experimental usefulness comparable across agents, budgets, and laboratories on a common scale, and a resource-efficiency analysis could weigh it against measured acquisition and inference costs.

Which simulator details matter? For an agent, the relevant question is whether an evolving strategy mix improves the final choice between deleveraging and a liquidity backstop. In our data it does not demonstrably do so: the prospective Adapt $-$ Fixed interval admits either sign, and complete-utility selectors from both laboratories recover nearly all target-optimal actions. This suggests a concrete evaluation practice: before treating added dynamics as necessary for a task, test whether they change the intervention ranking or reduce target regret [13, 18]. Because the simulator’s mechanisms are switchable by stage, the same test can be applied to each stage. Runtime savings and transfer to real markets remain separate empirical questions.

Limitations. The evidence covers one synthetic crash construction and two interventions, each with a single fixed implementation (one deleveraging sale; one backstop size). The fundamental value is constant, maker depth falls on a fixed schedule at the shock, the evolving strategy mix has two candidates (one of them signal-independent), and the shadow-trade horizon is one step. New constructors and independent target seeds support transfer within this construction, not to other constructions or to historical markets. With 24 worlds, the primary effect is clear in direction but modest in two-sided strength (exact sign-flip $p=0.075$ ). Incomplete Sol and Terra records limit prospective cross-deployment conclusions, and the placebo comparison leaves the contribution of world-specific evidence relative to tool interaction and generic crash information uncertain. The positive primary result therefore concerns the full laboratory-access condition for Luna within this construction. Finally, regret is measured in simulator utility units and is not calibrated to monetary outcomes.

title: From Scores to Safe Sets: Exact Safety--Constrained Decoding for Medication Recommendation
abstract: Recent generative medication recommendation systems ultimately produce sets of drugs, but drug--drug interaction (DDI) constraints depend on the set as a whole. A natural post-hoc approach is to first predict medications and then locally repair interacting pairs by removing one drug at a time. We ask whether this local repair step itself introduces avoidable error. Using fixed medication scores from FLAME's frozen classifier on MIMIC-III, we compare increasingly strong local repair strategies with an exact global decoder while holding the scores, output size, and DDI constraint fixed. The global decoder jointly selects the highest-scoring feasible medication set using mixed-integer linear programming. Across validation and test splits, global decoding consistently achieves higher Jaccard similarity than greedy repair, degree-aware repair, and degree-aware repair strengthened with exhaustive 1-swap local search. Its advantage is small under loose DDI constraints and becomes larger as the constraint tightens; on the test split it reaches +0.0064 Jaccard over the strongest local baseline at the strict DDI operating point. The finding also holds across a fine accuracy--DDI sweep at matched realized DDI exposure and under three score representations. At the strict setting, global decoding retains more true-positive medications while removing more false positives. These results show that medication recommendation is not only a representation-learning problem: even with a frozen clinical model, how its scores are converted into a constrained medication set can materially affect the final prediction.

body_start:
Abstract

Recent generative medication recommendation systems ultimately produce sets of drugs, but drug–drug interaction (DDI) constraints depend on the set as a whole. A natural post-hoc approach is to first predict medications and then locally repair interacting pairs by removing one drug at a time. We ask whether this local repair step itself introduces avoidable error. Using fixed medication scores from FLAME’s frozen classifier on MIMIC-III, we compare increasingly strong local repair strategies with an exact global decoder while holding the scores, output size, and DDI constraint fixed. The global decoder jointly selects the highest-scoring feasible medication set using mixed-integer linear programming. Across validation and test splits, global decoding consistently achieves higher Jaccard similarity than greedy repair, degree-aware repair, and degree-aware repair strengthened with exhaustive 1-swap local search. Its advantage is small under loose DDI constraints and becomes larger as the constraint tightens; on the test split it reaches +0.0064 Jaccard over the strongest local baseline at the strict DDI operating point. The finding also holds across a fine accuracy–DDI sweep at matched realized DDI exposure and under three score representations. At the strict setting, global decoding retains more true-positive medications while removing more false positives. These results show that medication recommendation is not only a representation-learning problem: even with a frozen clinical model, how its scores are converted into a constrained medication set can materially affect the final prediction.

## 1 Introduction

Medication recommendation from electronic health records (EHRs) is a canonical set-valued prediction problem. Given diagnoses, procedures, and longitudinal context, a model must recommend a combination of medications rather than a single label. This distinction matters because interactions are relational, duplicate or incompatible therapies arise at the set level, and the predicted medication set may need to satisfy multiple constraints simultaneously. A large literature has therefore developed increasingly structured medication recommenders, including sequence models, memory networks, graph-augmented models, molecular encoders, set-to-set predictors, causal representations, multimodal models, and more recently large-language-model (LLM) systems (Zhang et al., 2017; Le et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2019b; Shang et al., 2019a; Yang et al., 2021a; Yang et al., 2021b; Wu et al., 2022; Tan et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025; Lv et al., 2026; Huh et al., 2026). A recurring objective across this literature is to preserve recommendation accuracy while reducing harmful drug–drug interactions (DDIs) (Shang et al., 2019b; Yang et al., 2021b; Tan et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023).

Throughout this paper, references to “safety” refer only to the benchmark DDI constraint used in the evaluation. They should not be interpreted as establishing comprehensive clinical safety, clinical utility, or a prescribing recommendation for the resulting medication sets.

Most prior work attacks this tradeoff primarily through learning: DDI graphs are incorporated into representation learning, molecular structure is encoded to improve drug representations, DDI penalties are added to the training objective, or list-wise objectives are used to align recommendation behavior (Shang et al., 2019b; Yang et al., 2021b; Yang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Fan et al., 2025). A systematic survey of medication recommendation also highlights a basic difficulty with DDI-based post-processing: removing one interacting drug can discard treatment value elsewhere in the regimen (Ali et al., 2023). Prior work therefore mainly asks how to learn better scores or safer representations. We ask a complementary question: once a patient-specific scorer already exists, does error arise when those scores are converted into a DDI-constrained medication set? Our central finding is that it does: even strong local repair leaves measurable accuracy on the table relative to global constrained decoding. For modern generative medication recommenders, this final decoding step is the point where model-derived scores are converted into a coupled medication set.

A natural local strategy is to repair conflicts after prediction. Start from the model’s preferred set, identify a DDI conflict, remove one of the two drugs, and repeat until a target DDI level is reached. A stronger heuristic considers each drug’s conflict degree and removes high-degree nodes first, and stronger still, a local-search procedure repairs bad greedy commitments after the fact by searching every feasible swap. All three remain local: a removal is committed before the algorithm knows how that choice will constrain later removals and replacements.

The problem becomes combinatorial when conflicts are dense. In our evaluation regime, output sets contain approximately 27 medications on average, and a typical predicted set contains dozens of simultaneously active DDI edges. Removing one drug may resolve many edges at once but may also force the loss of a highly supported medication; retaining a high-scoring “hub” drug can make several other high-scoring medications mutually infeasible. The quality of a local decision therefore depends on the entire conflict graph, which motivates a global formulation that selects the full set jointly.

We formulate DDI-constrained decoding as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP). For each patient visit $q$ , a frozen scorer provides one score $s_{i}(q)$ per medication. We select exactly $K_{q}$ medications to maximize the total score, subject to an explicit budget $B_{q}$ on selected DDI edges. Every decoder returns the same number of medications and the same DDI budget, so the comparison isolates one factor: local versus global selection. Figure 1 summarizes this shared setup.

We instantiate the scorer with FLAME’s released drug-level classifier, $\pi_{\mathrm{cls}}$ (Fan et al., 2025), on MIMIC-III (Johnson et al., 2016), using the TWOSIDES-derived DDI graph released with FLAME’s preprocessing (Fan et al., 2025; Tatonetti et al., 2012). All methodological choices are made on a training split; a disjoint validation split confirms the phenomenon before a held-out test split is scored once. The three splits follow a 4:1:1 train/validation/test ratio over approximately 14,000 total visits. We compare exact global decoding with (i) greedy repair, (ii) degree-aware repair, and (iii) degree-aware repair strengthened with exhaustive 1-swap local search. Across loose, moderate, and strict DDI budgets, the ordering $J_{\mathrm{global}}>J_{\mathrm{1\text{-}swap}}>J_{\mathrm{degree}}>J_{\mathrm{greedy}}$ holds on both validation and test. The advantage grows as the DDI constraint tightens, holds when methods are compared at matched realized (not merely target) DDI exposure across a fine budget sweep, and holds under three different score representations.

Our contributions are:

1. 

A decoding-level view of DDI-constrained recommendation. We hold the patient–drug scorer, output cardinality, and DDI budget fixed and isolate the final set-selection problem.

2. 

A controlled comparison of local and global decoding. We compare exact MILP decoding with greedy repair, degree-aware repair, and degree-aware repair strengthened by exhaustive 1-swap local search.

3. 

Consistent and distinguishable evidence across splits and operating points. The advantage reproduces on validation and test, persists at matched realized DDI exposure over a fine DDI sweep, and holds under three score parameterizations.

4. 

A mechanistic account. Under strict DDI-constraint pressure, global decoding retains more true positives while removing more false positives, consistent with the cost of locally committing to coupled medication choices.

Figure 1: 
Controlled comparison of local repair and global DDI-constrained decoding.
A frozen FLAME scorer produces patient-specific medication scores $s(q)$ .
All decoding methods use the same scores, desired output cardinality $K_{q}$ , drug–drug interaction (DDI) graph $G$ , and patient-specific DDI budget $B_{q}$ .
Local methods construct or repair the medication set through sequential decisions, whereas the exact MILP jointly selects the entire set to maximize the frozen model score while satisfying the same cardinality and DDI constraints.
The resulting medication sets are compared using set accuracy and achieved DDI rate.
Thus, the experiment isolates the effect of the decoding strategy while keeping the underlying model scores and DDI constraints fixed.

## 2 Related work

## Medication recommendation from EHRs.

Medication recommendation has progressed from instance- and sequence-based prediction to increasingly structured set prediction. LEAP framed treatment-combination recommendation as sequential generation under multimorbidity (Zhang et al., 2017); DMNC modeled asynchronous longitudinal views with external memory (Le et al., 2018); GAMENet fused longitudinal patient representations with EHR and DDI graphs (Shang et al., 2019b); and G-BERT introduced graph-augmented pretraining for medical-code representations (Shang et al., 2019a). MICRON focused on medication changes across visits (Yang et al., 2021a), while COGNet used conditional generation with copy-or-predict behavior over historical medications (Wu et al., 2022). DAPSNet added patient-similarity retrieval to longitudinal representation learning (Wu et al., 2023). More recent work improves visit selection, rare-disease performance, causal patient-state modeling, or temporal treatment reasoning, including VITA, RAREMed, CausalMed, and time-aware dynamic-treatment approaches (Kim et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). Surveys summarize the rapid expansion of architectures and evaluation practices in this area (Ali et al., 2023).

## DDI-aware and set-structured recommendation.

DDI-aware recommendation is often incorporated during training. GAMENet integrates a DDI graph into its memory architecture (Shang et al., 2019b). SafeDrug uses molecular graph encoders together with a controllable DDI loss (Yang et al., 2021b). 4SDrug explicitly targets small and safe drug sets (Tan et al., 2022). MoleRec learns substructure-aware molecular representations and uses an annealed objective to balance recommendation accuracy and DDI safety (Yang et al., 2023). Carmen designs context-aware molecular and DDI graph embeddings (Chen et al., 2023), and DAPSNet includes a DDI-guided loss in a longitudinal patient-similarity model (Wu et al., 2023). These methods show that DDI information can improve the learned predictor. Our focus is orthogonal: we freeze the predictor and study the optimization problem induced at the final set-selection stage.

## Language models and generative medication recommendation.

Recent systems bring pretrained language models and LLMs into medication recommendation. LEADER distills knowledge from an LLM into a medication recommender (Liu et al., 2024); NLA-MMR aligns natural-language patient and drug representations with molecular information (Tan et al., 2024); LAMO fine-tunes LLMs for medication recommendation (Zhao et al., 2025); FLAME adds list-wise alignment and step-wise GRPO to a point-wise LLM-based medication classifier (Fan et al., 2025); GiantMed uses deep-model guidance to activate LLM reasoning near recommendation boundaries (Lv et al., 2026); and PACE-RAG studies patient-aware retrieval for clinical drug recommendation (Huh et al., 2026). Our experiments use FLAME only as a source of fixed patient–drug scores. The proposed decoder neither trains nor queries an additional language model, making it a modular inference layer that can in principle sit on top of any scorer.

## Constrained inference.

Mixed-integer optimization is a standard tool for exact discrete decision making under linear constraints (Nemhauser and Wolsey, 1988). The medication-recommendation literature frequently describes the task itself as combinatorial (Zhang et al., 2017; Tan et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Fan et al., 2025), but the dominant safety interventions in learned systems act through training losses, graph representations, sequential generation, or heuristic post-processing. We isolate the final inference problem and solve the fixed-score, fixed-cardinality, DDI-budgeted set-selection objective exactly, permitting a controlled comparison in which the score function is identical and only the decoder changes.

## 3 Problem formulation

Let $\mathcal{M}=\{1,\ldots,M\}$ denote the medication vocabulary, with $M=151$ in our experiments. For each patient visit $q$ , a frozen model provides scores

 $s(q)=[s_{1}(q),\ldots,s_{M}(q)]\in\mathbb{R}^{M},$ 

(1)

where larger $s_{i}(q)$ indicates stronger model evidence for medication $i$ . The base model also induces an initial medication set $\hat{Y}^{(0)}_{q}$ under its fixed operating point. We define

 $K_{q}=|\hat{Y}^{(0)}_{q}|$ 

(2)

and require every decoder to return exactly $K_{q}$ medications. This is the cardinality-matching condition the comparison depends on: since no decoder can alter its cardinality, none can appear to satisfy a looser DDI constraint by returning fewer drugs.

Let $G_{D}=(\mathcal{M},E_{D})$ be an undirected DDI graph, where an edge $(i,j)\in E_{D}$ indicates a flagged drug–drug interaction. For any predicted set $Y$ , we use the pairwise DDI rate

 $\mathrm{DDI}(Y)=\frac{|\{(i,j)\in E_{D}:i\in Y,j\in Y\}|}{\binom{|Y|}{2}}.$ 

(3)

We use three nominal target rates $\rho\in\{0.136,0.100,0.080\}$ , treated as loose, moderate, and strict prespecified DDI regimes rather than a search for an optimal operating point. Each rate is mapped to the nearest feasible integer edge budget

 $B_{q}(\rho)=\operatorname{round}\!\left(\rho\binom{K_{q}}{2}\right),$ 

(4)

using the same deterministic conversion for every decoder. Because of this discretization, we report achieved DDI rates in addition to the nominal targets. The task studied here is not to learn $s(q)$ ; it is to solve the decoding problem: among all medication sets of size $K_{q}$ whose selected DDI edge count does not exceed $B_{q}$ , choose a set that best respects the frozen scorer.

## 4 Exact DDI-constrained decoding

## 4.1 MILP formulation

For each medication $i$ , introduce a binary selection variable $x_{i}\in\{0,1\}$ . For each DDI edge $(i,j)\in E_{D}$ , introduce an auxiliary variable $y_{ij}\in[0,1]$ indicating whether both endpoints are selected. We solve

 $\displaystyle\max_{x,y}\quad$ 
 $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{M}s_{i}(q)x_{i}$ 

(5)

s.t.
 $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{M}x_{i}=K_{q},$ 

(6)

 $\displaystyle\sum_{(i,j)\in E_{D}}y_{ij}\leq B_{q},$ 

(7)

 $\displaystyle y_{ij}\geq x_{i}+x_{j}-1,\qquad\forall(i,j)\in E_{D},$ 

(8)

 $\displaystyle y_{ij}\leq x_{i},\quad y_{ij}\leq x_{j},\qquad\forall(i,j)\in E_{D},$ 

(9)

 $\displaystyle x_{i}\in\{0,1\},\quad 0\leq y_{ij}\leq 1.$ 

(10)

With binary $x_{i}$ , constraints (8)–(9) give the exact product $y_{ij}=x_{i}x_{j}$ , so Eq. (7) counts the selected DDI edges exactly. The formulation has 151 binary variables and 1,425 auxiliary edge variables, for 1,576 variables total (Appendix A).

The MILP never sees the ground-truth medication set during inference; it only sees the frozen model scores, target cardinality, DDI graph, and DDI budget. At global optimality, the MILP has objective value at least as high as any heuristic solution obeying the same constraints, but a higher score sum is not guaranteed to correspond to better clinical-label agreement, nor is the same decoded set guaranteed under a rescoring of $s(q)$ that preserves rank but not magnitude. We evaluate both questions directly in Section 7.

## 4.2 Why global optimization can differ from local repair

A local repair rule compares medications inside the conflict it is currently resolving. This can be suboptimal when a high-scoring drug participates in many conflicts: retaining that drug may force the subsequent removal of several slightly lower-scoring medications whose joint score is larger. The MILP evaluates those coupled consequences simultaneously. This effect should strengthen as $B_{q}$ decreases, since tighter budgets reduce the number of feasible combinations and give each local commitment more downstream consequences. We evaluate whether the advantage in Jaccard grows as DDI-constraint pressure increases, and whether it depends on which baseline, operating point, or score parameterization is used.

## 4.3 Implementation

We solve the MILP with scipy.optimize.milp, using the HiGHS mixed-integer optimization backend (Virtanen et al., 2020; Huangfu and Hall, 2018). No warm start, learning, or patient-specific tuning is required. Full solver settings are given in Appendix A.

## 5 Local repair baselines

## Greedy + refill.

We begin from the top- $K_{q}$ medications under the frozen score. While the selected set exceeds the DDI budget, the decoder finds a conflicting pair and removes the lower-scoring endpoint. Once the budget is met, it scans excluded medications in descending score order and refills the set with the highest-scoring candidate whose addition preserves feasibility, continuing until cardinality $K_{q}$ is restored.

## Degree-aware greedy + refill.

This baseline uses graph structure: at each repair step, it computes every selected medication’s current degree in the induced DDI subgraph and removes a medication with maximum conflict degree, breaking ties by lower model score. Refill is identical to the greedy baseline. Removing a high-degree medication can resolve several conflicts at once.

## Degree-awar
limitations: Our claims are intentionally scoped to one EHR benchmark, one frozen scorer, and a binary TWOSIDES-derived DDI graph (Tatonetti et al., 2012). The fixed-cardinality design isolates decoder choice but does not optimize regimen size, and the MILP inherits any systematic bias in the underlying scores. The DDI constraint is a benchmark safety signal rather than a complete clinical rule because it omits interaction severity and patient-specific context. Accordingly, the present evaluation does not establish the clinical safety or clinical utility of the resulting recommended medication sets. Broader validation across datasets, scorers, patient populations, and richer clinically informed constraints would be needed before evaluating the approach for potential clinical deployment. Runtime and scaling under larger vocabularies or richer constraints, as well as comparisons with stronger multi-swap or beam-search baselines, remain important directions for future evaluation.

title: When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models
abstract: Decision models return normalized probability distributions over candidate choices, which downstream applications can use to select among choices. Although their providers emphasize the reliability of these probabilities, calibration on tasks with a single correct choice does not establish their reliability when multiple choices are correct. We evaluate three decision models (Jev, Liquid d1, and GPT-6 Luna Decisions) on three diverse datasets (MetaTool, HotpotQA, and ECtHR) to study probability allocation and thresholding. Even when models rank every correct choice above every distractor, in 28% to 50% of those lists, at least one correct choice receives a probability below the uniform probability of 1/n, where n is the number of choices. We also present each model with five identical copies of a correct choice and observe probability disparities, with mean gaps ranging from 17 to 79 percentage points. We further show how these allocation disparities affect the recovery of multiple correct choices under probability thresholding. Decision-model probabilities can rank correct choices, but a probability threshold does not identify the set of correct choices.

## When Multiple Choices Are Correct:

Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models

Rushab Munot

Affiliation: Independent Researcher
body_start:
Abstract

Decision models return normalized probability distributions over candidate choices, which downstream applications can use to select among choices. Although their providers emphasize the reliability of these probabilities, calibration on tasks with a single correct choice does not establish their reliability when multiple choices are correct. We evaluate three decision models (Jev, Liquid d1, and GPT-6 Luna Decisions) on three diverse datasets (MetaTool, HotpotQA, and ECtHR) to study probability allocation and thresholding. Even when models rank every correct choice above every distractor, in 28% to 50% of those lists, at least one correct choice receives a probability below the uniform probability of $1/n$ , where $n$ is the number of choices. We also present each model with five identical copies of a correct choice and observe probability disparities, with mean gaps ranging from 17 to 79 percentage points. We further show how these allocation disparities affect the recovery of multiple correct choices under probability thresholding. Decision-model probabilities can rank correct choices, but a probability threshold does not identify the set of correct choices.

## 1 Introduction

Decision models are emerging as an alternative to generative language models for applications requiring structured decisions, offering lower inference costs and latency by returning predictions directly rather than generating text (Almeida, 2026; Liquid AI, 2026a). Three recently introduced models are TypeSafe AI’s Jev (Almeida, 2026), Liquid AI’s d1 (Liquid AI, 2026a), and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna Decisions (OpenAI, 2026). Despite differences in their implementations, these models expose a similar choice-based interface. Given contextual information, instructions, and a set of candidate choices, they return a probability distribution over the choices, with probabilities summing to one. Their providers emphasize the reliability and practical utility of these outputs. TypeSafe states that "Higher probability should correspond to a greater chance that the answer is correct" (TypeSafe AI, 2026a), while Liquid AI describes its decision models as returning "calibrated probabilities across a fixed set of outcomes" (Liquid AI, 2026b). OpenAI recommends setting probability thresholds for downstream routing, filtering, and review (OpenAI, 2026), and TypeSafe demonstrates using such thresholds to select additional correct choices beyond the highest-ranked choice (TypeSafe AI, 2026b). These claims and recommendations raise a question for tasks with multiple correct choices. Can normalized Choice probabilities reliably identify all correct choices, rather than only the highest-ranked one?

While categorical distributions must output probabilities that sum to 1, providers document that these are calibrated and recommend thresholds in practice. Since probabilities are a share of the total of 1, with more correct choices, the share of each correct choice goes down on average. However, since thresholding is the recommended way to use these models, for multiple correct choices, each correct choice must have a baseline probability. The constraint still allows an even split. Two correct choices in a list of 10 can each receive 0.5, and five identical copies can each receive 0.2. We hence study the allocation of unit probability over choices passed to the model.

Consider the HotpotQA question “Who is older, Maria Sharapova or Chanda Rubin?” (Yang et al., 2018). The question is accompanied by 10 candidate passages. One of those passages gives Rubin’s date of birth and another gives Sharapova’s. Both passages together are sufficient, but neither is sufficient alone. However, all three decision models assign a probability higher than 0.90 to Rubin’s passage and a probability lower than 0.10 to Sharapova’s passage. The Choice probabilities therefore concentrate on one of the two passages needed to answer the question. Table 1 shows the question, the two relevant passages and the probabilities. After replacing the names, tournaments, dates and locations with invented ones, the Choice probabilities remain uneven. Jev and Liquid d1 still favor the older player’s passage, but GPT-6 Luna Decisions now favors the younger player’s passage. Appendix A lists the full set of original and anonymized passages, along with the probabilities assigned by each model.

Recent work on decision models has measured accuracy and calibration on datasets with one correct choice (Porcedda, 2026). Deußer et al. (2026) evaluate Jev on 37 datasets and report that its Choice probabilities are calibrated on their tasks. They also find that rotating choices leaves aggregate accuracy unchanged. On yes/no questions, Jev’s probabilities rank well but are poorly placed relative to a threshold of 0.5. Liu (2026) finds that Jev gives unequal probabilities to the six faces of a fair die. Both studies test Jev only. Li et al. (2026) compare Jev’s answers to logically related yes/no and Choice questions and find differences between probabilities for events that should agree. TypeSafe states that the order of choices can affect Jev’s answer (TypeSafe AI, 2026d). Li and Chen (2026) find that restricting and renormalizing the original probabilities predicts aggregate accuracy after choices are removed. For generative language models, Zheng et al. (2024); Pezeshkpour and Hruschka (2024) show that choice order changes answers to multiple-choice questions. Blankenstein et al. (2026) find that language models selecting among functionally equivalent tools can favour particular providers. Wang et al. (2025) find that LLMs can select an offered answer even when none is correct. However, modern AI tasks require selecting more than one correct choice. Examples include selecting the tools an agent needs to complete a task, the diagnoses supported by a medical record, the passages relevant to a query in retrieval-augmented generation, and the vulnerability types present in code.

In this paper, we measure how decision models distribute probability over several correct choices. We specifically examine the gap between the maximum and minimum probabilities assigned to correct choices. We first evaluate the models on the choice lists in the datasets. We then modify the datasets’ choice lists while keeping the query and the instruction fixed to present five identical copies of a correct choice. Identical copies differ only in their place in the list and their random IDs, so they should get the same probability. We also check calibration on yes/no questions and observe miscalibration on intermediate probabilities. We study their behavior on three datasets, MetaTool (Huang et al., 2024), ECtHR (Chalkidis et al., 2022), and HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018).

Our results show that decision-model probabilities are not reliable for identifying multiple correct choices. When a list contains more than one correct choice, the mean gap between the highest and the lowest probabilities assigned to correct choices ranges from 55 to 74 percentage points across the three models and three datasets. A uniform distribution over $n$ choices assigns $1/n$ to each, representing no preference among them. The models rank every correct choice above every distractor in 52% to 85% of the lists. In 28% to 50% of those lists, a correct choice receives less than $1/n$ . Further, even when the models rank every correct choice above every distractor, the best single threshold gives the exact set in only 64% to 78% of those examples, and that threshold is low, ranging between 0.02 and 0.08, against the 0.25 that TypeSafe uses as an example in its documentation (Section 3).

The allocation of probabilities is uneven even when a list contains five identical copies of a correct choice. The mean gap between the highest and lowest (identical) copies ranges from 17 to 79 percentage points.
For lists containing exactly one correct choice, Jev’s ECE is 8 percentage points on MetaTool and 3 on ECtHR, consistent with Deußer et al. (2026). When multiple choices are correct, normalized Choice probabilities cannot be interpreted as independent probabilities of correctness. On yes/no questions about each choice, the ECE is 3 to 9 percentage points over all bins and 8 to 18 percentage points without the bin from 0 to 0.1.

## Models.

We study three decision models. We call Jev (jev-1.13.0) (Almeida, 2026) through TypeSafe’s API, and Liquid d1 (liquid/d1) (Liquid AI, 2026a) and GPT-6 Luna Decisions (openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions) (OpenAI, 2026) through Vercel AI Gateway (Vercel, 2026). Liquid AI and OpenAI publish no version for these two models, and our results refer to the models that the gateway served in October 2026. A request holds a query, an instruction and a list of named choices, each with a description. The answer holds the selected choice, which we call the prediction, and one probability per choice. These Choice probabilities sum to 1 (TypeSafe AI, 2026b). We call the highest probability of an answer its confidence. This is not the confidence field of Jev’s answer, which TypeSafe computes from the highest probability and the number of choices (TypeSafe AI, 2026c). Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions return probabilities with two decimals, and Liquid d1 with full precision. GPT-6 Luna Decisions can refuse a question and return no probabilities. Jev and Liquid d1 refused none. The three models received the same requests, and we sent each request once. Table 20 gives the number of examples and lists of each kind.

## Datasets.

We chose three datasets from different domains, all of which allow multiple correct choices, or have a subset of examples that do. MetaTool (Huang et al., 2024) is a tool selection task. The model sees the query and a list of tools and is asked to select the tools needed to solve the query. Its four tool selection subsets hold 4,287 queries. Of these, 995 have one correct tool among tools with similar descriptions, 1,800 have one correct tool among the tools of a scenario, 995 have no correct tool, and 497 have two correct tools. Some queries appear in more than one subset, and the answer to a repeated request counts once for each example.

The distractor setting of HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) gives a query and up to ten passages, two of which support the answer. While HotpotQA contains training, validation and test sets, we only use the validation set in this study.
ECtHR, Task A of LexGLUE (Chalkidis et al., 2022), is a legal multi-label classification task. Each example
gives the facts of a case and ten articles of the Convention and it asks the model to select the articles that the case violates. Of its 1,000 test cases, 655 have one violated article, 192 have two to four, and 153 have none. When several choices are correct, the instruction asks for all of them, for example “Choose every passage in the list that supports the answer to the question.” Table 2 gives the number of examples of each kind of list.

## Identical choices.

In our first experiment, for every example, we send five identical copies of one of its correct choices. The query and the instruction remain unchanged. Exactly identical copies are rejected by the APIs, hence we name each copy with a random ID. Identical copies are equally correct and equally relevant to the query, so a difference between their probabilities cannot come from their content. To place every copy once at every position, we send each list in its five cyclic permutations (Zheng et al., 2024; Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024).

We build these lists for 3,292 MetaTool queries, a seeded sample of 1,000 HotpotQA questions and the 847 ECtHR cases with a violated article, 25,695 lists per model. We report the mean probability of the highest and the lowest copy, the gap between them, and the share of predictions at each position. Under position-invariance and uniformity, we would expect the mean probability of each copy to be 0.20, and the gap to be 0.00.

## The gap between correct choices.

Next, we send the lists as the datasets give them. MetaTool gives 497 queries with two correct tools, and HotpotQA its questions. We send both in their released order. ECtHR gives 192 cases with two to four violated articles. We send each list in its ten cyclic permutations. For each answer, the gap is the highest minus the lowest probability given to a correct choice, and we report its mean. As a reference we use the uniform distribution, which gives each of $n$ choices $1/n$ and prefers none of them. We report the share of lists in which at least one correct choice gets less than $1/n$ . To separate this from ranking errors, we also report the share of lists in which every correct choice is above every distractor, and, among those lists, the share in which a correct choice still gets less than $1/n$ . These counts use only the released order of the ECtHR lists and leave out the 21 HotpotQA questions whose list has no distractor.

## Calibration.

A model is calibrated when, among the answers to which it gives a probability $p$ , a share $p$ is correct. For lists with exactly one correct choice, we define confidence as the highest probability assigned to any choice. For lists with several correct choices, this definition does not directly apply. We therefore convert each list into several yes/no questions, one per choice, based on the benchmarks’ format. For example, for HotpotQA we ask “Does this passage support the answer to the question?” for every (question, passage) pair. The models respond with a single probability of “yes”. We report the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) (Naeini et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017) over ten bins of equal width, which compares the mean confidence, or the mean probability of “yes”, with the observed share of correct predictions, or of true “yes” labels, in each bin. For the yes/no questions, we also report the ECE without the bin from 0 to 0.1.

## Selecting by a threshold.

Model providers suggest using a threshold (OpenAI, 2026), and TypeSafe uses one to select multiple correct choices (TypeSafe AI, 2026b). For example, TypeSafe’s documentation includes an example with three choices, two of which are correct, and uses a threshold of 0.25. A threshold $t$ selects every choice whose probability is at or above $t$ . In this experiment, we study whether there is a common threshold that selects all correct choices and no distractors across all examples in the dataset.

We start with examples answered both as lists and as yes/no questions, vary $t$ from 0 to 1, and compare the two formats. We define exact set accuracy as the share of examples in which every correct choice is selected and every distractor is rejected. We define recall as the proportion of correct choices above the threshold, and precision as the proportion of choices above the threshold that are correct. We compute precision, recall, and F1 from counts pooled across all examples. We plot exact set accuracy as a function of the threshold $t$ from 0 to 1, and precision, recall and F1 are reported in Appendix H.

## None of the above.

Following Tam et al. (2025), we send lists with no correct choice (Appendix E).

## 3 Results

limitations: We study three decision models, Jev, Liquid d1 and GPT-6 Luna Decisions, through their hosted APIs. Generative language models that select a choice in text are outside the scope of this study. We use three English datasets, MetaTool, HotpotQA and ECtHR, and take the labels of each dataset as the set of correct choices. We study selection by one threshold for all examples of a dataset and by one yes/no question per choice. Other tasks with several correct choices, such as the diagnoses supported by a medical record or the vulnerability types present in code, and other selection rules, such as a threshold per example or a fixed number of selected choices, are left to future work.
conclusion: When a list has several correct choices, decision models concentrate probability on one of them, even when every correct choice ranks above every distractor. Identical copies of a correct choice receive different probabilities and show model- and dataset-dependent position bias. Even with thresholds optimized on the evaluation data, exact set accuracy remains below the share of examples in which the models rank every correct choice above every distractor. Asking separate yes/no questions for each choice lowers this accuracy for 8 of the 9 models and datasets, and the resulting intermediate probabilities are miscalibrated. Choice probabilities can rank choices, but they should not be interpreted as the probability that each choice is correct.

title: TeachBack: Learning to Teach via Bidirectional Preference Optimization for On-Policy Self-Distillation
abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables a language model to learn from a Teacher instantiated from the same model but given access to privileged information, such as a reference solution. We find that access to sufficient privileged information allows the Teacher to generate highly accurate trajectories; however, accuracy alone does not guarantee that these trajectories are suitable for Student learning. Direct access to a complete solution may encourage shortened, reference-conditioned derivations that omit the exploration, verification, and self-correction required to solve problems without privileged information. We introduce TeachBack, a bidirectional preference-learning framework for on-policy self-distillation that learns not only from the Teacher but also how the Teacher should teach. TeachBack shapes the Teacher's generation behavior by controlling the length of the reference-reasoning suffix injected into the prompt and by varying the prompt style. While maintaining comparable Teacher accuracy, it encourages the Teacher to explore and re-solve problems, thereby reducing its reliance on the reference solution. At each rollout refresh, the shared policy generates both a privileged Teacher trajectory and a problem-only Student trajectory. A pairwise preference objective uses privileged Teacher trajectories to improve Student learning, while the reversed preference uses the Student's behavior to shape future Teacher supervision under the privileged condition. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks show that TeachBack consistently improves Student performance over existing OPSD methods and related baselines.

3.1 Teacher Construction: Reference-Suffix Injection and Prompt-Style Control
4.3 How Prompt Construction Changes Teacher Trajectories
body_start:
Abstract

On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables a language model to learn from a Teacher instantiated from the same model but given access to privileged information, such as a reference solution. We find that access to sufficient privileged information allows the Teacher to generate highly accurate trajectories; however, accuracy alone does not guarantee that these trajectories are suitable for Student learning. Direct access to a complete solution may encourage shortened, reference-conditioned derivations that omit the exploration, verification, and self-correction required to solve problems without privileged information.
We introduce TeachBack, a bidirectional preference-learning framework for on-policy self-distillation that learns not only from the Teacher but also how the Teacher should teach. TeachBack shapes the Teacher’s generation behavior by controlling the length of the reference-reasoning suffix injected into the prompt and by varying the prompt style. While maintaining comparable Teacher accuracy, it encourages the Teacher to explore and re-solve problems, thereby reducing its reliance on the reference solution. At each rollout refresh, the shared policy generates both a privileged Teacher trajectory and a problem-only Student trajectory. A pairwise preference objective uses privileged Teacher trajectories to improve Student learning, while the reversed preference uses the Student’s behavior to shape future Teacher supervision under the privileged condition. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks show that TeachBack consistently improves Student performance over existing OPSD methods and related baselines.

## 1 Introduction

On-policy distillation (Agarwal et al., 2024), which provides dense supervision by allowing a Student to sample reasoning trajectories from its current policy while a stronger Teacher evaluates the Student-generated prefixes, has emerged as the dominant post-training paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models. Building on this, On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) (Zhao et al., 2026) further removes the need for a separate Teacher by employing a unified, parameter-shared policy, receiving great attention recently. This policy allows the model to play two roles, where the model acts as a Student when given only the question, but switches to a privileged-information (PI) Teacher when provided with additional reasoning evidence, such as reference solutions. Despite eliminating the dependency on external models, recent studies reveal that OPSD may cause shorter responses and a degeneration of native reasoning behaviors, a failure mode commonly referred to as thinking collapse (Peng et al., 2026), which is particularly pronounced in models relying on long chain-of-thought reasoning.

Several approaches have been proposed to address this degradation. One representative line studies OPSD from the perspective of optimization, where an uncertain Student and a PI-conditioned Teacher can favor different continuations at high-entropy reasoning forks. More specifically, privileged targets can suppress the Student’s branching, verification, and backtracking when their token probabilities are directly matched (Kaur et al., 2026). To preserve these behaviors, AD-OPSD (Peng et al., 2026) anchors updates at high-risk tokens to a frozen base policy. Another line examines the supervision signal itself: reference conditioning can change the Teacher’s response style without providing correspondingly useful reasoning. RLCSD (Pan et al., 2026) contrasts correct and incorrect hints to cancel style shifts unrelated to correctness, while Purified OPSD (Shen et al., 2026) removes a reference-only component from the Teacher signal. The third line changes how the Student learns from that signal; PBSD (Yu et al., 2026a) uses reward-regularized preferences between Teacher and Student rollouts instead of directly matching their token distributions. Although these methods have made great achievements, they primarily regulate how the Student uses a Teacher signal that has already been generated, leaving open a more upstream question: can PI be used to construct a Teacher whose reasoning remains useful to a Student that cannot access PI?

Figure 1: Motivation for TeachBack. In standard OPSD, access to privileged information can lead the Teacher to produce a short solution that omits exploration and verification. TeachBack uses partial reference reasoning and Student feedback to encourage complete, self-contained Teacher trajectories that remain useful to a problem-only Student.

This question points to a Teacher-side way to mitigate thinking collapse: privileged information should guide the Teacher’s reasoning rather than serve as an authoritative solution to be copied. A problem-only Student must search among alternative paths, express uncertainty at ambiguous steps, verify intermediate conclusions, and recover from mistakes. As we design in Figure 1, a useful PI-conditioned Teacher should preserve these Student-compatible behaviors while using privileged information to check the explored path, correct unproductive branches, and converge more reliably to a correct answer. The desired Teacher therefore needs to balance three properties: high correctness under privileged information, low dependence on the wording or trajectory of the reference solution, and productive exploration that remains reproducible without PI. In particular, the Teacher should not simply compress the reference-conditioned response into a shorter answer. It should re-solve the original problem, use privileged information for verification, and produce a complete trajectory that is both reliable as supervision and rich enough for the Student to learn.

Based on this motivation, we propose TeachBack, which improves both the construction and transfer of privileged Teacher trajectories. First, TeachBack presents the Teacher with partial reference reasoning of varying lengths and prompt styles as optional working notes, then asks it to solve the original problem from the beginning. This encourages the Teacher to use PI to check its reasoning without simply following the reference. The shared policy then generates a Teacher trajectory with PI and a Student trajectory from the problem alone. We train with preferences in both directions: the Teacher trajectory guides Student learning, while the Student trajectory provides feedback on which reasoning paths the Teacher should retain. In this way, the Teacher learns to produce accurate, less reference-dependent supervision that the Student can learn from.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

• 

Through explicit Teacher rollouts, we reveal a substantial
reasoning-behavior gap between the PI-conditioned Teacher and the
problem-only Student, and show that highly accurate Teacher trajectories
are not necessarily suitable for Student learning.

• 

We construct the PI-conditioned Teacher by presenting a controllable
suffix of reference reasoning as optional working notes and varying the
surrounding prompt style. This encourages the Teacher to re-solve the problem
and produce complete reasoning with less reliance on the reference.

• 

We develop a bidirectional preference-learning framework over paired
Teacher and Student trajectories. Teacher-origin trajectories guide Student
learning, while Student-origin trajectories provide compatibility feedback
that shapes future Teacher supervision.

• 

Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks show that
TeachBack consistently improves Student’s reasoning performance and
outperforms existing OPSD and related baselines.

## 2 Related Work

On-policy distillation and privileged supervision.

Classical knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015; Kim & Rush, 2016; Gu et al., 2024) transfers a
stronger Teacher’s predictions or generated sequences to a Student.
On-policy distillation (OPD) (Agarwal et al., 2024) instead queries the
Teacher on Student-sampled prefixes, reducing the mismatch between training
and deployment states. On-policy self-distillation
(OPSD) (Zhao et al., 2026) uses one parameter-shared policy as a problem-only
Student and a privileged-information (PI) Teacher, and Privileged Information
Distillation (Penaloza et al., 2026) extends this setting to long-horizon
agents (Wang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). Recent studies show that privileged conditioning can suppress epistemic
verbalization, exploration, verification, and backtracking at high-entropy
reasoning forks, leading to thinking collapse and reference-induced style
drift (Kim et al., 2026; Kaur et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026).
Existing remedies modify the resulting Teacher signal: Purified
OPSD (Shen et al., 2026) removes the reference-induced component;
PAINT (Tan & Hong, 2026), Adaptive Teacher
Exposure (Han et al., 2026), and best-of- $N$ 
selection (Zhang et al., 2026) control privileged exposure or retain
selected rollouts; and AR-OPD (Zhang, 2026) and
DOPD (Yu et al., 2026b) constrain or route privileged supervision according
to local compatibility and relative advantage. These methods improve how an
already formed signal is filtered or transferred, leaving the construction of
a Student-compatible Teacher as an upstream problem.

Preference optimization and Teacher construction.

Preference optimization provides a sequence-level alternative to direct
token-distribution matching. DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) learns a
reference-relative policy from response preferences, while
SPIN (Chen et al., 2024) uses self-generated responses to form an iterative
preference signal. PBSD (Yu et al., 2026a) applies preference learning
to on-policy self-distillation by optimizing a reward-regularized preference
gap between PI-conditioned Teacher samples and on-policy Student samples
instead of directly matching Teacher probabilities. Related methods use
consensus gating (Stein et al., 2026) or
self-revision (He et al., 2026; Zelikman et al., 2022) to select or construct supervision (Li et al., 2026) before
distillation. TeachBack addresses the remaining Teacher-construction problem
by presenting a controllable ground-truth suffix as incomplete working notes,
varying the prompt framing, and using two cross-condition preference
directions: the Student-side objective transfers useful Teacher trajectories
under the problem-only condition, while the reversed objective uses Student
behavior to shape future privileged Teacher trajectories.

## 3 Method

Figure 2: Overview of TeachBack. (a) The Student receives the problem alone, while a reference-reasoning suffix is framed as optional working notes for the Teacher to re-solve the problem. (b) The shared policy samples paired Student and Teacher trajectories; both responses are replayed under both conditions and scored against a fixed reference policy. (c) Under the problem-only condition, the Teacher-origin response is preferred; under the PI-conditioned condition, the Student-origin response is preferred. The weighted losses update the shared policy before the next on-policy pair is generated. At test time, only the problem-only Student condition is used.

Given training examples $\mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i}^{*},a_{i}^{*})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ , where $x_{i}$ is a problem, $y_{i}^{*}$ is its reference reasoning, and $a_{i}^{*}$ is its correct answer, TeachBack uses a suffix of $y_{i}^{*}$ as privileged information (PI) and $a_{i}^{*}$ for answer verification. The Student and Teacher are conditional roles of one parameter-shared policy $\pi_{\theta}$ , rather than separate networks: the Student receives only the problem, while the Teacher receives the problem and a prompt containing PI. Training alternates paired rollout generation with bidirectional preference updates. Figure 2 summarizes Teacher construction, paired rollouts, cross-scoring, and the two preference updates.

## 3.1 Teacher Construction: Reference-Suffix Injection and Prompt-Style Control

For each problem $x$ , the Student context and PI-conditioned Teacher context are

 $c_{S}=\operatorname{BasePrompt}(x),\qquad c_{T}=\operatorname{WorkingNotesPrompt}\!\left(x,\operatorname{Tail}(y^{*})\right).$ 

(1)

Equation 1 shows the Working Notes configuration used in the main training runs. The suffix is extracted from the dataset reference rather than from the current Student response, so Student sampling errors do not change the privileged information in the Teacher prompt. We use a suffix instead of the complete reference because it provides answer-relevant information while leaving the Teacher responsible for reconstructing the earlier derivation. An authoritative solution framing may encourage the Teacher to continue or copy the suffix. Framing it as incomplete, non-terminal working notes instead prompts the Teacher to re-solve the problem, verify the notes, fill in missing steps, and produce a complete answer.

We study two related factors in Teacher construction. The suffix length controls how much privileged information is available, while the prompt style changes how that information is presented. We compare several styles, including authoritative reference, answer-only hint, and optional working notes; the answer-only and full-solution instruction styles also change the information content. These comparisons let us assess Teacher correctness and reasoning behavior separately from the downstream preference objective. Appendix A gives the audit setup, metric definitions, and prompt templates.

## 3.2 Paired On-Policy Rollouts and Cross-Scoring

Unlike conventional OPSD, which transfers privileged next-token predictions on Student-generated prefixes, TeachBack generates explicit trajectories from both conditional roles. At refresh $t$ , the current policy is held fixed while generating $G$ paired responses:

 $y_{S,i}^{(t,g)}\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot\mid c_{S,i}),\qquad y_{T,i}^{(t,g)}\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot\mid c_{T,i}),\quad g=1,\ldots,G.$ 

(2)

Both responses are sampled from the same policy state, so systematic differences between their rollout distributions arise from the prompt conditions rather than separate models. We retain the first $K$ valid response tokens for preference training; below, $y_{S}$ and $y_{T}$ denote these retained prefixes when used in scoring equations, with example and rollout indices omitted for readability. This prefix focuses the objective on the part of the trajectory where the model establishes a solution direction, explores alternatives, and begins verification; later tokens often elaborate a path that has already been selected. Generation budgets, truncation rules, and the longer diagnostic rollout cap are specified in Appendix C.

The sampled responses are replayed under both prompts:

 $\mathcal{Q}^{(t)}=\begin{bmatrix}c_{S}\oplus y_{S}^{(t)}&c_{S}\oplus y_{T}^{(t)}\\
c_{T}\oplus y_{S}^{(t)}&c_{T}\oplus y_{T}^{(t)}\end{bmatrix}.$ 

(3)

The current policy and a frozen initialization policy score the same response tokens in all four combinations. Within each row, the scoring condition is fixed and the response origin varies. In particular, $y_{T}$ replayed under $c_{S}$ lets us evaluate Teacher reasoning under the problem-only condition. Replaying $y_{S}$ under $c_{T}$ supplies the corresponding compatibility view for the Teacher role. After the preference update, the new policy generates the next paired batch.

## 3.3 Bidirectional Preference Optimization

Let $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}=\pi_{\theta_{0}}$ remain fixed throughout training. For condition $c$ and response $y$ , we use the length-normalized score relative to this frozen reference policy:

 $A_{\theta}^{c}(y)=\frac{1}{|y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|y|}\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{k}\mid c,y_{<k})}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{k}\mid c,y_{<k})}.$ 

(4)

Only valid response positions contribute. Length normalization prevents longer responses from receiving a larger score solely because they contain more log-probability terms, while the frozen reference anchors both conditional comparisons to the same initialization.

Student-side transfer.

Under the problem-only condition, we prefer the Teacher-origin response, $y_{T}\succ y_{S}$ , using

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{stu}}=-\mathbb{E}\log\sigma\!\left(\beta\left[A_{\theta}^{c_{S}}(y_{T})-A_{\theta}^{c_{S}}(y_{S})\right]\right).$ 

(5)

Here, $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid, $\beta>0$ scales the preference
margin, and the expectation is over training problems and paired rollouts
sampled from the fixed policy snapshot at the current refresh. We use
 $\beta=0.1$ .
Both responses are scored under $c_{S}$ . The margin therefore asks whether the trajectory generated with privileged information becomes preferable under the deployment condition. This transfers a trajectory-level teaching signal without requiring the Student to match the complete PI-conditioned next-token distribution. The label is determined by response origin, not by assuming that every Teacher sample is correct; Teacher correctness is measured separately in the experiments.

Teacher-side feedback.

Under the PI-conditioned condition, we reverse the ordering and prefer the Student-origin response, $y_{S}\succ y_{T}$ :

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tch}}=-\mathbb{E}\log\sigma\!\left(\beta\left[A_{\theta}^{c_{T}}(y_{S})-A_{\theta}^{c_{T}}(y_{T})\right]\right).$ 

(6)

The reversed preference does not claim that the Student answer is more accurate. A problem-only response can contain incremental derivation, verification, and backtracking that are absent from a concise privileged response. Favoring Student-origin responses under $c_{T}$ can feed Student-compatible reasoning back into the role that generates future Teacher targets, while the privileged suffix continues to support correctness. Because both roles share parameters, the Teacher-side update changes the next privileged rollout as well as the Student. It can also reinforce Student errors or unproductive verbos
conclusion:
We presented TeachBack, a bidirectional on-policy self-distillation framework
that transfers privileged Teacher trajectories to a problem-only Student and
uses Student behavior to shape future Teacher rollouts. Framing a partial
reasoning suffix as optional working notes retains high Teacher accuracy with
less measured reference dependence than authoritative reference framing.
Across the tested model scales, TeachBack improves aggregate mathematical and
logical reasoning. Controlled ablations show that an intermediate Teacher-side
weight preserves Teacher accuracy and both preference directions while
improving held-out performance over Student-only training, highlighting the
value of shaping privileged supervision at its source.

title: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model
abstract: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.

title: LaVGuard: Selective Decoding for Contextual Value Drift
abstract: A content-safe response can still promote priorities that conflict with its task: an assistant may demand compliance when asked to preserve autonomy. We study contextual value drift as a task-relative decoding problem with an explicit allowance for change. LaVGuard separates an authorized ten-dimensional profile from a frozen estimate of the values expressed in the visible prefix. A profile-relative density gate selects when to evaluate candidate continuations; their signed progress determines a logit tilt constrained by both changed-position and cumulative-KL budgets. We establish local surrogate improvement, pathwise budget feasibility, and a bound on response-distribution change. Profile conditioning raises boundary TPR at 5% FPR from .58 to .72. At the same .12 mean intervention ratio, the selection study reports risk-safety scores of .88 for LaVGuard and .72 for position-matched edits. The resulting interface makes task priorities actionable while keeping the extent of intervention explicit and bounded.
