body_start:
Abstract

A content-safe response can still promote priorities that conflict with its task: an assistant may demand compliance when asked to preserve autonomy. We study contextual value drift as a task-relative decoding problem with an explicit allowance for change. LaVGuard separates an authorized ten-dimensional profile from a frozen estimate of the values expressed in the visible prefix. A profile-relative density gate selects when to evaluate candidate continuations; their signed progress determines a logit tilt constrained by both changed-position and cumulative-KL budgets. We establish local surrogate improvement, pathwise budget feasibility, and a bound on response-distribution change. Profile conditioning raises boundary TPR at 5% FPR from $.58$ to $.72$ . At the same $.12$ mean intervention ratio, the selection study reports risk-safety scores of $.88$ for LaVGuard and $.72$ for position-matched edits. The resulting interface makes task priorities actionable while keeping the extent of intervention explicit and bounded.

## 1 Introduction

An assistant helping a team organize a project is asked to preserve each member’s autonomy. “Assign everyone a role and require compliance” contains no prohibited content, yet privileges conformity over the requested freedom of choice. “Offer clear roles and let members choose” respects both coordination and autonomy. What matters is not just which values an answer expresses, but whether their emphasis fits the authorized task. Figure 1 illustrates this distinction.

Figure 1: Task-relative selective decoding. The authorized profile and the frozen probe’s visible-prefix state meet in the residual; the two-dimensional region illustrates the fitted geometry. Boundary exceedance and remaining position and KL allowances enable candidate evaluation. The paired continuations express contrasting priorities under a shared content guard. Along the decoding ribbon, cinnabar marks a changed sampling kernel, counted by $I_{t}$ ; $K_{t}$ is that step’s conditional KL cost. Unchanged kernels consume neither allowance. The task, trajectory, responses, and ribbon are constructed illustrations; profile and state cells indicate dimensions.

We call a departure from the task’s authorized priorities contextual value drift. Values such as security, achievement, and self-direction can each be appropriate; their intended emphasis depends on the task. Value taxonomies provide a vocabulary for these co-occurring priorities (Schwartz, 1992; Yao et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2024). A task-relative controller therefore needs to distinguish the priorities expressed by a prefix from the priorities the application requests. It must also decide how much of the ongoing generation to change: acting at every position can spend intervention on language that already fits the task.

Existing methods make several parts of this problem tractable. ConVA selectively activates value directions (Jin et al., 2025); Values as Style learns a semantic–value editing interface for low-damage steering (Dai et al., 2026); AIMES adapts value-specific activation strengths from online observations (Bhattacharjee and Tandon, 2026). Controlled Decoding and Anchored Decoding connect generation to KL-regularized objectives and sequence-level divergence budgets, respectively (Mudgal et al., 2024; He et al., 2026). We address the joint decision these tools motivate: when does the current language depart from this task’s priorities, and how should a finite change allowance shape its continuation?

LaVGuard couples a task-relative trigger with two explicit resources: the number of positions changed and the cumulative divergence from the base decoder. An authorized profile is supplied before generation. A frozen, prefix-causal probe estimates ten value intensities from visible language, without reading the numeric profile. Subtracting the profile translates a learned residual geometry into the task’s activation region. At an active position, the model evaluates likely one-token continuations, favors progress toward a mixture-derived reference, and chooses a feasible tilt by scalar KL search. The content guard is shared with the base decoder.

Changing the authorized profile while holding the language state fixed can change whether intervention is warranted, without retraining the probe. Appendix J follows this decision through candidate scoring, sampling, and budget exhaustion.

Our evaluation tests profile conditioning, position selection, and budget control. Profile conditioning raises boundary TPR at 5% FPR from $.58$ to $.72$ (Table 1). At a shared mean intervention ratio of $.12$ , LaVGuard reaches a risk-safety score of $.88$ versus $.72$ for position-matched selection (Table 3). Removing the position budget increases the edit ratio to $.34$ , with risk safety of $.89$ and benign safety of $.73$ , compared with $.88$ and $.81$ for the full controller. These comparisons motivate selecting where to spend the allowance, as well as limiting its total size.

Our contributions are:

• 

A task-relative control interface. We separate authorized priorities from observed prefix values, making the same language state evaluable under different task profiles.

• 

Selective decoding with two resources. A profile-residual gate, candidate scoring, and a feasible scalar update jointly control changed positions and accumulated conditional KL.

• 

An analysis of what this control establishes. We connect the local candidate surrogate to the tilt, prove budget and response-distribution bounds, and evaluate the roles of profile conditioning, position selection, and the two allowances.

## 2 Related Work

## Values and task context.

Schwartz’s values describe co-occurring motivational priorities (Schwartz, 1992). FULCRA and ValueBench evaluate these priorities in language models (Yao et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2024); Social Chemistry and Moral Stories ground normative judgments in context (Forbes et al., 2020; Emelin et al., 2021). Value Alignment Tax studies cross-value effects (Chen and Shen, 2026). More recently, Liscio et al. (2026) track competing value orientations across conversations, showing that early steering effects can fade or reverse. LaVGuard makes the task reference explicit: an authorized profile and the observed prefix state remain separate inputs to a residual-based decision.

## Attribute and reward guidance.

PPLM, GeDi, DExperts, and FUDGE guide generation using attribute models or auxiliary distributions (Dathathri et al., 2020; Krause et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Yang and Klein, 2021). FUDGE predicts an eventual attribute from a prefix; our probe estimates values expressed in the visible text. DeAL uses reward-guided lookahead, IVG combines token- and chunk-level value functions, and Controlled Decoding trains prefix scorers for KL-regularized reward optimization (Huang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Mudgal et al., 2024). LaVGuard uses candidate reweighting with a task-relative trigger and a local prototype-progress score.

## Value editing and semantic preservation.

Representation Engineering, ITI, and CAA expose behavioral directions in hidden states (Zou et al., 2023a; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024). Values as Style learns a semantic–value interface with one-way semantic grounding; editing the value code while holding the semantic code fixed produces a residual-stream update (Dai et al., 2026). Selective Steering uses norm-preserving rotations at discriminatively selected layers (Dang and Ngo, 2026). These designs improve the intervention interface. LaVGuard controls the sampling kernel and accounts for its cumulative change relative to the base decoder.

## Selective and adaptive intervention.

ConVA gates value-vector activation with query and token classifiers (Jin et al., 2025). MAT-Steer learns token gates and multiple attribute directions with sparsity and orthogonality objectives (Nguyen et al., 2025). AIMES uses intermediate-layer vocabulary readouts to adapt each requested value’s steering strength during generation (Bhattacharjee and Tandon, 2026). These controllers adapt activation edits to the current input or state. LaVGuard combines a profile-translated residual boundary with explicit allowances for changed positions and conditional KL. Appendix L compares the observation, actuation, and accounting interfaces.

## Safety and divergence budgets.

SIREN detects harmfulness from internal features, while SafeDecoding, SafeInfer, and SaP target content safety (Jiao et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2024; Banerjee et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). Anchored Decoding budgets trajectory-wide divergence from a separate safe model for copyright-risk control (He et al., 2026). At the agent level, VoS learns intervention value from counterfactual continuations and calibrates a harm-budgeted trigger (Li et al., 2026). LaVGuard instead accounts for changed token positions and conditional KL against its base decoder along each response, while sharing the content guard with uncontrolled generation.

## 3 Task-Relative Value Control

Figure 2: One guarded decoding step. Four layer taps and a frozen probe yield the visible-prefix state. The external profile enters the residual; the mixture provides a gate and a posterior residual mean (star), translated and clipped into the scoring prototype. Boundary exceedance and remaining allowances enable evaluation of the top 32 candidate prefixes. Signed progress is scaled and clipped before a KL search selects the feasible tilt. Edited and unchanged kernels share one sampling path. The ledger records the kernel-change indicator $I_{t}$ and conditional cost $K_{t}=D_{KL}(\tilde{p}_{t}^{H}\|p_{t}^{H})$ before the sampled-prefix guard; a sample that triggers the guard retains its cost. Pre-step balances feed eligibility and KL search. Objects, bars, and geometry are schematic.

## 3.1 Profile, language state, and drift

Given prompt $x$ and context $c$ , a frozen autoregressive model generates $y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}$ with next-token distribution

 $p_{t}=p_{M}(\cdot\mid x,c,y_{<t})=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_{t}).$ 

(1)

Here $p_{t}$ is the actual sampling kernel. Context describes the task, affected parties, and stated constraints. Before generation, an authorized user or policy owner supplies a profile $\boldsymbol{\pi}(c)\in[0,1]^{10}$ . Each coordinate specifies a value intensity; the coordinates need not sum to one.

Let $\mathbf{q}(y,c)$ be an independently annotated value vector and $\mathcal{A}(c)$ the set of value expressions admissible for the task. Contextual drift is the event $\mathbf{q}(y,c)\notin\mathcal{A}(c)$ . Online control uses a learned prefix estimate $\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{<t}$ and a fitted admissible set $\widehat{\mathcal{A}}(c)$ . Evaluation uses independent compatibility judgments, keeping the intended behavior distinct from the controller’s estimate.

## Common content-safety policy.

A shared guard $H$ checks the empty prefix and each sampled prefix. If it activates, a common safe-completion rule replaces the response and terminates generation. Base and controlled decoders use this same rule. Write their conditional kernels as $p_{t}^{H}$ and $\tilde{p}_{t}^{H}$ ; they coincide on guard-stop transitions and otherwise equal $p_{t}$ and $\tilde{p}_{t}$ . This separates explicit content safety from control of priorities among permissible continuations.

## 3.2 An explicit allowance for decoder change

For each generated response, track changed positions and accumulated conditional KL:

 $\displaystyle I_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathbb{I}[\tilde{p}_{t}^{H}\neq p_{t}^{H}],\quad C_{t}^{tok}=\sum_{j\leq t}I_{j},$ 

(2)

 $\displaystyle C_{t}^{KL}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\sum_{j\leq t}D_{KL}(\tilde{p}_{j}^{H}\|p_{j}^{H}).$ 

The controller obeys

 $\begin{gathered}C_{T}^{tok}\leq B_{tok},\qquad C_{T}^{KL}\leq B_{KL},\\
D_{KL}(\tilde{p}_{t}^{H}\|p_{t}^{H})\leq\epsilon_{KL}.\end{gathered}$ 

(3)

 $B_{tok}$ is an integer budget; $C_{T}^{tok}/T$ is the realized intervention ratio. Common guard-stop transitions cost zero. A sampled token that triggers the guard retains its incurred cost, including when the output is subsequently replaced. These quantities account for LaVGuard’s changes to the generation process.

## 4 The LaVGuard Controller

## 4.1 Read the visible value trajectory

The probe pools the last $W$ visible positions of $[x;c;y_{<t}]$ at four depth-quartile layer taps $\mathcal{L}$ . Affine projections $P_{\ell}$ produce a shared-width representation:

 $\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\phi}_{<t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\operatorname*{concat}_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}P_{\ell}\left(\frac{1}{|J_{t}|}\sum_{j\in J_{t}}\mathbf{h}_{t,j}^{(\ell)}\right),$ 

(4)

 $\displaystyle\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{<t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\sigma(W_{v}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{<t}+\mathbf{b}_{v}).$ 

 $J_{t}$ contains the last $\min(W,n_{t})$ input positions. All features precede the sampling of $y_{t}$ . Numeric profile coordinates and annotation labels are excluded from the probe input; the probe reads the visible language, while the profile enters through the controller.

Training uses visible-prefix annotations at 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of each response. Annotators assign intensities in $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ ; their mean divided by four supplies a soft target, with an adjudicated vector taking precedence when present. Soft-label binary cross-entropy fits the probe while the backbone remains frozen. Validation MAE selects the probe, which is then frozen for boundary fitting and decoding (Appendix B).

## 4.2 Locate the state relative to the profile

Let $\mathbf{r}_{<t}=\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{<t}-\boldsymbol{\pi}(c)$ . A $K$ -component diagonal Gaussian mixture fitted to admissible training residuals defines

 $\displaystyle p_{adm}(\mathbf{r})$ 
 $\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\omega_{k}\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{r};\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k},\widetilde{\Sigma}_{k}),$ 

(5)

 $\displaystyle D(\mathbf{r})$ 
 $\displaystyle=-\log p_{adm}(\mathbf{r}),\quad b_{<t}=D(\mathbf{r}_{<t})-\tau.$ 

Diagonal variances are shrunk toward the global training variance. A threshold on family-max validation scores is selected under a benign-family FPR constraint, yielding

 $\widehat{\mathcal{A}}(c)=\{\mathbf{v}\in[0,1]^{10}:D(\mathbf{v}-\boldsymbol{\pi}(c))\leq\tau\}.$ 

(6)

The profile translates a shared residual geometry. Thus the same estimated state can lie inside the boundary for one task and outside it for another. Context enters this decision through the declared profile; the probe continues to measure the visible language. Appendix J gives a complete paired calculation of this contrast.

For candidate scoring, the mixture also defines a prototype reference:

 $\mathbf{v}^{*}_{<t}=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]}\left(\boldsymbol{\pi}(c)+\sum_{k}a_{k}(\mathbf{r}_{<t})\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}\right),$ 

(7)

where $a_{k}$ are posterior responsibilities. The density level set determines when to act; distance to this prototype determines which candidates to favor. These distinct geometric roles are developed in Appendix C.

## 4.3 Evaluate likely next-token continuations

When $b_{<t}>0$ and both budgets remain, take the top $M$ tokens $\mathcal{C}_{t}$ under $p_{t}$ . Append each candidate $w_{i}$ to the same prefix, evaluate the extended prefixes in batches, and score

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{t,i}^{cand}$ 
 $\displaystyle=f_{\theta}(x,c,y_{<t}\oplus w_{i}),$ 

(8)

 $\displaystyle\Delta_{t,i}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\|\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{<t}-\mathbf{v}^{*}_{<t}\|_{2}^{2}-\|\mathbf{v}_{t,i}^{cand}-\mathbf{v}^{*}_{<t}\|_{2}^{2},$ 

 $\displaystyle s_{t,i}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\Delta_{t,i},&i\in\mathcal{C}_{t},\\
0,&i\notin\mathcal{C}_{t}.\end{cases}$ 

This score measures one-step progress toward the prototype. Its zero extension defines the surrogate on unscored tokens. With a fixed positive scale $\sigma_{b}$ and clipping level $c_{z}$ , the proposed logit direction is

 $d_{t,i}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{[b_{<t}]_{+}}{\sigma_{b}}s_{t,i},-c_{z},c_{z}\right).$ 

(9)

Boundary exceedance scales the proposal, while candidate progress supplies its direction.

## 4.4 Allocate the remaining change budget

The two budgets regulate distinct decisions. The integer allowance determines whether another position can change; the KL allowance limits how far its sampling distribution can move. For the fixed candidate direction, consider the normalized exponential tilt

 $q_{\alpha}(i)=\frac{p_{t}(i)e^{\alpha d_{t,i}}}{Z_{t}(\alpha)},\quad Z_{t}(\alpha)=\sum_{j}p_{t}(j)e^{\alpha d_{t,j}}.$ 

For a nonconstant direction with budget available, choose

 $\displaystyle\eta_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\min\{\epsilon_{KL},B_{KL}-C_{t-1}^{KL}\},$ 

(10)

 $\displaystyle\alpha_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\max\{\alpha\in[0,1]:D_{KL}(q_{\alpha}\|p_{t})\leq\eta_{t}\}.$ 

Otherwise return $p_{t}$ . The scale searches a one-dimensional family with a fixed direction, rather than recomputing candidate preferences as the budget changes. Sample from $\tilde{p}_{t}=q_{\alpha_{t}}$ and update the counters. Constant directions preserve the distribution and consume no position budget. title: NormTune: Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Reasoning-Intensive Tasks
abstract: Full fine-tuning has achieved remarkable success on reasoning-intensive tasks, but it often requires substantial GPU resource consumption. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) provides a promising alternative for reducing this cost, yet we observe a substantial performance gap on reasoning-intensive tasks. In this paper, we present three key observations showing that this gap is closely associated with norm-related under-adaptation, where PEFT produces markedly smaller weight-update norms than full fine-tuning. Based on these observations, we propose Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (NormTune), a simple yet effective strategy that adaptively strengthens insufficiently updated layers according to their weight-update norms. Extensive experiments show that NormTune consistently enhances multiple PEFT methods across challenging reasoning benchmarks. Specifically, when trained on S1K-1.1, integrating NormTune into rank-8 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA yields substantial average accuracy improvements of 24.24\%, 11.33\%, and 16.21\% , respectively, across AIME 2024, MATH 500, GPQA, and AIME 2025. Moreover, NormTune-enhanced rank-256 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA achieve performance comparable to S1 full fine-tuning, with respective average gains of 2.17\%, 0.93\%, and 3.00\% over this baseline.

headings: NormTune: Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Reasoning-Intensive Tasks
body_start:
Abstract

Full fine-tuning has achieved remarkable success on reasoning-intensive tasks, but it often requires substantial GPU resource consumption.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) provides a promising alternative for reducing this cost, yet we observe a substantial performance gap on reasoning-intensive tasks. In this paper, we present three key observations showing that this gap is closely associated with norm-related under-adaptation, where PEFT produces markedly smaller weight-update norms than full fine-tuning.
Based on these observations, we propose Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (NormTune), a simple yet effective strategy that adaptively strengthens insufficiently updated layers according to their weight-update norms.
Extensive experiments show that NormTune consistently enhances multiple PEFT methods across challenging reasoning benchmarks.
Specifically, when trained on S1K-1.1, integrating NormTune into rank-8 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA yields substantial average accuracy improvements of 24.24%, 11.33%, and 16.21% , respectively, across AIME 2024, MATH 500, GPQA, and AIME 2025.
Moreover, NormTune-enhanced rank-256 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA achieve performance comparable to S1 full fine-tuning, with respective average gains of 2.17%, 0.93%, and 3.00% over this baseline.

## 1 Introduction

Recent studies (Wu et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2024; Guo et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2025a; Xie et al., 2024) find that, for challenging reasoning tasks, carefully increasing inference-time compute can significantly boost performance.
However, most of these approaches depend on substantial compute budgets, specialized training pipelines, or complex inference-time search, making them expensive, hard to reproduce, and impractical for broad adoption. To address these limitations, many studies(Muennighoff et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025b) have explored simpler and more reproducible alternatives based on supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
These methods, however, still depend on full fine-tuning, which becomes progressively less practical as model scale increases, particularly in compute-constrained settings.
For example, full fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (Team, 2024) on a dataset with a 32K context length requires 562.07 GB of memory even with gradient checkpointing, making it difficult to apply under limited compute resources.
To address this challenge, we consider parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods (Hu et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2024a; Feng et al., 2025), which adapt large pretrained models to downstream tasks by updating only a small subset of parameters while keeping the backbone model frozen.

Motivated by this efficiency, we apply PEFT to reasoning-intensive adaptation, while noting that its reduced training cost may come with non-negligible performance risks in such challenging settings. Thus we investigate the question: Can low-rank PEFT retain the Full-FT comparable adaptation capability? As shown on the right side of Figure 1(a), existing PEFT methods exhibit a substantial performance drop on reasoning-intensive tasks, failing to reach 90 % of the full fine-tuning performance commonly used criterion for effective low-dimensional adaptation (Aghajanyan et al., 2021). In contrast, PEFT remains effective on tasks involving shorter reasoning chains and long-context understanding, as shown in the left and middle panels of Figure 1(a).
To examine this gap, we present three key observations.
Observation 1: PEFT methods exhibit a much larger loss contribution on reasoning tokens such as transition, self-verification, template, and reasoning-boundary tokens compared with Full-FT at earlier training. During training, PEFT methods exhibit a smaller relative reduction in loss on normal tokens (i.e., all tokens other than reasoning tokens) than on reasoning tokens, whereas Full-FT exhibits the opposite pattern, as shown in Figure 1(b).
Observation 2: The gradients induced by reasoning token and normal token losses exhibit substantial conflicts across most trainable parameters in earlier layers.
However, the total token gradients remain aligned with the normal token optimization direction, while its effective magnitude is partially reduced by the conflicting reasoning token gradients. This gradient interference weakens the effective parameter updates in earlier layers.
Observation 3: PEFT methods induce substantially smaller weight-update norms than full fine-tuning, especially in earlier layers.
To achieve performance comparable to Full-FT, we expect PEFT methods to exhibit similar layer-wise weight-update magnitudes as Full-FT. Based on this observation, we propose Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (NormTune), which reduces the gradients conflicts in earlier layers, reallocates optimization strength toward under-adapted layers and improves model performance.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

• 

We systematically investigate the limitations of PEFT on reasoning-intensive tasks and present three key observation, revealing that PEFT induces substantially smaller fine-tuning-induced weight changes, which is closely associated with its performance degradation.

• 

Motivated by these observations, we propose a novel PEFT method named NormTune, which reduces the gradients conflicts in earlier layers and reallocates optimization strength toward under-adapted layers. To the best of our knowledge, NormTune is the first approach that enables PEFT methods to achieve comparable performance relative to full fine-tuning on reasoning-intensive tasks.

• 

Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of NormTune. Specifically, when trained on S1K-1.1, NormTune improves rank-8 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA by 24.24%, 11.33%, and 16.21% in average accuracy across AIME 2024, MATH 500, GPQA, and AIME 2025, respectively. Moreover, NormTune-enhanced rank-256 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA achieve performance comparable to S1 full fine-tuning, with respective average gains of 2.17%, 0.93%, and 3.00% over this baseline.

## 2 Methodology

## 2.1 Key Observations On Reasoning-Intensive Tasks

Observation 1: PEFT methods exhibit a much larger loss contribution on reasoning tokens compared with Full-FT at earlier training.
To investigate the accuracy gap between PEFT and Full-FT on reasoning-intensive tasks, we analyze how training loss is distributed across tokens and how it evolves during fine-tuning, motivated by prior work Lin et al. (2024b); Pang et al. (2025).
Specifically, we sample 16 sequences from S1K-1.1 (Muennighoff et al., 2025) and evaluate token-level cross-entropy losses on the same sequences at training step 30, immediately after warm-up, and step 310, at the end of training, using Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct.
We inspect the high-loss tail using the empirical 99th percentile ( $P_{99}$ )Sato et al. (2022) of token-level losses as a cutoff. Most tokens above this threshold correspond to transitions, self-verification expressions, templates, or reasoning boundaries such as “Alternatively” and “Wait”.. For this analysis, we refer to tokens serving these four roles as reasoning tokens, and to all remaining tokens as normal tokens. As shown in Figure 1(b), PEFT methods exhibit a much larger loss contribution on reasoning tokens compared with Full-FT at earlier training. After training at step 310 , PEFT methods exhibit a smaller relative reduction in loss on normal tokens than on reasoning tokens, whereas Full-FT exhibits the opposite pattern. This indicates that PEFT disproportionately allocates its optimization capacity toward adapting reasoning token patterns, while providing insufficient adaptation for normal token representations compared with Full-FT.

Observation 2: The gradients induced by reasoning token and normal token losses exhibit substantial conflicts across most trainable parameters in earlier layers.

To understand how different token groups affect the optimization dynamics of PEFT methods, we decompose the training loss into reasoning token and normal token components.
Let $\theta$ denote all trainable LoRA parameters.
The total loss can be rewritten as

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}(\theta)$ 
 $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}|}\left(\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{reasoning}}}\ell_{i,t}(\theta)+\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{normal}}}\ell_{i,t}(\theta)\right)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reasoning}}(\theta)+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{normal}}(\theta),$ 

(1)

where $\mathcal{I}$ denote total tokens, $i$ is sequence and the $t$ is prediction position.
Because both loss terms are differentiable with respect to the LoRA parameters $\theta$ , taking the gradient of Eq. 1 yields $\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=\nabla_{\theta}\left(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{special}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{normal}}\right)=\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{special}}+\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{normal}}.$ 
Therefore, the update direction of LoRA parameters is determined by the combination of two independent optimization signals:
the gradient induced by reasoning tokens and the gradient induced by normal tokens.
We define their gradient alignment using cosine similarity. Specifically, for
 $\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{special}}$ and $\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{normal}}$ , the cosine similarity is defined as
 $\mathrm{CosSim}(\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{special}},\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{normal}})=\frac{\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{special}}^{\top}\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{normal}}}{\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{special}}\|_{2}\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{normal}}\|_{2}}$ .
We also measure their alignment with the overall optimization direction
 $\mathrm{CosSim}(\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{special}},\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}})$ and
 $\mathrm{CosSim}(\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{normal}},\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}})$ .
As shown in Figure 4, the gradients induced by special-token and normal-token losses exhibit substantial conflicts across most trainable parameters in earlier layers.
However, this behavior is reversed in deeper layers, where the two optimization signals become more compatible.
Although earlier layers exhibit
conflicts between the two token-group gradients, the total gradient remains positively aligned with the normal-token gradient. This
indicates that the special-token gradient does not reverse the
normal-token optimization direction, but reduces its effective update magnitude.

Observation 3: PEFT methods induce substantially smaller weight-update norms than full fine-tuning, especially in earlier layers.

Motivated by norm-based generalization theory Bartlett et al. (2017); Galanti et al. (2023); Nagarajan and Kolter (2019), which links network norm to model capacity and generalization, we analyze the magnitude of fine-tuning-induced weight changes as a proxy for layer-wise adaptation strength.
Specifically, for module $m$ in layer $l$ , we define the parameter update under fine-tuning strategy $\tau$ as
 $\Delta W_{l,m}^{\tau}=W_{l,m}^{\tau}-W_{l,m}^{0}$ ,
where $W_{l,m}^{0}$ denotes the corresponding base-model weight and $W_{l,m}^{\tau}$ denotes the fine-tuned weight. Here, $\tau\in\{\mathrm{Full},\mathrm{PEFT}\}$ , where $\mathrm{Full}$ represents full fine-tuning and $\mathrm{PEFT}\in\{\mathrm{LoRA},\mathrm{Bone},\mathrm{MoRA}\}$ .
To quantify the adaptation strength of each layer, we aggregate the entry-wise $L_{1}$ norm of the effective weight updates over all target modules in that layer:

 $U_{l}^{\tau}=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}_{l}}\left\|\Delta W_{l,m}^{\tau}\right\|_{1,1},where\left\|\Delta W_{l,m}^{\tau}\right\|_{1,1}=\sum_{i,j}\left|\Delta W_{l,m,ij}^{\tau}\right|.$ 

(2)

Here, $\mathcal{M}_{l}$ denotes the set of target modules in layer $l$ , including the attention projections $\{Q,K,V,O\}$ and the MLP projections $\{\mathrm{Gate},\mathrm{Up},\mathrm{Down}\}$ . In addition, the LoRA scaling factor $s=\alpha/r=2$ , which is already incorporated in this function.
Based on this metric, Figure 2(a) shows that PEFT methods with rank 256 induce substantially smaller weight-update norms than full fine-tuning, with the gap being particularly pronounced in earlier layers. This indicates that PEFT provides much weaker effective adaptation in these layers.
Furthermore, we visualize the layer-wise weight-update norms of rank-8 PEFT methods on other tasks, as shown in Figure 3. Unlike reasoning-intensive tasks, these benchmarks do not exhibit significant under-adaptation in earlier layers, suggesting that the insufficient layer adaptation observed in PEFT is particularly associated with reasoning-intensive fine-tuning.

(a) 
Gradient alignment across early and late layers, measured by
 $\mathrm{CosSim}(\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reasoning}},\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{normal}})$ and
 $\mathrm{CosSim}(\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}},\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{normal}})$ . The corresponding Full-FT results are provided in Figure 7.

(b) Layer 4 MLP down ( $A$ )

(c) Layer 41 attention Q ( $B$ ) 

(d) Layer 53 attention V ( $A$ )

(e) Layer 57 MLP gate ( $B$ )

Figure 4: 
Gradient alignment analysis between token groups and layer-wise optimization directions.
The left panel shows the cosine similarity between different gradients.
The right panels visualize representative gradient directions and the L1 norms of the gradients for different LoRA parameters (LoRA A and B) across early and late layers after 30 training steps.

## 2.2 NormTune

Overall, the three observations suggest that improving PEFT on reasoning-intensive tasks requires stronger adaptation for normal tokens, particularly in earlier layers. Observation 1 reveals an imbalance in token-level loss reduction, suggesting insufficient adaptation for normal tokens relative to Full-FT. Observation 2 provides a explanation: although reasoning-token and normal-token gradients conflict in earlier layers, the total gradient remains positively aligned with the normal-token gradient. This interference therefore attenuates the gradient component along the normal-token direction while preserving its positive alignment. This pattern is consistent with Observation 3, which shows substantially smaller weight-update norms in these layers under PEFT.
These findings motivate increasing the learning rates of under-adapted layers to compensate for attenuated updates.
Specially, for fixed parameters, gradients, and optimizer state, increasing a layer’s learning rate scales the magnitude of its parameter update without changing its direction.

Motivated by these observations,
we propose Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (NormTune), which assigns larger learning rates to weakly updated layers based on their weight-update norms, thereby improving the adaptation of under-trained layers.
In general, $U_{l}^{\mathrm{Full}}$ , i.e., the layer-wise weight-update norm obtained from full fine-tuning, can serve as an ideal reference scale for calibrating PEFT learning, encouraging $U_{l}^{\mathrm{PEFT}}$ to align with the adaptation magnitude of full fine-tuning. However, obtaining $U_{l}^{\mathrm{Full}}$ requires performing full fine-tuning, which is impractical due to its substantial training time and computational cost. Here,we first examine whether the layer-wise norm statistics from PEFT can serve as a practical alternative. Empirically, we observe that after a complete PEFT run, the maximum-to-minimum ratio of layer-wise update norms, $\max_{l}U_{l}^{\mathrm{PEFT}}/\min_{l}U_{l}^{\mathrm{PEFT}}$ , is close to that of full fine-tuning, with both ratios being approximately $6\times$ . This indicates that although PEFT produces much smaller absolute update norms, it still captures a similar relative range of layer-wise adaptation magnitudes.

Nevertheless, obtaining $U_{l}^{\mathrm{PEFT}}$ from a completed PEFT run remains costly. We therefore introduce a lightweight probing procedure that performs only 30 PEFT training steps. As shown in Figure 2(b), the early-stage update norms $U_{l}^{\mathrm{PEFT},s}$ already exhibit a comparable maximum-to-minimum ratio of approximately $6\times$ . Based on this observation, we adopt this early-stage statistic as an efficient proxy for estimating the desired layer-wise adaptation range.
Directly assigning a distinct learning rate to each layer may be sensitive to local fluctuations in $U_{l}^{\mathrm{PEFT},s}$ .
We therefore group layers into $n$ buckets according to their update magnitudes inspired by Zhang et al. (2025).
Let $U_{\min}^{\mathrm{PEFT},s}=\min_{l}U_{l}^{\mathrm{PEFT},s}$ , $U_{\max}^{\mathrm{PEFT},s}=\max_{l}U_{l}^{\mathrm{PEFT},s}$ .

conclusion:
In this work, we studied parameter-efficient fine-tuning for reasoning-intensive tasks with test-time scaling.
Through three key observations, we propose Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (NormTune), which adaptively enhances under-trained layers and thereby substantially improves performance on reasoning-intensive tasks.
Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that NormTune consistently improves different PEFT methods and can achieve performance comparable to full fine-tuning with substantially lower resource consumption.

title: StochIKM: Automated High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Individual Patient Data from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves
abstract: Individual patient data are the gold standard for secondary analysis of time-to-event evidence, but they are rarely released, and reconstruction from a published Kaplan-Meier figure could help. Existing methods all claim high fidelity, each judged by whichever agreements it happens to achieve, and each returns a single dataset although the map from figure to data is not bijective. We define fidelity explicitly: a dataset is admissible when it reproduces the risk table exactly, follows the digitized curve to within the image resolution, and respects the printed median, interval and event count. We propose StochIKM, a stochastic algorithm that digitizes the figure with a vision-capable language model and uses the high-fidelity definition as constraints, returning an admissible set of individual patient datasets. A solution is guaranteed to exist whenever the figure has been read correctly, so a failure indicts either the published figure or its digitization. In simulation and in 79 arms from published oncology trials, StochIKM reproduces the published risk tables and medians more closely than LLM-improved IPDfromKM, a high-impact alternative.

vision-capable language model and uses the high-fidelity definition as constraints, returning an admissible set of individual patient datasets. A
solution is guaranteed to exist whenever the figure has been read correctly, so
a failure indicts either the published figure or its digitization. In simulation and in 79 arms from
published oncology trials, StochIKM reproduces the published risk tables and
medians more closely than LLM-improved IPDfromKM 20, a high-impact alternative.

\copyyear

2026
\startpage1
\historydates

\authormark

KE et al.

\corres

Wei Wei () and Guannan Gong ()

## 1 Introduction

Individual patient data (IPD) are the currency of meta-analysis. For studies reporting time-to-event outcomes, access to IPD enables individual-participant-data meta-analysis 42, 31; assessment of modelling assumptions 32, 45 and sensitivity analysis; extrapolation beyond the observed follow-up for the evaluation of health technologies 19;
hypothesis generation for future studies; and emulation of randomized comparisons between treatments never studied head to head 9, 29.

The original IPD, however, are rarely accessible because of confidentiality and proprietary considerations. Even where data-sharing platforms exist, requests are often fulfilled for only a small number of applicants 18, 7. Reconstructing IPD from the published
Kaplan–Meier (K–M) curve offers a promising alternative, but the quality of such synthetic IPD is not guaranteed and requires careful evaluation. Where a ground truth is observed, as in supervised learning, accuracy is the distance from the truth. As the true IPD are rarely available, the question becomes how completely a reconstruction agrees with what the publication reports. Faith is “the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1, KJV). In information theory, fidelity is defined as the expected distortion between a source and its reproduction under a stated distortion measure, and a code is judged against a fidelity criterion fixed in advance 37, 3. Although authors who reconstruct K–M figures have measured fidelity in different ways, the idea beneath is common to all: a reconstruction is faithful to the extent that it reproduces what the original publication reported.

Recovering information from published survival curves is not new.
Parmar et al. Super and
Tierney et al. Super showed how a hazard ratio and its variance could be
recovered from a published curve together with the reported numbers at risk. Guyot et al. Super introduced an algorithm that inverts the K–M product-limit formula one risk-table interval at a time, assuming that
censoring is spread uniformly within each interval, and so produces a
complete set of event and censoring times. Liu et al. Super refined that algorithm, correcting a boundary condition so that the K–M curve is mathematically plausible, and developed software that clinicians could use. Since then, reporting standards have improved the quality of survival figures 27, 24, and vision-capable large language models (LLMs) are able to parse the elements of a figure simply by prompt engineering 21. These developments reduce the burden of extracting information from published figures but do not resolve the statistical ambiguity inherent in reconstructing patient-level records from aggregate survival data.

Three methodological challenges remain. First, fidelity has been checked as an afterthought, against inconsistent criteria: agreement with the plotted
curve and the hazard ratio 8; with reported events, numbers
at risk, survival probabilities and medians 20;
or with a synthetic ground truth 51, rather than enforced as part of the reconstruction. Some reconstructed IPD therefore do not agree with the published risk table 8, 20. Second, a published K–M curve does not identify the original IPD uniquely. Missing or overlapping censoring marks, sparse risk tables and the finite resolution of the figure admit many event and censoring configurations. Reported confidence intervals for the median carry additional information about sampling variability, but existing methods neither use them as constraints nor return more than a single IPD. Third, reconstruction depends heavily on digitization. Manual digitization is labor-intensive and prone to operator error 20, whereas automated extraction may degrade when figures are low-resolution rasters, curves overlap, or arms are distinguished only by line type or similar colours 51.

To address these limitations, we propose StochIKM, an automated stochastic algorithm for generating high-fidelity IPD from published K–M curves. StochIKM makes three contributions to the three challenges. First, it defines fidelity by three constraints: each admissible IPD must reproduce the reported numbers at risk exactly, remain within a prespecified maximum absolute deviation from the extracted K–M curve, and agree within prespecified tolerances with the reported number of events, median survival and its confidence interval, when available. StochIKM enforces them within its loop. Second, StochIKM generates a set of $\Omega$ admissible datasets rather than one, so that the uncertainty of reconstruction can be propagated into downstream analysis. Third, under idealized conditions of internally consistent reporting, an error-free K–M figure and exact extraction of the plotted information, we establish the existence of at least one dataset satisfying the fidelity criteria.

## 2 Methods

## Step 1: Digitization

StochIKM reconstructs IPD that satisfy the built-in high-fidelity constraints (“admissible” IPD) from a published paper that contains a K–M curve and an accompanying risk table. First, a vision-capable LLM (in this paper, GPT-5) automatically extracts, or “digitizes”, the information of interest. For simplicity, we present the notation for one treatment arm. The digitized elements fall into two categories. The first are numbers that can be checked directly against the original paper, denoted with an asterisk: i) from the risk table, the numbers of
patients at risk $r^{*}_{0}=n^{*},r^{*}_{1},\ldots,r^{*}_{K}$ , where $n^{*}$ is the arm-specific sample size; ii) the median overall survival (mOS) $M^{*}$ and its interval $(M^{*}_{L},M^{*}_{U})$ ; and iii) the number of events $D^{*}$ . These elements contain no digitization error. The second are elements that can be obtained only through the vision capability of the LLM, denoted with a hat: i) the coordinate system of the plotting area, that is, the pixel positions of the two axes and of their labelled ticks, by which a pixel is converted into a time and a survival probability; ii)
the curve of the arm, traced by its colour and read at times $0=\hat{\tau}_{0}<\hat{\tau}_{1}<\cdots<\hat{\tau}_{J}$ with heights $\hat{s}_{j}=\hat{S}(\hat{\tau}_{j})$ , where consecutive read times define the fine
intervals $F_{j}=(\hat{\tau}_{j-1},\hat{\tau}_{j}]$ ; and iii) the visible drops of that curve, each a vertical segment whose time and whose heights immediately above and
below it reveal that at least one event occurred there (Figure 1B). These elements may contain digitization errors, and the resolution of the image bounds how large they can be: a drop can be located in time only to about one pixel column, $\delta_{t}$ , and a height can be read only to about half the width of the drawn
line, $\delta_{s}$ . Censoring marks may be printed but not used in this paper; we return to them in the Discussion.

Figure 1: The StochIKM algorithm. A Flow chart of one run. B–G A toy example carried through the steps of A: one arm of
24 patients with a risk table at 0, 6, 12 and 18 months, a printed median with its
confidence interval, and 14 printed events; C–F follow the second risk-table
interval, $I_{2}$ .

## Step 2: Reconstruction of admissible IPD

A reconstruction is of high fidelity if it closely agrees with
the published K–M curve and the information commonly reported with it, and
an IPD that meets this standard is called admissible. Fidelity is imposed through three sequential constraints. A tilde denotes a quantity of the reconstruction: the survival $\tilde{S}$ , the mOS and its interval ( $\tilde{M}$ , $\tilde{M}_{L}$ , $\tilde{M}_{U}$ ), and the number of events $\tilde{d}_{k}$ in each risk-table interval. The zeroth-order, or risk-table, constraint requires that at every
risk-table time the reconstruction leaves exactly $r^{*}_{k}$ patients at risk (Figure 1E),

 $\tilde{n}(t^{*}_{k})=r^{*}_{k},\qquad k=1,\ldots,K.$ 

(1)

The first-order, or curve, constraint requires that at every read time the K–M
curve of the reconstruction agrees with the digitized curve to within
 $\delta_{s}$ (Figure 1F),

 $\max_{j=1,\ldots,J}\bigl|\hat{s}_{j}-\tilde{S}(\hat{\tau}_{j})\bigr|\leq\delta_{s},$ 

(2)

and that every event is placed within $\delta_{t}$ of the drop that revealed it.
The second-order, or reported-summaries, constraint uses the quantities the
publication prints alongside the figure (Figure 1G),

 $\begin{gathered}\bigl|\tilde{M}-M^{*}\bigr|\leq\varepsilon_{t},\\
\frac{\bigl|(\tilde{M}_{L},\tilde{M}_{U})\cap(M^{*}_{L},M^{*}_{U})\bigr|}{\bigl|(\tilde{M}_{L},\tilde{M}_{U})\cup(M^{*}_{L},M^{*}_{U})\bigr|}\geq\rho,\\
\sum_{k=1}^{K}\tilde{d}_{k}=D^{*},\end{gathered}$ 

(3)

where $(\tilde{M}_{L},\tilde{M}_{U})$ is the Brookmeyer–Crowley interval
4, and $\varepsilon_{t}$ and $\rho$ are fixed in advance.
Each part of (3) is used only when the publication prints the corresponding quantity, and an endpoint that is not reached is set to $t^{*}_{K}$ ; a figure with no
printed median and no printed number of events is reconstructed under (1) and (2)
alone. The algorithm below generates one candidate dataset at a time and keeps it
only if (1)–(3) hold, repeating until $\Omega$ admissible datasets have been collected.

The reconstruction proceeds one risk-table interval $I_{k}=(t^{*}_{k-1},t^{*}_{k}]$ at a time, from $I_{1}$ to
 $I_{K}$ , carrying forward the number of patients still at risk and the
reconstructed survival (Figure 1A). Within $I_{k}$ it
must determine the number of events $\tilde{d}_{k}$ and the number of censored patients
 $\tilde{c}_{k}$ , whose sum must be the attrition $\alpha^{*}_{k}=r^{*}_{k-1}-r^{*}_{k}$ obtained in Step 1.

Initialization.

Set $\tilde{q}_{0}=1$ and $\tilde{n}_{1}=n^{*}$ , and recall
that each $I_{k}$ is the union of the fine intervals $F_{j}$ , $j\in J_{k}$ 
(Figure 1B).

Step 2.1: the censoring.

With no censoring,
 $r^{*}_{k-1}\hat{S}(t^{*}_{k})/\hat{S}(t^{*}_{k-1})$ patients would be at risk at
 $t^{*}_{k}$ , and the shortfall against $r^{*}_{k}$ gives a starting value for
 $\tilde{c}_{k}$ , corrected for the fact that the events see about
 $r^{*}_{k-1}-\tilde{c}_{k}/2$ patients rather than $r^{*}_{k-1}$ . With probability
 $\omega$ this value is replaced by a uniform draw from
 $\{0,1,\ldots,\alpha^{*}_{k}\}$ ; this randomization is what lets the search reach every possible configuration, as Proposition 2.1 requires. The censoring times are drawn
independently and uniformly on $I_{k}$ , and $\tilde{c}_{j}$ of them fall in $F_{j}$ 
(Figure 1C).

Step 2.2: the events.

Events of $F_{j}$ are placed in the event window $W_{j}$ , equal to
the last $\delta_{t}$ of $F_{j}$ when the curve drops at $\hat{\tau}_{j}$ and to all of
 $F_{j}$ otherwise,
and a reference time $\tilde{u}_{j}$ , uniform on $W_{j}$ , fixes which censorings of
 $F_{j}$ come before them (Figure 1D). Inverting the K–M product
one fine interval at a time gives
 $\tilde{m}_{j}=\tilde{n}_{j}-\#\{\text{censorings of }F_{j}\text{ before }\tilde{u}_{j}\}$ and

 $\begin{gathered}\tilde{d}_{j}=\Bigl[\tilde{m}_{j}\Bigl(1-\frac{\hat{s}_{j}}{\tilde{q}_{j-1}}\Bigr)\Bigr],\\
\tilde{q}_{j}=\tilde{q}_{j-1}\Bigl(1-\frac{\tilde{d}_{j}}{\tilde{m}_{j}}\Bigr),\end{gathered}$ 

with $\tilde{n}_{j+1}=\tilde{n}_{j}-\tilde{d}_{j}-\tilde{c}_{j}$ . Given the censorings,
this step is deterministic.

Step 2.3: matching the risk table.

If
 $\tilde{n}(t^{*}_{k})=r^{*}_{k-1}-\tilde{d}_{k}-\tilde{c}_{k}$ is not $r^{*}_{k}$ , the
discrepancy is charged to censoring, $\tilde{c}_{k}\leftarrow\alpha^{*}_{k}-\tilde{d}_{k}$ ,
and $I_{k}$ is recomputed (Figure 1E). Once $r^{*}_{k}$ is
attained, $\tilde{c}_{k}\pm 1$ and $\tilde{c}_{k}\pm 2$ are tried as well, and one of
those that also reach $r^{*}_{k}$ is chosen at random.

Step 2.4: fidelity check.

Constraint (1) now holds by construction;
constraint (2) is checked over $j\in J_{k}$ (Figure 1F); and
constraint (3) is checked as soon as it is decidable, that is, once the upper
confidence limit of the reconstructed curve has fallen to one half
(Figure 1G). A failed interval is attempted again from Step 2.1,
and after $N$ failures the run is discarded and restarted from $I_{1}$ (dashed
paths of Figure 1A).

Steps 2.1–2.4 are repeated for $k=1,\ldots,K$ ; a run that reaches the end of $I_{K}$ 
yields one admissible IPD $\tilde{D}_{\ell}=\{(\tilde{y}_{i}^{(\ell)},\tilde{\Delta}_{i}^{(\ell)})\}_{i=1}^{n^{*}}$ , and runs continue until $\tilde{D}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{D}_{\Omega}$ have been
collected.

Proposition 2.1 (Under perfect digitization, StochIKM guarantees a solution.).

Suppose the risk table and the printed summaries are transcribed correctly, and every
survival probability $\hat{s}_{j}$ read from the figure is within $\delta_{s}$ of the curve
printed in the publication (perfect digitization). Then the original patient data of the trial satisfy constraints (1)–(3); in particular, the admissible set is not empty.

Proof 2.2.

Write $x^{0}$ for the original data. Since the risk table is read correctly,
 $\tilde{n}(t^{*}_{k})=r^{*}_{k}$ holds at $x^{0}$ for every $k$ , which is (1), and
exactly $\alpha^{*}_{k}$ patients leave the risk set in each $I_{k}$ . The K–M curve
of $x^{0}$ is the published curve $S$ , so at every read time
 $|\hat{s}_{j}-S(\hat{\tau}_{j})|\leq\delta_{s}$ by assumption, which is (2); each event
of $x^{0}$ produced the drop that revealed it, so it lies in that drop’s window.
The printed summaries $M^{*}$ , $(M^{*}_{L},M^{*}_{U})$ and $D^{*}$ are computed from
 $x^{0}$ , so (3) holds at $x^{0}$ up to the rounding of the printed digits, which
 $\varepsilon_{t}$ absorbs.

## Step 3: Relaxation

Every quantity denoted with a hat is read from an image, which may be of poor quality or even contain mistakes, and the LLM may misread a legend or a colour. The premise of Proposition 2.1, the perfect digitization assumption, fails and the admissible set may be empty. Repeated failure therefore has two possible causes: the search has not yet found a solution, or the digitization is
inconsistent with the published summaries and no solution exists. Step 3, relaxing constraints (1)–(3) lower the thresholds to a certain extent, and still produce result of fidelity given imperfect digitization. If $R$ runs produce no admissible dataset, the constraint
responsible for most of the failures is identified and relaxed by one level, and
the search restarts; the levels are fixed in advance and applied in the same
order for every figure. The second-order constraint has three parts and they are relaxed separately. The number of events is the commonest cause of failure, a dataset is
accepted if $\bigl|\sum_{k}\tilde{d}_{k}-D^{*}\bigr|\leq\tau D^{*}$ , with $\tau=0.035$ , and if
that is still not enough, $\delta_{s}$ is widened as for the first-order constraint while the
tolerance is kept. The number of events is a sum over
every interval, and configurations that meet every other constraint often miss it by a few
events, so a small tolerance raises the efficiency of the search considerably while the risk
table, the curve, the median and its interval keep their full fidelity. A discrepancy in number of events per arm may be attributed to a systematic mis-reading besides the digitization: the reported total number of events may count events that occurred after the last time point the figure shows, a practice that varies with the authors and the journals. The tolerance $\tau$ is
the largest discrepancy observed in the case study, 9 of 262 events. For the median and its
interval, $\varepsilon_{t}$ is doubled and $\rho$ lowered to $0.6$ , then $\varepsilon_{t}$ 
doubled again and $\rho$ lowered to $0.4$ , then the interval condition is dropped, then the
median condition is dropped. For the first-order constraint, $\delta_{s}$ is multiplied by
 $1.5$ at each level, up to a ceiling $\delta_{s}^{\max}$ . The zeroth-order
constraint is never relaxed. If no admissible dataset is obtained once every level has been exhausted, the figure is declared irreconcilable and no IPD is returned. A reconstruction obtained after relaxation is reported together with the
levels used.

Throughout, the tolerances $\delta_{t}$ and $\delta_{s}$ are fixed by the resolution
of the figure, one pixel column and half the width of the drawn line
respectively, and $\varepsilon_{t}$ is $\delta_{t}$ plus half the last printed digit
of $M^{*}$ . The remaining constants are used for every
figure in this paper: the probability of the uniform draw in Step 2.1 is
 $\omega=0.1$ ; an interval is attempted $N=200$ times before the run is discarded;
the required overlap of the two intervals is $\rho=0.8$ ; the portfolio size is
 $\Omega=50$ ; relaxation begins after $R=40\Omega$ runs without an admissible dataset
conclusion:
Reconstruction methods routinely claim high fidelity, but each has measured it
differently, and no criterion has been agreed
upon 8, 20, 51. Our principal
contribution is to propose one: a reconstruction is admissible when it reproduces
the risk table exactly, follows the digitized curve to within the resolution of
the image, and respects the summaries printed beside the figure. Because that criterion does not identify a single
dataset, StochIKM returns a portfolio of $\Omega$ admissible ones, and the spread
across them measures what the publication left undetermined.

We build directly on Liu et al. Super, whose algorithm depends on manual,
software-assisted tracing and returns a single IPD, and whose authors
anticipated both the automation of the reading and the multiplicity of the
answer. Vision-capable language models have made the first possible, and the
constrained sampling scheme developed here makes the second explicit. Over 97
published arms the reconstruction reproduced every risk table and matched the
published median to within one month in all of them, and
Proposition 2.1 shows that, when the figure is traced exactly, an
admissible set exists. A failure of producing result therefore indicates either an imperfect figure-tracing or imperfect quality of the source figure.

Limitations lie in the figure-reading part: we are not able to use censoring marks. Many figures draw them, and they carry exactly the information determining IPDs. The K–M curve and the risk table determine how many patients
are censored between two events but not when. Authors and journals draw these marks in
different ways, and adjacent marks merge into one, so the vision-language models available to
us cannot yet read them reliably. If a highly capable large language model could read the marks, then it would boost the algorithm on efficiency: with the censoring times given, the events in each interval would follow
deterministically from the steps of the curve, so the search for $\tilde{c}_{k}$ would no longer be needed. Under perfect digitization
it would recover the original true patient data themselves, up to tied events
(Supplementary material); a partial reading, which separates some marks and only
counts the others, would already narrow the admissible set. More broadly, what limits
StochIKM is the vision of the model that reads the figure. Given how quickly vision-language models have improved, we expect this
limitation to ease, and the algorithm is ready to take adva

body_start:
Abstract

A coding agent that rewrites its own scaffold has to choose which proposed edit to expand before that edit has been evaluated, and the search then has to return one agent.
Each run fits one linear readout on the parent’s steering-split solve rate and eight coordinates of the proposed diff, from 96 scaffold edits labeled by four evaluations of a 16-instance fit split, and then freezes the coefficients.
HumanEval+ reserves 48 instances as the steering split and Polyglot reserves 64.
That split scores parents and keeps an archive of four nodes.
Huxley–Gödel Machine selection draws a parent by Thompson sampling on the steering counts of nodes that have already been evaluated, and it expands the child that parent proposes.
Every method then returns the earliest evaluated node whose steering-split solve count is maximal.
The tables report the held-out score of that node on the other 100 HumanEval+ instances and the other 145 Polyglot instances, next to the root scaffold and the calibration edit with the highest fit-split label.
Twelve runs of GPT-4o return a node at 87.0% on held-out HumanEval+, against 84.2% for the parent-rate ablation.
On that split Huxley–Gödel Machine selection returns 85.1%, the root is at 81.2%, and the calibration-best edit is at 82.8%.
On the same split Claude Sonnet 4.5 returns 86.6%, beside 86.5% for Huxley–Gödel Machine selection, 85.3% for the parent-rate ablation, and 85.1% for the calibration-best edit.

## 1 Introduction

A coding agent that rewrites its own scaffold has to rank the edits it proposes before any of them has been evaluated, because the checker runs on one child per keep step and the child that is kept becomes a parent of the edits that follow.
The Darwin Gödel Machine adds a child to its archive only after that child has been evaluated, and it samples parents from observed scores (Zhang et al., 2026).
The Huxley–Gödel Machine draws a parent by Thompson sampling on the success and failure counts of evaluated nodes and expands the child that parent proposes (Wang et al., 2026).
AIDE scores a candidate after the evaluator has run it (Jiang et al., 2025).
Surrogate-assisted evolution fits a predictor of fitness from earlier evaluations of similar individuals (Jin, 2011).
The readout is that kind of predictor, applied to the diff before the child is expanded.
It is a linear score on the parent’s steering-split solve rate and eight coordinates of the diff.
The ablation uses the same archive and expands by the parent’s steering rate alone.
When the keep steps end, the readout, the parent-rate ablation, and Huxley–Gödel Machine selection each return the earliest evaluated node whose steering-split solve count is maximal.
The held-out score of that node is the comparison, together with the root and the calibration edit whose fit-split label is highest.
Huxley–Gödel Machine selection draws $\theta$ from $\mathrm{Beta}(1+n_{s},1+n_{f})$ for each evaluated node, using that node’s steering counts, and expands the child of the parent with the largest draw.
Every run of every method spends the same number of checker evaluations: the readout and the ablation label 96 calibration edits and then expand 24 children, and Huxley–Gödel Machine selection expands 144 children on Polyglot and 176 on HumanEval+.
Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) are fit separately (OpenAI, 2024).
The held-out splits are 100 HumanEval+ instances and 145 Polyglot instances (Liu et al., 2023; Gauthier, 2024).
Table 1 is the held-out score of the returned node for the readout, the parent-rate ablation, and Huxley–Gödel Machine selection.
Table 2 is the child the readout and the parent-rate ablation expand at the first keep step, and Figure 1 plots the returned node.
Theorem 1 gives the mean of that parent draw, $(1+n_{s})/(2+n_{s}+n_{f})$ , on the steering counts of an evaluated node.
The proof is in Appendix A.

Figure 1: Held-out solve rate of the returned node, twelve runs.
Points are means and bars are run standard deviations.
For the readout, the parent-rate ablation, and Huxley–Gödel Machine selection, the node is the earliest evaluated node whose steering-split solve count is maximal.
The root is the starting scaffold, and calibration best is the edit with the highest fit-split label.
On HumanEval+ with GPT-4o the readout is the highest mean.
On HumanEval+ with Claude Sonnet 4.5 the readout sits with Huxley–Gödel Machine selection, the parent-rate node, and the calibration-best edit.
Table 1 reports these means.

• 

The readout ranks eight scaffold diffs at each keep step, and every method returns the earliest evaluated node whose steering-split solve count is maximal (Algorithm 1, Figures 2 and 3).

• 

Huxley–Gödel Machine selection draws a parent from $\mathrm{Beta}(1+n_{s},1+n_{f})$ on the steering counts of evaluated nodes and expands that parent’s child (Theorem 1, Figure 3).

• 

On held-out HumanEval+, GPT-4o’s returned node leads the parent-rate ablation, and the same table reports Huxley–Gödel Machine selection, the root, and the calibration-best edit (Table 1, Figure 1).

## 2 Method

## 2.1 Birth-time readout

The root is a scaffold: a system prompt and a loop that writes a solution, runs the unit tests, and retries once.
A proposal is a unified diff of that scaffold.
The readout scores that diff from the parent’s steering-split solve rate and from eight coordinates of the diff, before the diff is expanded.
The diff is embedded by text-embedding-3-small as a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{1536}$ .
Each run draws its own projection, with i.i.d. standard normal entries and rows scaled to unit length, and it maps that vector onto the coordinates $e$ .
The birth feature of the full readout is $X=(R_{\mathrm{par}},e)\in\mathbb{R}^{9}$ .
Both $R_{\mathrm{par}}$ and the label $R$ are solve rates in $[0,1]$ .

Before the search, each run calibrates its own readout.

title: GRAM: Group-wise Rank-Aware Model Merging via Subspace Alignment
abstract: Merging different models into a single model is highly desirable for multi-task deployment, particularly in regulated domains like healthcare. In such settings, models are often locally fine-tuned due to strict data privacy policies, necessitating that aggregation operates exclusively on the fine-tuned weights. Existing methods apply a uniform merge across all tasks, ignoring the geometric relationships among their learned subspaces. When task updates occupy misaligned subspaces, projecting them onto a shared low-rank basis discards task-relevant directions, a failure mode named \emph{subspace interference}. Through this study, we show that the per-task projection error of a merged model is governed by the principal-angle alignment between each task and the shared subspace, so that grouping geometrically compatible tasks provably reduces this error within each group. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{Group-wise Rank-Aware Model Merging (GRAM)}, which uses the principal-angle geometry of task vectors to decide which tasks should be merged together and then performs a standard SVD-based merge within each coalition; the pipeline requires only the fine-tuned weights at merge time. With only one additional model ($\nK{=}2$), GRAM significantly mitigates subspace interference and consistently outperforms prior merging methods across language understanding (GLUE with Flan-T5), 8-task CLIP vision, and medical instruction tuning (Qwen2-7B-Instruct with four English/Chinese medical LoRAs).
