Results by Instance Order Patterns.

Figure 2 shows
the accuracy of each LLM across four representative order patterns.77
 7

 Since several patterns show similar trends,
Figure 2 and Section 4.2
focus
on four representative patterns, including random, majority-first, majority-middle and majority-last, with results for all seven patterns provided in the appendix. 
Models generally achieve their highest accuracy under the majority-first pattern, while accuracy under majority-last and particularly majority-middle
often falls
below the random baseline.
This systematic variation shows that the models’ predictions are
strongly influenced
by where the majority signal is placed, rendering them
sensitive
to order permutations.
Although no single pattern yields the lowest accuracy across all plotted LLMs, over half of the models perform worst under majority-middle, suggesting a “lost-in-the-middle” effect (Liu et al., 2024).
Full results a
limitations:
We study LLM reliability in multi-instance processing (MIP) through
the lens of permutation invariance. This is a necessary reliability criterion
for unordered instance sets, and its violation is already sufficient to show
that a model is unreliable in this setting. However, MIP reliability has other
important dimensions that we do not fully cover, such as robustness to task
formulation, language variations (we study only English), calibration, aggregation faithfulness, and transparency of
intermediate decisions.
Future work should
therefore examine a broader set of reliability criteria and investigate the different
mechanisms underlying MIP failures.

Our goal is primarily diagnostic.
We design a controlled probe to assess whether the evaluated LLMs satisfy permutation invariance and to characterise behaviours associated with its violations.
We therefore do not provide a comprehensive method for improving
MIP reliability. Our prompt-based
experiments
show that the tested prompting approaches do not consistently resolve
the failures we observe.
More systematic solutions may be needed, such as specialised training, explicit instance-level decomposition, tool-assisted processing, deterministic or verifiable aggregation, or agentic workflows that separate instance processing from aggregation.

Finally, our behavioural analysis relies on indirect evidence from reasoning traces and attribution signals.
Some evaluated models do
not produce reasoning traces, while others do not reveal them through the API.
Even when traces are available, they may be incomplete or may not fully reflect
the model’s internal computation, and our automatic ID extraction may contain false positives. Thus, they offer observable but potentially unfaithful evidence
of how reasoning LLMs approach a task (Turpin et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026b).
Attribution signals are likewise descriptive rather than causal: Input
 $\times$ Gradient is a local, first-order measure tied to the chosen decision
score and the observed input.
We therefore treat these analyses as complementary evidence of positional
imbalance, rather than direct measurements of the model’s internal computation.
Developing more faithful and explainable methods for analysing MIP behaviour
remains an important direction for future work.
conclusion:
Our controlled majority-label probe identifies instance order as a concrete source of aggregation errors in multi-instance processing.
Across fifteen LLMs and five tasks, accuracy varies widely across order patterns, with
generally higher accuracy when
majority-label instances appear first. Since the task is order-independent, these results reveal clear violations of permutation invariance
despite the instance sets remaining unchanged, with the bias towards early instances suggesting broader reliability issues in MIP.

Available reasoning traces
often
mention only a fraction of the input and disproportionately reference early instances, while gradient-based attribution profiles are also non-uniform across instance positions. We also explore prompt variants that explicitly instruct models to check all instances, but these do not consistently improve permutation robustness.
Together, these findings suggest that models may rely on shortcuts in MIP, even when the task requires them to consider every instance.

Several takeaways and implications emerge from our findings.
First, evaluations of MIP should report both accuracy and variation across input orders.
Second, future work should
investigate models and workflows that process
instances systematically and aggregate verifiable intermediate decisions without sensitivity to presentation order.
Such approaches could help ensure that all required instances are considered, regardless of their positions, and give users greater confidence in the results.
Finally, future work should investigate mechanisms that enable models to recognise when they cannot fully complete a task and alert users accordingly.

title: AutoFraming: Synthesizing Dynamic Frames of C Code with LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in synthesizing formal specifications from source code. However, existing approaches primarily focus on functional contracts and loop invariants, while largely neglecting frame conditions, which specify the memory locations that may or may not be modified during execution and constitute an essential part of formal specifications. To address this limitation, we propose an LLM-based approach for synthesizing ACSL frame specifications alongside functional contracts from C code. Our approach analyzes code property graphs (CPGs) to extract frame-relevant information from the input code and leverages this information to guide the LLM in generating accurate frame conditions. The resulting specifications capture both region-separation constraints and data dependencies that govern variable modifications. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. On a benchmark of 84 ACSL-compliant functions from non-trivial real-world systems, our method successfully synthesizes error-free frame specifications for 92.9% of the functions, representing a 179% relative improvement over state-of-the-art techniques. On a second benchmark consisting of 51 functions, the success rate increases from 80.4% to 96.1%. Furthermore, when integrated as an auxiliary component into existing LLM-based ACSL-synthesis frameworks, our approach improves frame-specification generation performance by up to 61.9%.

IV-C RQ1: How effectively does AutoFraming synthesize frame specifications?
IV-D RQ2: How do CPG-derived frame information and frame-constrained projection contribute
IV-E RQ3: Can AutoFraming improve existing frameworks as a frame synthesis component?
body_start:
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in synthesizing formal specifications from source code. However, existing approaches primarily focus on functional contracts and loop invariants, while largely neglecting frame conditions, which specify the memory locations that may or may not be modified during execution and constitute an essential part of formal specifications.
To address this limitation, we propose an LLM-based approach for synthesizing ACSL frame specifications alongside functional contracts from C code. Our approach analyzes code property graphs (CPGs) to extract frame-relevant information from the input code and leverages this information to guide the LLM in generating accurate frame conditions. The resulting specifications capture both region-separation constraints and data dependencies that govern variable modifications.
Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. On a benchmark of 84 ACSL-compliant functions from non-trivial real-world systems, our method successfully synthesizes error-free frame specifications for 92.9% of the functions, representing a 179% relative improvement over state-of-the-art techniques. On a second benchmark consisting of 51 functions, the success rate increases from 80.4% to 96.1%. Furthermore, when integrated as an auxiliary component into existing LLM-based ACSL-synthesis frameworks, our approach improves frame-specification generation performance by up to 61.9%.

Index Terms: 
deductive verification, frame specification, ACSL, Frama-C, code property
graph, large language models, program analysis

## I Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong potential for generating formal specifications from source code. For C programs, several approaches [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] have explored using LLMs to synthesize ACSL specifications, often with feedback from static analyzers or verification tools. These techniques can generate useful functional specifications, such as preconditions, postconditions, and loop invariants, and can substantially reduce the manual effort required for deductive verification. However, little attention has been paid to frame conditions: the part of a specification that describes what memory a function may affect, what values those effects depend on, and what memory must remain independent. Without accurate frame information, a verified function cannot be safely reused by callers, because the caller cannot know which parts of the program state are preserved.

This limitation is especially important for C programs. Recent approaches such as AutoSpec [4] and Preguss [5] push LLM-based specification generation further by combining models with program information and verification feedback. However, their treatment of frame information remains limited. They primarily optimize for whether the generated specification can help discharge verification conditions, while frame completeness is not directly measured. In particular, evaluations based mainly on WP proof success may overlook missing memory-dependence information or imprecise aliasing assumptions, because a proof can succeed even when the contract does not fully describe what state a caller may rely on after the function returns. This gap is difficult to close for C: pointers, arrays, pointer arithmetic, loops, and library calls can hide which memory regions may overlap and which input values may influence each write. As a result, a generated contract may look correct to the verifier but still be too weak for precise modular reasoning. Section II shows a small example where an apparently verified contract still permits an invalid aliased call.

To address this problem, we propose AutoFraming, an approach for synthesizing frame specifications for C programs. AutoFraming analyzes frame-relevant information from a code property graph (CPG) [6], including possible memory interference, caller-visible writes, loop-indexed write ranges, and data dependencies. It then projects this information into a fixed-frame skeleton that captures which memory regions must be kept independent and which inputs may influence each written location. The LLM is used to assemble the full contract and repair remaining verification failures, while the frame-critical structure is generated and preserved during refinement.

We evaluate AutoFraming on two benchmarks: 84 functions from real-world C systems and 51 academic verification examples. On the real-world benchmark, AutoFraming synthesizes error-free frame specifications for 92.9% of functions, a 179% relative improvement over the state-of-the-art baseline. On the academic benchmark, it improves the error-free frame rate from 80.4% to 96.1%. When used as an auxiliary frame-synthesis component for existing specification-generation tools, AutoFraming further improves error-free frame performance by up to 61.9%. Ablation results show that the CPG-derived frame information and deterministic projections are essential to the improvement.

The contribution of this paper is summarized as follows: AutoFraming provides an effective approach to the novel problem of synthesizing
error-free frame conditions with LLMs.
It conducts frame analysis, including caller-visible roots, access windows, interfering pointer pairs, write-set locations, and dependence footprints. It then projects frame-related information into ACSL specification, including region separation for caller-visible memory regions and data dependence for write-set locations.
Moreover, AutoFraming can be used in other ACSL synthesis frameworks, such as Preguss and AutoSpec, to improve their capability of synthesizing frame conditions.

## II A Motivating Example

Consider the C function parse_value, shown below, which reads two values from the memory region pointed to by buf and stores their sum in the memory location pointed to by eaten.

Listing 1: Source code of the motivating example.

⬇

int parse_value(const uint16_t *buf, uint16_t len, uint16_t *eaten) {

 if (len < 2 || buf == NULL || eaten == NULL) return -1;

 *eaten = buf[0];

 *eaten = (uint16_t)(*eaten + buf[1]);

 return 0;

}

To call parse_value, the client needs to provide actual parameters for *buf and *eaten, such as the following:

⬇

uint16_t buf[2] = { 3, 5 };

uint16_t out;

parse_value(buf, 2, &out);

Without a formal specification for parse_value, clients have no precise way to determine whether a call satisfies the function’s assumptions or achieves its intended behavior. To address this issue, we can prompt an LLM to synthesize the following ACSL [7] specification directly from the source code of parse_value:

Listing 2: Preliminary ACSL specification generated by prompting an LLM

⬇

/*@ requires len > 0;

 requires buf != \null;

 ensures \result == 0 || \result == -1; */

int parse_value(const uint16_t *buf, uint16_t len, uint16_t *eaten);

The generated comment enclosed by /*@ and */ defines the ACSL contract for parse_value, including its precondition (the requires clauses) and postcondition (the ensures clause). The precondition specifies the conditions that callers must satisfy before invoking parse_value; specifically, len must be positive and buf must be non-null. The postcondition specifies the property that must hold when parse_value returns, namely that the return value is either 0 or -1.

The ACSL specification can be verified with Frama-C and one of its plug-ins (e.g., WP or Eva) [8]. Given a function and its ACSL contract, Frama-C generates a set of proof obligations, called goals, each expressed as a logical formula whose validity establishes a specific aspect of the contract. These goals are then dispatched to automated SMT solvers. The proportion of discharged goals, referred to as the goal ratio (proved/total), indicates the extent to which the contract has been verified. A goal ratio of $1$ (i.e., a full proof) means that every proof obligation has been discharged, establishing that the implementation satisfies the specified contract for all executions. Otherwise, the result is only a partial proof, indicating that some proof obligations remain unresolved. It is important to note, however, that a full proof does not necessarily imply that the code is correct. Rather, it only guarantees conformance to the given specification. If the specification is incomplete or inaccurate, the implementation may still satisfy it while failing to capture the intended behavior. For example, Frama-C with the WP plugin reports a full proof for the preliminary LLM-generated ACSL contract shown above, even though the contract only partially captures the intended behavior of parse_value. The generated precondition is overly restrictive. It requires len to be positive and buf to be non-null, even though parse_value handles the cases where len is non-positive or buf is NULL without error.

To improve the quality of synthesized ACSL specifications, existing approaches leverage the results of static code analysis to prompt LLMs and refine the specifications.
The following ACSL specification is generated by Preguss [5], the state-of-the-art method:

Listing 3: ACSL specification generated by existing approaches

⬇

/*@ requires \valid_read(buf + (0..len-1));

 requires \valid(eaten);

 assigns *eaten;

 ensures \result == 0 || \result == -1; */

int parse_value(const uint16_t *buf, uint16_t len, uint16_t *eaten);

The requires clauses specify the validity conditions for buf and eaten. The assigns clause, assigns *eaten;, defines the function’s frame condition by specifying that only the memory location referenced by eaten may be modified during execution. Consequently, all other program state, including buf, len, and the memory referenced by buf, must remain unchanged. More generally, the assigns clause consists of a list of variable names or memory locations (referred to as a write set or footprint).

However, the above frame specification is insufficient even though the verification result is a full proof. Consider the following call:

⬇

uint16_t buf[2] = { 3, 5 };

parse_value(buf, 2, &buf[1]);

The call satisfies
both precondition clauses, i.e., buf is readable and &buf[1] is
valid. Although the intended value for *eaten (i.e., buf[1]) is
buf[0] + buf[1] = 8, the actual outcome is 3 + 3 = 6 because parse_value reads buf[1]
after writing through *eaten, so the write clobbers
buf[1] first and the call computes 3 + 3.

The problem arises because the same object, buf, is passed to both pointer parameters, *buf and *eaten. However, parse_value operates correctly only when these pointers refer to separate, non-overlapping memory locations. Therefore, the ACSL specification must explicitly capture this separation requirement to prevent invalid function calls and ensure correct verification.

In summary, existing LLM-based approaches to ACSL specification synthesis do not explicitly address the frame problem, particularly dynamic frame conditions such as the memory separation requirement illustrated above. Dynamic frame conditions precisely specify the memory locations that a function is permitted to read or modify, ensuring that changes to one object cannot inadvertently affect the state of another unrelated object. The goal of this paper is to enable LLMs to synthesize ACSL specifications with accurate frame conditions for C programs that are ACSL-compliant, i.e., programs whose behavior can be completely specified in ACSL. The following specification for the example illustrates the desired result:

Listing 4: ACSL specification with dynamic frames

⬇

/*@ requires \valid_read(buf + (0..len-1));

 requires \valid(eaten);

 requires \separated(buf + (0..len-1), eaten);

 assigns *eaten

 \from buf[0..len-1], len;

 ensures \result == 0 || \result == -1; */

int parse_value(const uint16_t *buf, uint16_t len, uint16_t *eaten);

The additional requires clause,
\separated(buf + (0..len-1), eaten);
specifies that the memory region referenced by buf must be disjoint from the memory location referenced by eaten. The assigns clause,
*eaten \from buf[0..len-1], len;
defines both the function’s write set and the data dependencies of the modified location, stating that only *eaten may be updated and that its value depends solely on buf[0..len-1] and len.
Synthesizing the region separation requirement and the data dependency of the write set is a challenging problem. Because C programs do not expose their memory footprint directly in the source syntax. Pointer aliasing, array ranges, pointer arithmetic, loops, globals, and library calls can hide both the regions that may interfere with one another and the inputs that may affect each write. Therefore, synthesizing accurate dynamic frames requires recovering caller-visible memory regions, separation assumptions, and write dependencies from program structure rather than treating frame clauses as ordinary text to be generated.

## III The design of AutoFraming

## III-A Overview

AutoFraming leverages the code property graph (CPG) representation of C code to synthesize its frame specifications. Given an unannotated function, AutoFraming generates an ACSL specification whose frame part describes not only the memory locations that may be modified, but also the memory regions that must remain disjoint and the caller-visible inputs that may influence each write. Although AutoFraming outputs a complete ACSL specification, this paper focuses on the synthesis of frame conditions. Figure 1 shows the three-stage workflow of AutoFraming.

Stage 1: AutoFraming first constructs the call graph and analyzes functions in bottom-up order, ensuring that verified callee contracts are available when analyzing their callers. For each function $f$ , AutoFraming builds a CPG and extracts the frame-related information $\Phi_{f}$ , which captures the caller-visible roots of memory accesses, accessed regions of pointer roots, pointer pairs whose aliasing may interfere with caller-visible writes, write-set locations used as frame carriers, and the dependence footprint of each write-set location.

Fig. 1: AutoFraming Pipeline for CPG-guided Frame Specification Synthesis.

Stage 2: AutoFraming projects $\Phi_{f}$ into a frame skeleton. The separation projection turns interfering pointer regions into disjointness requirements, while the dependence projection attaches caller-visible dependence footprints to write-set locations. AutoFraming treats projected frame obligations as required constraints.
A candidate is rejected if it deletes or weakens them, but the current
implementation may still allow equivalent or stronger rewritings that
change the proof burden.

Stage 3: AutoFraming asks the LLM to assemble a verifier-checkable contract around the frame skeleton and uses Frama-C feedback to repair remaining failures. During refinement, candidate contracts are accepted only if they preserve the projected frame conditions, avoid degenerate frames, and make proof progress. This design lets AutoFraming use the LLM for auxiliary annotations and repair while keeping the frame-critical content grounded in program analysis.

## III-B CPG-Based Frame Analysis

For each function $f$ , AutoFraming extracts from its CPG the information needed to synthesize the dynamic frame. A CPG overlays three program views on one graph [9]: the abstract syntax tree (AST), which exposes declarations and assignment targets; the
control-flow graph (CFG), which exposes branches, loops, and execution paths; and the program dependence graph (PDG), which exposes data and control dependencies. This combination is essential because frame synthesis is not a purely syntactic task: write-set locations come from syntax, region extents often come from loops and guards, and dependence footprints require following value and control flow.

AutoFraming represents the frame-related information as

 $\Phi_{f}=(\mathcal{R}_{f},\Omega_{f},\mathcal{I}_{f},\mathcal{L}_{f},\Delta_{f}).$ 

The first three components help address the region-separation issue:
which caller-visible regions must be disjoint? The last two deal with the data dependency issue: what does each write set location depend on?

## CPG-to-information extraction.

AutoFraming derives each component of $\Phi_{f}$ by querying specific CPG
nodes and edges rather than by passing the whole graph to the LLM. AST
nodes provide syntactic roots and memory-access forms: parameter and
global declarations identify caller-visible roots; dereference,
array-subscript, field-access, assignment, and update nodes identify
reads and writes; and declaration and cast nodes provide type information
for alias compatibility. CFG edges provide the execution context of these
accesses: loop headers, back edges, and branch guards are used to recover
loop-indexed access ranges and conditional bounds. PDG edges provide
dependence information: data-dependence edges connect values to the
expressions they influence, while control-dependence edges connect guards
to the writes whose execution they control. Together, these CPG views
determine the five information components used by AutoFraming:
caller-visible roots, access windows, interfering pointer pairs,
write-set locations, and dependence footprints.

conclusion: We have presented AutoFraming for synthesizing ACSL frame specifications for C programs. It extracts frame-related information and projects the information into a deterministic frame skeleton, and uses the LLM only to complete and repair the surrounding contract under verifier feedback. Our experimental results show that grounding LLM-based specification synthesis in explicit program structure and frame-specific constraints leads to more complete and reusable frame specifications than existing generators. Future work will extend AutoFraming to richer heap abstractions, recursive data structures, inter-procedural library summaries, and additional specification languages and verifiers.

title: GRAIL: From Saliency to Semantics in Time-Series Explanation
abstract: Explaining a time-series model requires both locating the evidence and extracting meaningful knowledge from it. Yet a single timestep is not a semantic unit: the meaningful patterns live across many samples, not in any one of them. Per-timestep saliency is therefore noisy, high-dimensional, and unstable. Existing methods address this by introducing fixed-size windows and treating them as independent players in a cooperative game. Evaluating a coalition of such players requires defining a ``baseline'' region, which prior work tackles with fixed counterfactuals (e.g., a flat line, noise, or a spectral surrogate). This choice frequently dominates the resulting explanation, obscuring the model's true decisions. To address these issues, we propose GRAIL, a region-based time-series explanation framework that uses domain-specific intervals, such as the P-wave and the QRS complex of an electrocardiogram (ECG) beat, as players. We describe each region with human-readable features and generate counterfactual baselines with an on-manifold conditional generator. Such a choice of players also admits non-temporal features: static covariates enter as singleton players attributed with the temporal regions on one scale, so a patient's tabular evidence (e.g., age, sex) is weighed directly against the signal. We attribute the predictions to the features via Owen values with common-random-number variance reduction. Experimental results on both synthetic and real data show that the proposed framework produces faithful and robust explanations, evaluated under matched on- and off-manifold operators, offering meaningful knowledge to domain experts.

4.3 Temporal Signal and Covariates on One Scale
body_start:
Abstract

Explaining a time-series model requires both locating the evidence and extracting meaningful knowledge from it. Yet a single timestep is not a semantic unit: the meaningful patterns live across many samples, not in any one of them. Per-timestep saliency is therefore noisy, high-dimensional, and unstable. Existing methods address this by introducing fixed-size windows and treating them as independent players in a cooperative game. Evaluating a coalition of such players requires defining a “baseline” region, which prior work tackles with fixed counterfactuals (e.g., a flat line, noise, or a spectral surrogate). This choice frequently dominates the resulting explanation, obscuring the model’s true decisions.

To address these issues, we propose GRAIL, a region-based time-series explanation framework that uses domain-specific intervals, such as the P-wave and the QRS complex of an electrocardiogram (ECG) beat, as players. We describe each region with human-readable features and generate counterfactual baselines with an on-manifold conditional generator. Such a choice of players also admits non-temporal features: static covariates enter as singleton players attributed with the temporal regions on one scale, so a patient’s tabular evidence (e.g., age, sex) is weighed directly against the signal. We attribute the predictions to the features via Owen values with common-random-number variance reduction. Experimental results on both synthetic and real data show that the proposed framework produces faithful and robust explanations, evaluated under matched on- and off-manifold operators, offering meaningful knowledge to domain experts.

1KAIST

2NYU

enver@kaist.ac.kr, ys1001@nyu.edu, jaesik.choi@kaist.ac.kr, stoyanovich@nyu.edu

## 1 Introduction

Deep learning models are increasingly deployed on high-stakes time series, from clinical data to industrial sensors and financial data. Wherever they are used, deploying them hinges on a question that’s hard to answer for time series: which part of the signal drove a decision, in terms a domain expert can act on.

(a) a cardiologist-delineated ECG beat

(b) an explanation of the LVH-positive prediction by GRAIL

Figure 1: From saliency to semantics on one LUDB beat. (a) A real ECG beat split into P, QRS, T, and the isoelectric background. Two samples of equal amplitude ( $+1.04$ ) fall in different regions, so a per-timestep view cannot separate them. (b) GRAIL scores each region and static covariate (age, sex) on a single log-odds scale for this beat, which the model correctly classifies as LVH-absent. The prediction relies primarily on the QRS region, even though the patient’s age and T region would suggest otherwise.

Example 1.

Consider a cardiologist inspecting a single heartbeat (Figure 1(a)). Rather than reasoning sample by sample, the cardiologist reads a sequence of named regions: the P-wave (atrial activation), the QRS complex (the sharp ventricular spike), and the T-wave (ventricular recovery), and attaches clinical meaning to each. Left-ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), for instance, is read chiefly from the QRS voltage. A saliency map that reports “sample 137 was important” may localize evidence, but it does not directly express the regional pattern or its clinical meaning.

In the game, a present feature keeps its observed value while an absent one triggers on-manifold regeneration, so every coalition is a plausible real signal. Predictive patterns typically span multiple samples, rendering per-timestep saliency maps high-dimensional, unstable, and difficult for domain experts to interpret (Ismail et al. 2020). This motivates our first design choice: explain in the domain expert’s units. We take the unit of explanation to be the region, a contiguous, named interval corresponding to a recognizable event: the P/QRS/T waves of an ECG beat, or an injected pulse, a seasonal stretch, or a trend in a synthetic signal. Regions are few, human-readable, and carry a prior, since cardiology tells us which region should distinguish an LVH from a normal beat.

Additionally, models are routinely given non-temporal information alongside the temporal signal. Returning to Example 1, a cardiologist reads an ECG differently depending on the patient’s sex and age, since the voltage criteria for left-ventricular hypertrophy are sex-specific and normal intervals shift with age. This motivates our second design choice: to place the signal and covariates on a common scale. A faithful explanation must weigh such covariates against the waveform, so a model’s reliance on demographics in addition to morphology can be read directly from the model. Figure 1(b) provides a clinically meaningful explanation of the correct diagnosis: the model calls this 68-year-old LVH-positive despite a normal QRS, consistent with the lower QRS-voltage threshold that LVH criteria apply at older ages.

## Our approach.

We propose GRAIL (Generative Region Attribution with Interpretable Labels), a framework that explains time-series predictions in domain-aligned units. GRAIL produces feature-based, additive explanations via a cooperative game: each region and each covariate is a player, and its value is its contribution to the prediction across all coalitions, so the contributions sum to the model’s output. Scoring a coalition requires saying what the signal looks like when a region is absent, but there is no canonical “off” state for a stretch of a time series such as an ECG: prior work fills it with a fixed counterfactual, a flat line, noise, or a spectrally matched surrogate, an arbitrary choice that frequently dominates the resulting explanation (Sundararajan and Najmi 2020). The choice of the absent state is thus not an implementation detail; it is the explanation. In this work, we stop choosing from a fixed menu and instead build the counterfactual: an interpretable codec encodes each region as named features, and a conditional generator regenerates an absent region on the data manifold, so every coalition remains a plausible real signal.

GRAIL attributes the model’s log-odds to regions and covariates with Owen values (Owen 1972) (a two-level Shapley value (Shapley 1953), features nested in regions) estimated by a common-random-number sweep, and always reports the residual $\rho$ , so the accounting is exactly complete. Figure 2 shows the pipeline of GRAIL, which also amortizes into a fast single-pass surrogate for deployment.

## Contributions.

1. 

A region-and-covariate cooperative game. We cast time-series attribution as a cooperative game whose players are semantic temporal regions and non-temporal covariates, credited on one common scale, so reliance on metadata is read off alongside the waveform. To our knowledge, no prior time-series explainer accommodates both (Section 3.1).

2. 

An exact, on-manifold attribution. GRAIL plays the game by generating each absent region on the data manifold rather than from a fixed filler, and attributes with exactly-complete Owen values (CRN-estimated). This is the faithful but slow reference; a model-aware segmenter recovers regions absent a prior (Section 3.2).

3. 

A fast surrogate for deployment. GRAIL-fast amortizes the game into one forward pass, $\sim$ $10^{3}\times$ cheaper and still exactly complete, though its on-manifold faithfulness holds only on real data
(Section 3.3).

4. 

A comprehensive benchmark. An at-scale comparison over four families of benchmarks, including real ECG, scoring every method under matched on- and off-manifold operators with paired significance tests against concept- and group-level Shapley baselines, with kernel, generator, reference, and segmenter ablations (Section 4).

## 2 Related Work

## Attribution and time-series explainers.

Attribution via Shapley values (Shapley 1953; Lundberg and Lee 2017) depends on how an “absent” feature is modeled (Sundararajan and Najmi 2020; Janzing et al. 2020; Covert et al. 2021). Most time-series explainers give per-timestep saliency (Theissler et al. 2022); those at a coarser grain group timesteps into windows or segments (WindowSHAP (Nayebi et al. 2023), TimeSHAP (Bento et al. 2021), TS-MULE (Schlegel et al. 2021), LIMESegment (Sivill and Flach 2022), Dynamask (Crabbé and Van Der Schaar 2021)), but all fill the absent state with a fixed, off-manifold filler. Instead, we make the removal operator a conditional generator that stays on-manifold and lift the flat Shapley game to a two-level Owen value (Owen 1972) over features nested within regions.

## Closest comparators and evaluation.

Nearest to us are methods that highlight time series players: C-SHAP (Jutte et al. 2025) uses signal concepts, while GroupSegment-SHAP (Kim and Park 2026). We also benchmark these approaches. They redefine the player but keep an off-manifold mean-replacement operator, whereas we hold the player structure fixed and change the operator, and neither admits non-temporal covariates. CausalConceptTS (Lopez Alcaraz and Strodthoff 2025) shares our generative premise but imputes over full recordings, and ManifoldShap (Taufiq et al. 2023) restricts the interventional background to an on-manifold region rather than generating it. Our per-region generation keeps an exact Owen sweep affordable. Because perturbation faithfulness is confounded by the removal operator (Hooker et al. 2019; Jethani et al. 2021), we score every method under both a matched on-manifold and a neutral off-manifold operator, and amortize the exact game for deployment (Jethani et al. 2022). Appendix A expands each baseline and the hierarchical-credit connection.

## 3 The GRAIL framework

GRAIL represents time-series attribution as a cooperative game and solves it on the data manifold. We define the game and its players, semantic regions together with non-temporal covariates in Section 3.1; play it exactly, generating each absent region’s counterfactual on-manifold and attributing with exactly-complete Owen values in Section 3.2; and amortize the exact game into a fast single-pass surrogate for deployment in Section 3.3.

## 3.1 Defining the Cooperative Game

We write a signal as $x\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times T}$ over $C$ channels ( $C=1$ for a univariate series) and denote the model’s logit for the target class by $f$ . A segmenter partitions $x$ into named regions $R_{1},\dots,R_{M}$ , each keyed by (channel, span), and a codec (an interpretable encoder paired with a conditional generator) encodes each region as human-readable features $\hat{\theta}_{r}$ . The players $N$ are the region features, grouped into Owen coalition blocks $B$ . Static covariates are treated as singleton players appended after the regions, so that signal and tabular evidence are evaluated on a single scale. This ensures no contribution leakage into $v(\emptyset)$ .

For a coalition $S\subseteq N$ we pin each present feature to its observed value and draw each absent feature from a reference,

 $\theta_{i}(S,\omega)=\begin{cases}\hat{\theta}_{i},&i\in S\quad(\text{present: observed}),\\
F^{-1}_{p_{0,i}}(u_{i}),&i\notin S\quad(\text{absent: generated}),\end{cases}$ 

(1)

with $u_{i}\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1]$ and $F^{-1}_{p_{0,i}}$ the quantile function of feature $i$ ’s reference marginal (App. B). Each region is then regenerated from its features by a conditional generator, conditioned only on its own channel since boundary continuity is a within-channel property. Folding the reference draws $u$ and generator noise $\varepsilon$ into a fixed base randomness $\omega=(\varepsilon,u)$ makes the assembled signal a deterministic function $x^{\prime}(S,\omega)$ , and the coalition value is the expected logit

 $v(S)=\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\!\big[\,f(x^{\prime}(S,\omega))\,\big].$ 

(2)

With $v(\emptyset)$ defined, the Shapley/Owen axioms hold automatically, and attributions aggregate by additivity from features to regions and, for multivariate signals, from regions to channels (Section 4.3). ## Intervention and reference semantics.

The interventional default draws absent features from the marginal $p_{0}$ , isolating what the model uses, while the conditional draw takes them from $p(\theta_{\bar{S}}\mid\theta_{S})$ , crediting shared information. This is referred to as the interventional-versus-observational
distinction (Janzing et al. 2020). A marginal reference is assumption-free, whereas a class-conditional reference draws the absent value from a labeled cohort: the normal cohort (default), so each $\phi_{i}$ reads as its deviation from normal; the sample’s own class; or a foil, giving the contrastive “why this class rather than another.” Conditional draws use a Gaussian copula that stays deterministic in $u$ (so CRN coupling survives) and collapses exactly to the marginal when the conditioning set is empty, so any difference is attributable to conditioning alone; App. F compares the four references.

## 3.2 Playing the Game On-manifold

Playing the game means evaluating coalition values, each of which requires regenerating the absent regions on the data manifold. The codec’s generator makes “feature absent $\to$ regenerate region” well-defined.

Our default generator is a Gaussian process (GP) posterior: a distribution over plausible region shapes given the retained features and the region’s boundary. A present feature conditions the GP on its value, an absent feature is set to the reference, and the region is sampled from that posterior. This keeps every coalition on the data manifold. For example, a spectrally and autocorrelation-matched GP sample of an ECG resembles the original form rather than a flat or noisy filler. The generator is swappable. Replacing it changes only the region sampler, not the game, estimator, or residual. A learned conditional VAE (Kingma and Welling 2014; Sohn et al. 2015) keeps the analytic encoder but replaces the GP sampler, improving off-manifold behavior at a small on-manifold cost, and swapping only the GP kernel (RBF, Matérn, or spectral) alters the counterfactual’s texture for robustness (App. D). The exact GP game is our on-manifold reference: its closed-form posterior is what keeps an exact Owen sweep affordable, since a learned generator pays a per-coalition sampling cost it cannot amortize.

## Owen values and exact completeness.

We attribute feature importance with Owen values, the average marginal contribution of a region-feature under permutations that preserve the block (region) structure. Since features are nested in regions, their Owen values roll up consistently. For instance, values of the QRS region’s R-amplitude and width should sum to the QRS’s Shapley value (Owen consistency), so the “regions $\to$ features” explanation is coherent. A telescoping common-random-number (CRN) sweep estimates every player from $|N|{+}1$ model calls along one nested chain:

 $\phi_{i}\;\mathrel{+}=\;f(x^{\prime}(S\cup\{i\},\omega))-f(x^{\prime}(S,\omega)).$ 

(3)

Reusing the same $\omega$ across adjacent coalitions, each term measures the effect of toggling feature $i$ rather than the gap between two noise draws. Antithetic pairing and a cached unit-variance Cholesky factor ( $O(n^{3})\!\to\!O(n^{2})$ ) reduce cost further. The estimator is efficient at any budget: $\sum_{i}\phi_{i}=v(N)-v(\emptyset)$ holds to machine precision because it follows from the telescoping sweep, not from averaging permutations.

The reconstruction residual $\rho=f(x)-v(N)$ is the part of the decision that the feature representation cannot reproduce, since even the all-present coalition regenerates $x$ only approximately. We are required to always report $\rho$ because neglecting it breaks efficiency. Additionally, a large $\rho$ indicates an off-manifold generator. Therefore, to make the accounting exactly complete, we add a lossless morphology-residual player per region that restores the region’s exact residual when present ( $v(N)=f(x)$ , $\rho\to 0$ ) and regenerates normally when absent, so the opaque residual becomes one attributable named channel. Finally, to recover within-region resolution, we distribute each $\phi_{r}$ across its timesteps by a normalized occlusion profile ( $\sum_{t\in r}\text{saliency}_{t}=\phi_{r}$ ); in Example 1, this concentrates saliency at the R-peak within QRS.

## Region discovery with GRAIL-auto

When no region prior is available, the segmenter must find regions itself. The proposed segmenter model adopts three sources of information: a prior, when available; Pruned Exact Linear Time (PELT) change points (Killick et al. 2012); and a model-aware segmenter. The signal-only default is PELT change, which reacts only to the signal. Our model-aware segmenter instead learns a selector (trained REAL-X-style (Jethani et al. 2021) with the generator as imputer) that reads regions from a thresholded mask. Since the amortized surrogate is trained on a single model, the model-randomization sanity check requires retraining the surrogate. Although the method achieves high performance on non-stationary data, we need to explore additional signals that a GP cannot represent. The exact generator saturates the logit, which the residual $\rho$ detects, and the swappable cVAE and DDPM generators mitigate this effect. Automated region discovery is improved but still unsolved. Further lessons that generalize beyond GRAIL, an expert-rule agreement analysis, and the scope of our reimplementations, diffusion arm, and multivariate claims are developed in Appendix K.
conclusion: Meaningful time-series explanation begins with the choice of the right unit, the region, and the non-temporal covariates a model uses alongside it. Having fixed the players, an explanation is governed by the definition of a "baseline" region, defined by a counterfactual. Instead of choosing a fixed filler, the proposed method generates an absent region on the data manifold. Then it attributes the logit via Owen values estimated with common random numbers, and always reports the residual. Since all players share a single scale, the model’s overreliance on static data rather than time series can be assessed. Experiments show that the exact game is the most faithful on-manifold on every family and exactly complete. On real ECG data, GRAIL almost reaches the same off-manifold performance as other baselines. Finally, we attempt to ease the deployment process by introducing an amortized surrogate that reduces runtime on real data; a faithfulness-aware segmenter that enables region discovery without ground truth; and a game that supports multi-lead signals by recovering the clinically expected leads.

We keep realised fitness φas the selector and reference performance θas the unused ruler. Every measurement uses gemini-3.1-flash-lite on one negotiation task, and no fixed-oracle arm was run. In the open loop, tactic append grafts short donor rules and is admitted. Free rewrite moves only a third of the requested dose and is rejected. Template append pastes raw donor replies into the child. Its movement clears the bound on the first probe but not on the re-probe, and it is left undetermined. body_start:
Abstract.

Large language model (LLM) agents are often improved by iterating
until a fixed verifier is done. Once that verifier saturates, the
loop has nothing left to climb. We instead score agents against the
current population, and a frozen panel records whether anyone got
better. The panel mean can rise inside the seeds by elimination alone.
We therefore count a run as training only when its final mean beats
the best generation-zero member. A merge is admitted only when the
child moves toward the donor, past the child the same operator produces
at zero dose, and the lower confidence bound on that movement reaches
half the requested dose. That is the admission test. A detectable
shortfall rejects the operator, and the test is otherwise undetermined.
We keep realised fitness $\phi$ as the selector and reference performance
 $\theta$ as the unused ruler. Every measurement uses gemini-3.1-flash-lite
on one negotiation task, and no fixed-oracle arm was run. In the open
loop, tactic append grafts short donor rules and is admitted. Free
rewrite moves only a third of the requested dose and is rejected.
Template append pastes raw donor replies into the child. Its movement
clears the bound on the first probe but not on the re-probe, and it
is left undetermined. A held-out re-probe on the five situations the
merge never saw confirms that both appends move, and it does not rescue
free rewrite. Neither append rises with the dose. Constrained rewrite
is admitted in the open loop and was not run in the closed loop, which
changes only the operator. The population, the scores and the task
stay fixed. No free-rewrite run beats the best generation-zero member.
Every tactic-append run and every template-append run does. Sampled
loop children keep that split. Free rewrite moves no further toward
the donor, and both appends still clear the bound, by less than in
the open loop.

Keywords: 
Large language model agents, competitive training, competitive coevolution,
prompt evolution, heritability, merge operators

## 1. Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents are usually improved by iterating
until a fixed verifier is satisfied (Shinn et al., 2023),
and the same shape governs fine-tuning and human feedback (Ouyang et al., 2022).
Once the verifier is satisfied, the loop has nothing left to climb.
We therefore score each agent against opponents drawn from the current
population, and no weights are updated. Realised fitness $\phi$ is
then relative. It ranks the population at every generation, but it
cannot certify progress, because a population in which every agent
improves still faces only itself. We read progress instead on reference
performance $\theta$ against a panel frozen at initialisation, and
 $\phi$ stays the selector. That decoupling is the setting of this
paper, not its contribution.

The setting has a weakness, and that weakness motivates the paper.
The panel mean can rise inside the seeds by elimination alone, because
selection keeps the better seeds and discards the worse. A climb therefore
does not show that children inherit anything from their donors. Whether
they do is a property of the merge operator, and that operator is
what we test.

The objects are concrete. Each agent is one frozen LLM with its own
system prompt, and the population is a set of such prompts. A merge
takes a recipient prompt, a behavioural trace of a donor and a requested
dose $\beta$ , the fraction of the donor the child is asked to inherit,
and it returns a child prompt. We study four such operators (Table
1). Two rewrite the recipient and two append
to it. Their effect is read on a behaviour profile, the frequencies
with which a prompt claims each issue of a negotiation game, or accepts,
on a fixed battery of scripted situations.

We ask two questions.

RQ1.: 

Given a requested dose $\beta$ , does an operator move the
child toward the donor, past the child the same operator produces
at $\beta=0$ , by the requested dose? We call that the admission test.
An operator is admitted when the lower confidence bound on that movement
reaches half of $\beta$ , it is rejected when a shortfall below $\beta$ 
is detected, and it is otherwise undetermined.

RQ2.: 

Does the open-loop verdict predict the closed loop? When
only the operator changes and the population, the scores and the task
stay fixed, do admitted operators carry the population past the best
generation-zero member, and do rejected ones stay inside the seeds?

The scope is deliberately narrow. We measure transmission, not efficiency.
No fixed-oracle arm was run, and we make no claim that competitive
scoring trains faster than a fixed verifier. Every measurement uses
gemini-3.1-flash-lite on one negotiation task.

We offer two contributions. The first is the admission test of RQ1.
It scores a merge against the operator’s own zero-dose child rather
than against the recipient, and that baseline is what separates inherited
movement from paraphrase drift. It admits on a confidence bound rather
than on a failure to detect a shortfall. The second is the closed-loop
protocol of RQ2. A run counts as training only when its final mean
beats the best generation-zero member, which elimination alone cannot
do, and sampled loop children are re-tested with the same admission
test.

## 2. Related Work

The trajectory of LLM systems has run from the static model to the
tool-using agent (Yao et al., 2022) and cooperating multi-agent
systems (Wu et al., 2023). Unlike those orchestration
frameworks, our agents never divide a task between them, and the output
is a population rather than a workflow. Closest to our work are methods
that optimise a prompt or an agent program against a task metric.
Some use textual gradients (Pryzant et al., 2023)
or an LLM acting as the optimiser or compiler (Yang et al., 2024).
Others run an evolutionary search over prompt strings (Guo et al., 2023),
including language-model crossover (Meyerson et al., 2023) and self-referential
prompt evolution (Fernando et al., 2023). Those methods
use the parents as in-context examples and sample a new complete prompt.
They do not keep the recipient and append the donor.

By contrast, each merge here takes a recipient prompt, a donor and
a requested dose $\beta$ , the fraction of the donor the child is
asked to inherit. We measure that family in Section 4
against its own $\beta=0$ child, the child the same operator produces
at zero dose with the donor still in view, and we contrast it with
a recipient-preserving graft. Headless-chicken crossover replaces
one parent with a random individual (Angeline, 1997),
but our control keeps both parents and sets the dose to zero. The
graft itself has precedent. ExpeL and Agent Workflow Memory distil
rules from experience and append them to a prompt (Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024).
Those rules come from the agent’s own history, but our donor is a
rival’s trace. What is new here is the audit of that graft.

The same neighbourhood now includes later LLM evolution. AlphaEvolve
(Novikov et al., 2025) edits an existing program, and GEPA
(Agrawal et al., 2025) edits an existing prompt in light of its rollouts.
ShinkaEvolve and the Darwin Gödel Machine (Lange et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025)
evolve programs against a task metric, and EvoAgent (Yuan et al., 2025)
evolves a specialist into a multi-agent system by mutation and crossover
of agent settings. None of them scores the change against the operator’s
own zero-dose child.

The setting inherits from classical evolutionary computation. Competitive
coevolution (Hillis, 1990; Rosin and Belew, 1997) and
its reinforcement-learning counterpart self-play (Silver et al., 2018)
induce the frequency-dependent dynamics we analyse (Hofbauer and Sigmund, 1998).
More recently, foundation-model self-play has brought these dynamics
to LLM-driven evolution (Dharna et al., 2025). That method freezes
the model as well, but it uses the model as a code-level search operator
that writes a new program from the opponent and the match result.
We instead keep the model as the player, and the genome is a prompt
that must inherit. That tradition also supplies our measurement problem
and its pathologies of disengagement, cycling and mediocre stable
states (Watson and Pollack, 2001). The frozen panel of Section
3.1 is the simplest of its archives
(Lanctot et al., 2017).

The merge itself also has classical counterparts. Geometric semantic
crossover places the child on the segment between its parents (Moraglio et al., 2012).
We call that placement a blend. A blend inherits exactly the requested
dose, but it never leaves the hull of the seeds. Open-ended and quality-diversity
search (Lehman and Stanley, 2011) instead seeks the variation a blend
cannot supply, a child outside the hull of its seeds. Remark 3.2
distinguishes that hull escape from inherited change.

## 3. A Coevolutionary Training Model

We model competitive survival as a steady-state coevolutionary process
over a fixed population of $N$ agents. Each generation adds $k$ 
children by a merge operator and removes $k$ agents by rank-proportional
elimination, returning the population to $N$ . No weights are updated,
and evolution acts on strategies alone. An agent is scored against
its current rivals rather than a fixed oracle.

## 3.1. Population, Competitive Fitness, and Reference Performance

Let the population at generation $t$ be $P_{t}=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{N}\}$ 
of fixed size $N$ . Each agent carries a strategy, its prompt and
configuration, in a space $\mathcal{A}$ . An embedding $\psi:\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ 
(in Section 4, a behaviour profile) is an instrument
for measuring transmission, and convexity of $\mathcal{A}$ is not
assumed. A competitive task is a two-party interaction with match
function $m(a_{i},a_{j})\in[0,1]$ , the expected score agent $i$ 
obtains against agent $j$ . The interaction need not be zero-sum.

An agent’s realised fitness is its expected match score against opponents
drawn from the current population,

(1)

 $\phi_{i}(P_{t})=\frac{1}{|O_{i}|}\sum_{j\in O_{i}}m(a_{i},a_{j}),\qquad O_{i}\subseteq P_{t}\setminus\{a_{i}\}.$ 

Here, $O_{i}$ is a fixed-size set of opponents drawn uniformly without
replacement, independently of the strategies. Because its opponents
are population members, $\phi_{i}$ depends on which strategies its
rivals currently use, and the same strategy scores differently as
that mix shifts.

Because $\phi_{i}$ is relative, it cannot by itself certify progress.
If every agent improves, all still face one another and the mean is
unmoved. We therefore fix a reference panel $B$ , at initialisation
and never subject to selection, and define agent $i$ ’s reference
performance,

(2)

 $\theta_{i}=\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{b\in B}m(a_{i},b).$ 

Since $B$ never changes, $\theta_{i}$ is an external ruler, the
counterpart of the coevolutionary master tournament (Nolfi and Pagliuca, 2024).
Progress is the mean reference performance $\bar{\theta}_{t}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\theta_{i}$ .
Finally, sorting agents by $\phi_{i}(P_{t})$ assigns each a rank
 $r_{i}\in\{1,\dots,N\}$ , with $r_{i}=1$ the fittest.

## 3.2. Reproduction Operator

At each generation, $k$ recipients are drawn uniformly with replacement
from the original $N$ scored agents. For each recipient $b$ , a donor
 $d$ is drawn by the rank-Boltzmann rule (A3) below. The recipient
then requests a dose $\beta\in[0,\beta_{\max}]$ , a control in the
prompt rather than a geometric weight, and a child is spawned by a
(possibly stochastic) merge operator $T$ , $a_{\mathrm{clone}}\sim T(a_{b},a_{d},\beta)$ .
A behavioural trace of the donor may also enter $T$ as a prompt ingredient.
The theory itself uses $T$ only through two derived quantities, the
fidelity and the residual defined next, identified on LLM merge operators
in Section 4.

Write $x=\psi(a)$ for the embedding of a strategy. The child is the
recipient, plus a fraction $\tau$ of the donor increment (what was
inherited), plus an orthogonal residual $\xi$ . Formally, any realised
child with $x_{d}\neq x_{b}$ decomposes uniquely as

(3)

 $x_{\mathrm{clone}}=x_{b}+\tau(x_{d}-x_{b})+\xi.$ 

The realised fidelity

(4)

 $\tau=\frac{(x_{\mathrm{clone}}-x_{b})^{\top}(x_{d}-x_{b})}{\lVert x_{d}-x_{b}\rVert^{2}}$ 

is the coefficient that makes the residual $\xi$ orthogonal to the
donor-recipient difference (Fig. 1). The fidelity
of an operator at a requested $\beta$ , $\tau(\beta)$ , is its expectation
under $T$ . If reference performance is affine in the embedding, the
same split holds on the panel, $\theta_{\mathrm{clone}}=\theta_{b}+\tau(\theta_{d}-\theta_{b})+\varepsilon$ ,
with $\mu=\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon]$ the operator bias. The expectation
is under $T$ for a given pair, as for $\tau(\beta)$ . Orthogonality
fixes each realised $\xi$ but does not make its mean vanish, and
 $\mu$ is the panel reading of that mean shift. The realised residual
 $\xi$ , not its mean, may leave the convex hull of the current population.

Figure 1. The decomposition of Eq. 3 in the embedding.
Points are population members $\psi(a)$ . The child $x_{\mathrm{clone}}$ 
is the recipient $x_{b}$ plus a fraction $\tau$ of the donor increment,
the projection of Eq. 4, plus the orthogonal residual
 $\xi$ . The dashed polygon is the hull of $\psi(P_{t})$ , which the
residual may leave.

We adopt four modelling assumptions. (A1) A child satisfies Eq. 3
in the embedding, with fidelity $\tau(\beta)$ and orthogonal residual
 $\xi$ . Both are properties of the operator family, identified empirically.
(A2) A merge leaves the recipient unchanged, and the operator bias
 $\mu$ lands in the child alone. That bias does not vary with the
dose, and it is read at $\beta=0$ , where a rewrite still paraphrases
while an append copies. (A3) The donor is drawn with probability $\Pr(d=i)\propto e^{-\eta\,(r_{i}-1)}$ ,
decaying in realised-fitness rank with inverse temperature $\eta>0$ .
(A4) Conditional on $(a_{b},a_{d},\beta)$ , the residual $\xi$ is
independent across children and generations. It need not be independent
of $\beta$ , and the $\beta=0$ rewrite is the baseline law of $\xi$ .

Requested $\beta$ and fidelity $\tau$ are different objects. The
requested dose follows the rule

(5)

 $\beta^{*}(\phi_{b},\phi_{d})=\min\!\left(\beta_{\max},\ \max\!\left(0,\ \frac{\phi_{d}-\phi_{b}}{\kappa}\right)\right).$ 

That rule requests a dose only from a fitter donor and raises it with
the fitness gap, up to the cap $\beta_{\max}$ . The scale $\kappa$ 
is the gap at which the requested dose would reach one. It reads $\beta$ 
as the fraction inherited, which holds for a blend, where $\tau(\beta)=\beta$ .
If $\tau$ is instead flat in $\beta$ , as the appends are, the same
rule is a misspecified policy. If $\tau$ is a small fraction of $\beta$ ,
as free rewrite is, the rule under-delivers at every dose.

## 3.3. Population Dynamics

Children enter unscored, hence immune to elimination in the current
generation. Each generation then removes $k$ agents sequentially
without replacement, with weight equal to rank. The least-fit agent
therefore carries the greatest weight, and it is the most likely to
leave. What that removal moves is the mean reference performance $\bar{\theta}_{t}$ .

Since the recipient is drawn uniformly, $\mathbb{E}[\theta_{b}]=\bar{\theta}_{t}$ .
One generation of $k$ merges and $k$ removals then changes the panel
mean by

(6)

 $\Delta\bar{\theta}_{t}=\frac{k}{N}\Bigl[\,\mathbb{E}[\tau(\beta)(\theta_{d}-\theta_{b})]+\mu-\tfrac{2}{N+1}\mathrm{Cov}_{i}(r_{i},\theta_{i})\Bigr].$ 

The first term is the fidelity term, the second is the bias term,
and the third is the selection term, which is one rank-weighted removal
 $\mathbb{E}[\theta_{\mathrm{elim}}]-\bar{\theta}_{t}$ written out.
Because rank one is the fittest, the covariance is negative whenever
reference performance tracks realised fitness, and the selection term
then lifts the mean even when no child inherits anything. The decomposition
is exact for $k=1$ and holds to leading order in $k/N$ otherwise
(Price, 1970). For a convex blend, the fidelity term
becomes $\mathbb{E}[\beta^{*}(\phi_{b},\phi_{d})\,(\theta_{d}-\theta_{b})]$ 
and $\mu=0$ .

## 3.4. Fidelity and the Operator Envelope

Section 3.3 accounts for one generation
of change. This subsection asks two questions of the operator. First,
what does selection achieve when the child does not respond to dose?
Second, how far can any operator carry the population from its seeds?

Proposition 3.1 (Response to selection is gated by dose).

Let $z$ be any trait that is affine
in the embedding, $\theta$ among them when reference performance
is. The one-generation response of the mean to selection on the donor
increment $z_{d}-z_{b}$ is the fidelity term. If $\tau(\beta)$ does
not vary with the requested dose, the increment is inherited at a
rate the dose cannot set, and raising the dose with the donor’s advantage
does no extra work. The extreme case $\tau(\beta)=0$ is included.
Then the increment is not inherited at all, however large the donor’s
advantage.

Remark 3.2 (Ceiling is the operator envelope).

Every later strategy lies in the closed support
of the finite iterates of $T$ starting from $P_{0}$ . If $\theta$ 
is continuous, $\sup_{i}\theta_{i}(P_{t})$ cannot exceed the supremum
of $\theta$ on that support. In general this supremum need not equal
 $\max_{i}\theta_{i}(P_{0})$ . Under a blend with $\tau(\beta)=\beta$ 
and vanishing residual, the embedding stays in the hull of $P_{0}$ .
When reference performance is affine in the embedding, no agent surpasses
the best member of $P_{0}$ . That is why a noiseless blend cannot
beat the best seed. Leaving the parent line is necessary to clear
the best seed, and it is not sufficient. A residual that is mere noise
can also clear the best seed, hence a large unsigned residual does
not by itself admit a merge.

## 4. Identifying Fidelity on LLM Merge Operators

This section answers RQ1. It measures a single merg
conclusion:
Iterating against a fixed verifier stops once the verifier is satisfied.
Scoring against the current population keeps a target that moves with
the population, and the frozen panel with the best-seed bar reports
whether that movement is progress. The gain is not efficiency, which
we did not measure against a fixed-oracle arm, but a target that does
not saturate and a reading of progress that elimination cannot fake.

Competitive survival guarantees a ranking at every generation (Section
3), and a frozen panel records whether
the population climbed (Eq. 2). A ranking by itself
does not certify progress, and elimination alone can lift the panel
mean without anyone leaving the seeds. Training is therefore read
against the best seed, not against the starting mean. Whether a run
can clear that mark is a property of the operator, not of the tournament.

On RQ1, free rewrite leaves the parent line, but it moves only a third
of the requested dose and is rejected. Tactic append clears the half-dose
bound on both probes and leaves the line without pasting raw donor
replies, and the held-out situations confirm it. Template append makes
no model call and pastes raw donor replies. Its movement is real on
the five situations the merge never saw, but its bound clears the
bar on one probe of the full battery of Section 4
and not on the other, hence it is undetermined, and neither append
rises with the dose. On RQ2, the open-loop verdict predicted the closed
loop for both decided operators that entered it, and the undetermined
operator trained as well. In the closed loop, no free-rewrite run
clears that mark, and every tactic-append run and every template-append
run does. Sampled loop children keep that split, and both appends
clear the admission bound inside the loop while free rewrite is rejected.
Every measurement uses one model on one negotiation task, with sixteen
pairs in the open loop and three runs per operator in the closed loop,
and both appends drive the population toward copies of a few agents.

Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.

body_start:
Abstract

Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities in authoring interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench’s testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.

## 1 Introduction

Coding agents have become increasingly capable of building interactive software. Recent benchmarks have expanded beyond algorithmic problems (Jimenez et al., 2024) to end-to-end interactive applications, evaluating how models handle dynamic user input in web and desktop environments (Lu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Extended reality (XR) introduces a distinct set of challenges for code generation. Unlike 2D software governed by discrete event loops, XR applications operate within continuous 3D physical spaces. Functional correctness depends on the real-time coordination of head and hand kinematics, spatial coordinate transformations, environmental sensing, mixed-reality rendering, and physical ergonomics. Consequently, generating XR software requires reasoning about spatial mathematics, runtime sensor lifecycles, and embodied interaction semantics that are absent in flat-screen software engineering.

Despite these demands, evaluating coding agents in XR remains largely unexplored due to an execution and verification bottleneck. Existing coding benchmarks rely on programmatic unit tests (Jimenez et al., 2024) or browser action runners (Lu et al., 2025), which cannot verify spatial scene graphs or continuous 3D tracking inputs. Conversely, 3D code-generation benchmarks focus primarily on generating static shapes rather than reactive software (Gao et al., 2026), while prior XR benchmarks focus on hardware performance and runtime systems rather than evaluating generative code synthesis (Huzaifa et al., 2021; Bierbaum et al., 2003; Popescu et al., 2025). Evaluating agent-generated XR software requires an automated and comprehensive testing suite capable of simulating physical environments, exercising embodied user actions, and verifying runtime behavior across diverse implementations.

We present GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench comprises 112 expert-curated tasks across two tiers: (1) SDK engineering tasks, consisting of 24 feature implementations and 21 bug repairs in core subsystems such as occlusion shaders, raycast reprojection, and gestural state machines; (2) Application generation tasks, consisting of 67 end-to-end experiences spanning education, healthcare, daily living, design, and entertainment, distilled from a taxonomy of 436 peer-reviewed XR systems papers. To support reproducible, headless execution without the proprietary GUI navigation and multi-gigabyte build toolchains of desktop game engines, all tasks are built on XR Blocks (Li et al., 2025), an open-source WebXR framework. To test candidate implementation at scale, we introduce GenXR-Test, the first set of testing tools that pair deterministic kinematic actors with adaptive VLM-controlled agents in simulated XR environments, evaluating runtime results through both scene-graph assertions and scoped visual checks.

To validate our authored evaluation suite, eight blinded XR experts evaluated 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Across 372 evaluation runs, our automated suite achieved 96.5% mean accuracy against human expert ground truth with a 4.0% flakiness rate, demonstrating that simulator-based evaluation reliably reflects physical device execution. We evaluate 10 model configurations on the full benchmark. The strongest configuration achieves an overall Pass@1 of 50.9%, with performance dropping to 29.2% on SDK feature tasks. Diagnostic analysis reveals recurring failure modes across models: 64.4% of failed runs exhibit coordinate-transformation errors, 44.9% encounter asynchronous sensor initialization races, and 34.5% fail to distinguish bimanual interaction semantics.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

• 

GenXR-Bench: An open-source benchmark of 112 expert-authored tasks evaluating coding agents on XR software engineering, spanning SDK-level feature development, bug repair, and end-to-end application synthesis.

• 

GenXR-Test: XR tooling for automated evaluations using scripted kinematic actors, adaptive VLM agents, runtime state assertions, and scoped visual checks in simulated 3D environments.

• 

Hardware-Grounded Validation: A validation study across 372 physical XR device trials demonstrating that simulator-based evaluation achieves 96.5% agreement with expert human judgment with low flakiness (4.0%).

• 

Empirical Analysis of Coding Agents in XR: An evaluation of 10 model configurations identifying key bottlenecks in frontier models, including coordinate-frame handling, sensor lifecycles, and embodied interaction semantics.

## 2.1 Interactive Software Engineering Benchmarks

Interactive software often requires its own set of runtime evaluations. Recent agent benchmarks treat interactivity as the benchmark itself, using operating systems and interactive worlds to evaluate agents in controlled application environments (Xie et al., 2024; Rawles et al., 2025; Trivedi et al., 2024; Koh et al., 2024), while embodied-agent benchmarks similarly test long action sequences in fixed 3D environments (Kolve et al., 2017; Puig et al., 2018; Savva et al., 2019; Shridhar et al., 2020). Interactive software generation benchmarks often leverage these systems to evaluate generated software: website development benchmarks use agent-controlled browser actions to evaluate functionality (Lu et al., 2025; Koh et al., 2024); ArtifactsBench (Zhang et al., 2025), Interaction2Code (Xiao et al., 2025), and InteractScience (Chen et al., 2026b) combine runtime interaction and rendering with multimodal evaluations using vision-language models as judges (Zheng et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024); game-development benchmarks (Chi et al., 2026; La et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a) combine functional, visual, and behavioral evaluations with interaction testing. GenXR-Bench extends runtime evaluations to XR software by simulating embodied interactions and environmental sensing to become the first benchmark to formalize evaluations of physically grounded interactive applications beyond relying purely on LLM judges. A systematic comparison of GenXR-Bench against these existing benchmarks is shown in Table 1.

## 2.2 Generative 3D and XR Authoring

Natural-language 3D authoring predates coding agents, with early systems such as WordsEye (Coyne and Sproat, 2001) and the framework proposed by Chang et al. (2014) translating text into virtual scenes. Recent approaches use language models to generate procedural content and interactive environments (Sun et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024b; Yang et al., 2024c). As a result, code-based 3D generation benchmarks increasingly extend evaluation beyond simple primitives to perceptually and physically correct models (Gao et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2025b). In XR, Text2VRScene (Yin et al., 2024) and VRCopilot (Zhang et al., 2024) allow users to use language to author new scenes and layouts. LLMR generates XR application features in real time (De La Torre et al., 2024); DreamCodeVR generates object behaviors from speech within VR (Giunchi et al., 2024); and LLMER produces structured specifications that control XR objects (Chen et al., 2025). GenAssist explores iterative agentic rendering loops to refine XR applications guided by human ratings (Srinidhi et al., 2026). XARP (Caetano et al., 2026) and XR Blocks (Li et al., 2025) introduce agent-native XR authoring toolkits for easy XR code generation. Closest to our work, Du et al. (2026) demonstrate that current LLMs can author XR applications that initialize without errors. GenXR-Bench continues this work, building upon the XR Blocks framework validated by Du et al. (2026) to systematically verify whether candidate implementations satisfy task-specific functional and interactive requirements across diverse XR development tasks.

## 2.3 Automated XR Testing

XR presents unique evaluation challenges because runtime behaviors depend continuously on the user’s kinematics, physical environment, and spatial interaction dynamics (Bowman et al., 2001). Automated XR testing spans from replaying device input with state checkpoints (Bierbaum et al., 2003), categorizing WebXR (Li et al., 2020) and Unity (Rzig et al., 2023) bugs, and formalizing XR interface heuristics (Nielsen and Molich, 1990; Gu et al., 2025a; Utting et al., 2012). The OpenXR Conformance Test Suite checks whether XR runtimes implement OpenXR interfaces consistently (Khronos OpenXR Working Group, 2025). VR-ReST derives functional tests from requirements and scene-graph structure (Corrêa Souza et al., 2018). Other work simulates user actions through camera-based exploration and scripted XR controllers (Wang, 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Gu and Rojas, 2025; Zhu et al., 2025). XRintTest constructs an interaction-flow graph in existing Unity scenes (Gu et al., 2026). Commercial solutions such as Meta XR Operator (Meta, 2026) integrate an LLM-driven tester into XR development to run natural-language tasks in Unity. Closest to our work are XR benchmarks that target end-to-end systems (Huzaifa et al., 2021), machine-learning workloads (Kwon et al., 2023), and performance criteria (Popescu et al., 2025). We extend prior works by introducing GenXR-Test, which empowers task authors to define implementation-agnostic functional tests executed deterministically within a reproducible simulator environment.

Figure 2: Authoring workflow of GenXR-Bench. Human icon indicates human-authored and robot icon indicates LLM-authored. Both icons indicate LLM generated with human guidance.

## 3 GenXR-Bench

GenXR-Bench consists of 112 expert-curated XR software engineering tasks. Each task contains a natural-language specification, an editable project scaffold, and a held-out evaluation suite. The specification defines the required implementation and observable behavior. The scaffold provides the relevant code, tools, interfaces, documentation, and assets needed to complete the task. The evaluation suite contains human-authored tests written using GenXR-Test described in Section 3.4.

All tasks use XR Blocks 

0.21.0
 (Li et al., 2025), a web framework for building cross-platform XR applications. Prior work has demonstrated that LLMs can generate complete XR Blocks applications from a single prompt (Du et al., 2026). Using a common web framework reduces variation caused by engine-specific editors, deployment workflows, and device toolchains that often require complex GUI navigation. All agents were given access to XR Blocks DevTools, a suite of tools for debugging, running, and developing XR Blocks applications that simplifies multimodal development.

## 3.1 Benchmark Composition

GenXR-Bench covers three types of XR development tasks motivated by real-world use cases: feature implementation, bug repair, and application generation. Examples are shown in Appendix D.

SDK feature implementation. 
Feature tasks require agents to implement a missing XR Blocks capability while retaining the surrounding SDK, interfaces, documentation, and relevant examples. Tasks cover capabilities such as hand interaction, sensing, spatial design, and rendering that form the primitive features for core XR development. These tasks are designed to evaluate an agent’s ability to implement and understand low-level XR functionality and focus on software engineering.

SDK bug repair.
